It switches on decoder->event.type: any type not listed below returns -pte_bad_query. enabled sets variant.enabled.resumed when decoder->ip equals the event ip and calls pt_insn_process_enabled; async_disabled returns -pte_bad_query when the ip is not suppressed and does not equal variant.async_disabled.at, and then (like disabled) calls pt_insn_process_disabled; async_branch returns -pte_bad_query unless decoder->ip equals variant.async_branch.from and calls pt_insn_process_async_branch; async_paging and async_vmcs check the ip (when not suppressed) and, like paging and vmcs, call their process function; overflow, exec_mode, tsx and stop call their process functions; exstop and mwait return -pte_bad_query on an IP mismatch when the ip is not suppressed and decoder->enabled is set; pwre, pwrx, ptwrite, tick, cbr and mnt do nothing special. A negative status from a process function or an IP-mismatch return leaves decoder->process_event set, since it is cleared only after the event copy. Then it copies min(size, sizeof(event)) bytes to uevent, clears decoder->process_event, and if decoder->process_insn is set calls pt_insn_check_insn_event (negative status returned; a status with pts_event_pending returned) and then pt_insn_proceed_postponed (negative status returned). It finally returns the result of pt_insn_check_ip_event(decoder, NULL, NULL). I did not read the process helpers.

functions.name: apl12_resume_disabled
functions.prose_contract: Static helper for erratum APL12 that replays packets from the query decoder's position to the resume point offset bytes ahead, then resumes with tracing treated as disabled. Returns -pte_internal if decoder is NULL; gets the current offset with pt_qry_get_offset and syncs pkt to it with pt_pkt_sync_set (negative results returned). It then loops reading packets with pt_pkt_next and the offset after each with pt_pkt_get_offset: if reading a packet fails with -pte_eos it returns 0 without advancing decoder->pos and without creating an event (timing state may already have been updated by earlier replayed packets); other read/offset errors are returned; when the offset after a packet reaches begin+offset it stops (returning -pte_internal if it jumped past it). For each packet before that point, mode, pip and vmcs packets give -pte_internal, tsc, cbr, tma, mtc and cyc packets are applied to decoder->time and decoder->tcal with pt_qry_apply_* (a negative result is returned), and all others are skipped. After the loop it does decoder->pos += offset and returns pt_qry_event_ovf_disabled(decoder), which prepares a standalone overflow event with ip_suppressed set, clears decoder->enabled, stores it in decoder->event and returns -pte_internal if no event could be allocated or otherwise the result of pt_qry_event_time (not read, so its sign is not claimed).

functions.name: pt_time_update_mtc
functions.prose_contract: Updates the timing state from an MTC packet. Returns -pte_internal if time, packet or config is NULL (nothing changed). If time->have_tsc is set and time->have_tma is clear it returns 0 with no state changed. Otherwise it computes ctc = (uint32_t)packet->ctc << config->mtc_freq; sets time->ctc_cyc to ctc if time->fc or time->lost_cyc was nonzero or time->have_mtc was clear at entry; sets time->have_mtc to 1, time->fc to 0, time->ctc to ctc and time->lost_cyc to 0. Then: if have_mtc was clear at entry and have_tma is clear it returns 0 (tsc and base unchanged); if have_mtc was clear at entry and have_tma is set and the entry value of time->ctc has bits outside pt_pl_tma_ctc_mask it returns -pte_internal (tsc and base unchanged); on the first MTC with a TMA seen it extends the previous ctc with estimated high bits from this MTC. It then calls pt_time_ctc_delta; on failure it increments time->lost_mtc and returns that error. It calls pt_time_ctc_fc; on failure it returns that error without touching lost_mtc. On success it sets time->base and time->tsc to the entry base plus the computed TSC delta and returns 0. Because have_mtc, fc, ctc and lost_cyc are written before the later checks, those fields are already changed on the error returns after that point.

functions.name: stress
functions.prose_contract: Static test helper taking a fixture cfix and a worker function. When FEATURE_THREADS is defined it runs ptu_test(ptunit_thrd_create, &cfix->thrd, worker, cfix) in a loop num_threads times, so every thread handle is stored through the same &cfix->thrd (the fixture keeps a handle; what happens to earlier handles is not checked here) and the return values of the spawned workers are not examined here. Then, in all builds, it calls worker(cfix) in the calling thread and checks ptu_int_eq(errcode, 0). It ends with return ptu_passed(). The ptu_test and ptu_int_eq macros are defined in ptunit headers that are not in this source tree; they are the places where a thread-creation failure or a nonzero worker result is reported, and, as is usual for such macros, a failed assertion is expected to return a failed result from stress instead of reaching the final return, but I could not read their definition to confirm that.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Program entry of editmap (a sendmail map editor); the slice cut the head, K&R definition at editmap.c:74. It zeroes the SMDB params (cache size 1 MB), derives progname, sets RunAsUid/RealUid and gid from getuid/getgid, fills RealUserName from getpwuid (or "Unknown UID n"), and parses options "C:fquxN" (-C config file, -f no case folding, -q query, -u update, -x remove, -N include the terminating NUL in key and value, anything else calls usage). It adds SFF_* flags depending on the DontBlameSendmail bits, then requires exactly one of -q/-u/-x and the matching operand count (query and remove need exactly 3 operands after the options, update needs more than 3) or calls usage. It takes type, map name and key (and value for update), lower-cases the key unless -f. With HASFCHOWN it opens the sendmail.cf file (exit EX_NOINPUT if it cannot be opened) and scans for an O TrustedUser line to set TrustedUid. It opens the map with smdb_open_database (read-only for query; read/write and create otherwise); on failure it prints a message (with a recompile hint for an unsupported type) and exits EX_CANTCREAT. It syncs the database, and if geteuid() == 0 and TrustedUid != 0 it tries to change the owner (failure only prints a warning). Query: smdb_get; any error (not only not-found) prints a message and sets exit status EX_UNAVAILABLE, otherwise it prints the value. Update: smdb_put; failure prints a message and sets EX_IOERR. Remove: smdb_del; SMDBE_NOT_FOUND prints a message but leaves the status EX_OK, SMDBE_OK is silent, any other error prints a message and sets EX_IOERR. It then closes the database (close failure prints a message and sets EX_IOERR), frees it and calls exit(exitstat). It does not return normally.

functions.name: mi_milteropen
functions.prose_contract: K&R function mi_milteropen(conn, backlog, rmsocket, name) that creates, binds and listens on the milter socket described by conn ("protocol:filename" or "protocol:port@host" or a bare address); slice cut the head, function starts at listener.c:122. It returns the listening socket or INVALID_SOCKET. It returns INVALID_SOCKET if conn is NULL or empty; if the protocol part is unknown or no default protocol is available; for AF_UNIX if the path is too long or safefile reports it as unsafe; for inet/inet6 if the port is neither numeric nor a known service name or the host cannot be parsed or resolved; if socket() fails; if setting close-on-exec or SO_REUSEADDR fails (the socket is closed); if rmsocket is set and the path exists but stat fails with an error other than ENOENT, is not a socket, or cannot be unlinked (socket closed); if bind or listen fails (socket closed); and if malloc of the global sockpath for the UNIX path fails (socket closed). On success for a UNIX socket it stores a copy of the path in the global sockpath. The function modifies the caller's conn string in place by temporarily writing NUL at the ':' and at the '@'. The ':' is restored only on the success path of the protocol parse, so returning for an unknown protocol leaves a NUL there; the '@' is restored only after the port has been parsed, so returning for an invalid port or unknown service name leaves a NUL there. Sets the global L_socksize and may set other listener globals.

functions.name: mi_listener
functions.prose_contract: K&R function mi_listener(conn, dbg, smfi, timeout, backlog): the milter accept loop. It calls mi_opensocket and, when _FFR_WORKERS_POOL is compiled in, mi_pool_controller_init; either failure returns MI_FAILURE immediately (these early returns do not reach the smutex_destroy of L_Mutex at the end). Then, while mi_stop() returns MILTER_CONT, it locks L_Mutex and selects on listenfd with a MI_CHK_TIME timeout: an invalid listenfd, a select exception on the socket, MAX_FAILS_S select failures (EINTR just retries) , MAX_FAILS_A accept failures, MAX_FAILS_M malloc failures or MAX_FAILS_T thread-creation failures set ret to MI_FAILURE and leave the loop; a timeout loops again. After accept it closes and rejects the connection if the client address looks incomplete or the descriptor is not usable with select, and for transient accept errors (EINTR, EAGAIN, ECONNABORTED, EMFILE, ENFILE, ENOBUFS, ENOMEM, ENOSR, EWOULDBLOCK) it just continues without counting. Accepted connections get close-on-exec and SO_KEEPALIVE (failures only logged) and a freshly malloced context (if malloc fails the socket is closed), whose callback mask is filled from smfi, and it starts a session (mi_start_session or thread_create; a failure closes the socket and frees ctx). After the loop, if ret is not MI_SUCCESS it calls mi_stop_milters(MILTER_ABRT), otherwise it logs a stop/abort message if mi_stop was not MILTER_CONT and calls mi_closener. It then destroys L_Mutex and returns ret. I did not read mi_opensocket, mi_stop or the session-start helpers.

functions.name: smfi_setreply
functions.prose_contract: K&R function smfi_setreply(ctx, rcode, xcode, message) that stores a custom SMTP reply in ctx->ctx_reply. It returns MI_FAILURE, leaving ctx->ctx_reply unchanged, if rcode or ctx is NULL; if rcode is not exactly 3 characters long; if rcode does not start with '4' or '5' followed by two ASCII digits; if xcode is non-NULL but myisenhsc(xcode, NUL) rejects it (it must start with 2, 4 or 5, a dot, 1 to 3 digits, a dot, 1 to 3 digits and then the end of the string, so its length is between 5 and 9 characters); if message is non-NULL and contains CR or LF or is longer than MAXREPLYLEN; or if malloc fails. Otherwise it builds the string "rcode ", then xcode if given, then (a space only when xcode was given, then) message if given, frees any previous ctx->ctx_reply, stores the new buffer there and returns MI_SUCCESS. The caller keeps ownership of the argument strings; ctx owns the new buffer.

functions.name: smfi_setmlreply
functions.prose_contract: smfi_setmlreply(ctx, rcode, xcode, ...) stores a multi-line SMTP reply in ctx->ctx_reply from a NULL-terminated list of text arguments. It returns MI_FAILURE, leaving ctx->ctx_reply unchanged, if rcode or ctx is NULL; if rcode is not exactly 3 characters or does not start with '4' or '5' followed by two digits; if xcode is non-NULL and myisenhsc(xcode, NUL) rejects it (otherwise "4.0.0" or "5.0.0" is used depending on the first digit of rcode); if any text argument is longer than MAXREPLYLEN or contains CR or LF, or if more than MAXREPLIES text arguments are given (the scan stops at the first such argument and the call fails); or if malloc fails. Otherwise it allocates a buffer sized for the code, xcode and each line, writes "rcode-xcode" or "rcode xcode" (the separator is a space only when exactly one text argument was counted, otherwise a hyphen), then " first text" and for each further text argument CRLF, the code and separator (space for the last line) and the text, frees any previous ctx->ctx_reply, stores the buffer there and returns MI_SUCCESS. With zero text arguments the stored string is rcode, a hyphen and xcode with no text.

functions.name: sm_heap_report
functions.prose_contract: Writes a report of the heap-checking tables to a stream; slice cut the head and the definition is at heap.c:758. It is compiled only in the branch of the #if at line 114 that applies when SM_HEAP_CHECK is nonzero (the #else at line 212 up to the #endif at 837, whose comment says !SM_HEAP_CHECK for the enclosing test), and at run time it returns immediately without writing anything if HEAP_CHECK (sm_debug_active(&SmHeapCheck, 1)) is false or verbosity <= 0. Otherwise it walks every entry of SmHeapTable: with verbosity > 2 it prints one line per entry (group, pointer, size, optional tag and number), with verbosity exactly 2 only entries whose group is not 0, and with verbosity 1 none; it totals sizes by group 0, group 1 and other groups. It then reads the current time, formats it into a static buffer with localtime (the result of localtime is not checked for NULL), prints a summary line with pid, time, SmHeapMaxTotal, the grand total and group totals, and prints a "BUG" line if the grand total differs from SmHeapTotal. Returns nothing and does not change the heap tables; it does change the function-static time string.

functions.name: sm_io_setvbuf
functions.prose_contract: sm_io_setvbuf(fp, timeout, buf, mode, size) sets the buffering of an SM_FILE_T. It first requires fp to have SmFileMagic (SM_REQUIRE_ISA). If mode is not SM_IO_NBF, a mode other than SM_IO_FBF, SM_IO_LBF or SM_IO_NOW, or size > INT_MAX, returns SM_IO_EOF with fp not yet touched. Otherwise it converts the timeout, flushes the old buffer with sm_flush (result ignored), frees any unread-pushback buffer, clears f_r and f_lbfsize, frees the old buffer only if it was malloced (flag SMMBF; a buffer supplied by an earlier caller is not freed), and clears the buffering and EOF flags. With SM_IO_NBF it switches to unbuffered mode (one-byte f_nbuf buffer) and returns 0. Otherwise it asks sm_whatbuf for the optimal size; size 0 means use that size with a library-allocated buffer; if buf is NULL it sm_mallocs size bytes: if that fails it remembers SM_IO_EOF as the result and, if size differs from the optimal size, retries with the optimal size; if still no buffer it switches to unbuffered mode and returns SM_IO_EOF; if the retry succeeds the stream is left buffered with the optimal size and the function returns SM_IO_EOF. A buffer it allocated is marked SMMBF. It then sets SMNPT if the size differs from the optimal size, sets the line/now/full flag for mode, installs the buffer, sets f_w or f_lbfsize for write streams (f_w = 0 for read streams), registers sm_cleanup with atexit and returns 0 (or SM_IO_EOF after a successful retry).

functions.name: sm_io_fopen
functions.prose_contract: sm_io_fopen(pathname, flags, ...) opens a file with open(2) and wraps it in an SM_FILE_T of type SmFtStdio. Slice cut the head; the packet name sm_sysfopen does not exist in libsm, the code shown is the tail of sm_io_fopen (head at stdio.c:470). If flags contains O_CREAT it reads the mode argument with va_arg, else mode is 0. It maps the access mode in flags (O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_RDWR) to SMRD, SMWR or SMRW; any other value calls sm_abort. It obtains a stream with sm_fp(SmFtStdio, ioflags, NULL) (its result is used without a NULL check) and sets fp->f_file to open(pathname, flags, mode). If open returns -1 it clears the stream flags and magic so the slot is unused and returns NULL; otherwise it returns the new stream. It does not itself set f_cookie or do any buffering setup beyond what sm_fp does.

functions.name: sm_strseek
functions.prose_contract: sm_strseek(fp, offset, whence) repositions a string-backed stream. It computes a target ret from whence: SM_IO_SEEK_SET gives offset, SM_IO_SEEK_CUR gives the current strio_offset plus offset, SM_IO_SEEK_END gives strio_size (the offset argument is not added in the code). Any other whence sets errno to EINVAL and returns -1. If ret is negative or exceeds (size_t)-1 it returns -1 without setting errno. If ret is greater than the current strio_size it calls sm_strgrow(s, ret): on success it recomputes (goto reseek) with the same arguments, on failure it returns -1 (errno set by sm_strgrow). Otherwise it stores ret in strio_offset and returns it.

functions.name: notify_rd
functions.prose_contract: Test receiver for the sm_notify mechanism, notify_rd(nproc, nmsgs). It calls sm_notify_start(true, 0); if that is negative it prints a perror message and returns -1. Then it loops nmsgs * nproc times; in each iteration it calls sm_notify_rcv with a 5 second timeout, recording SM_TEST(r >= 0) each time, and repeats while the result is 0; if the result is negative it prints a diagnostic and returns that negative value at once. A received message is NUL-terminated at buf[r] when r < sizeof(buf) and at the last byte of buf, then checked with SM_TEST for: prefix "qf0001", length greater than the prefix, a decimal pid after the prefix that validpid() maps to an index below nproc, a '_' followed by a message number n with 0 <= n < nmsgs, and msgs[pidx][n] being NUL before it is set to 'f'. The SM_TEST checks only record failures; they do not change the return value. After the loop it returns 0. Global state used or changed: the msgs table, Verbose, stderr output, and whatever sm_notify_start sets up.

functions.name: sm_vfscanf
functions.prose_contract: sm_vfscanf(fp, timeout, fmt0, ap) is the scanf-style scanner on an SM_FILE_T; slice cut the head, the function starts at vfscanf.c:109. A timeout of SM_TIME_DEFAULT becomes fp->f_timeout; if the timeout is SM_TIME_IMMEDIATE it sets errno to EAGAIN and returns SM_IO_EOF without reading. For other finite timeouts it arms an alarm event via sm_seteventm and a setjmp(ScanTimeOut): if the alarm fires it sets errno to EAGAIN and returns SM_IO_EOF (this path does not clear the event itself). It then walks the format: when the format string ends it clears the event and returns nassigned (which can be 0). Whitespace in the format skips input whitespace; literal characters must match the next input character or the scan stops with match failure; a '%' followed by NUL clears the event and returns SM_IO_EOF; conversions that need input first try to refill the buffer and go to input failure at end of input. Conversions store through pointers taken from ap and each stored one increments nassigned (%n stores the count of characters read and does not count). A match failure (for example no digits for a number, an empty %[ set, or a literal mismatch) clears the event and returns nassigned. Input failure (end of file or error before a conversion could start) clears the event and returns nassigned if it is non-zero, otherwise -1. I read the control flow and returns, not every conversion body in the 600-odd lines.

functions.name: smdb_cdb_open
functions.prose_contract: smdb_cdb_open(database, db_name, mode, mode_mask, sff, type, user_info, db_params) opens a cdb map (only compiled with CDB defined); slice shows only the tail of the function at smcdb.c:428-566. It sets *database to NULL, then builds the file name with the extension (error returned), calls smdb_setup_file (error returned) and smdb_lock_file (error returned); if the file did not exist and O_CREAT is in mode it will truncate instead of create (mode |= O_TRUNC, clears O_CREAT and O_EXCL). It allocates the SMDB_DATABASE and cdb map objects; if either allocation fails it unlocks the lock file, frees what was allocated and returns SMDBE_MALLOC. It opens the file with open(file name, mode, DBMMODE): failure gives SMDBE_BAD_OPEN via the error exit. It sets cdbmap_create for a non-read-only mode and calls cdb_init (O_RDONLY) or cdb_make_start (other modes); a nonzero result gives SMDBE_BAD_OPEN via the error exit; otherwise result is set to SMDBE_OK (the else branch at 521-527 can never run because result is 0 there) and smdb_filechanged is called. If that returns SMDBE_OK it installs the smcdb_* method pointers in the database object, stores sm_cdbmap in smdb_impl, sets *database and returns SMDBE_OK. Any other result falls to the error exit, which unlocks the lock file through sm_cdbmap->smcdb_lock_fd, frees sm_cdbmap, frees the database object with smdb_free_database and returns the result; the opened db_fd is not closed there (the close is only a comment).

functions.name: smdb_lockfile
functions.prose_contract: smdb_lockfile(fd, type) tries to lock a file descriptor and returns a bool. On systems without flock (!HASFLOCK) it builds an fcntl lock request from type (LOCK_UN gives F_UNLCK, LOCK_EX gives F_WRLCK, otherwise F_RDLCK) and uses F_SETLK for LOCK_NB, F_SETLKW otherwise; with flock it calls flock(fd, type). Either way it retries while the call fails with EINTR. It returns true if the call succeeds (this includes a successful LOCK_UN unlock, so true does not necessarily mean a lock was acquired); in the fcntl variant it also returns true when the call fails with EINVAL. Otherwise it returns false with errno set to the saved error: in the fcntl variant any failure other than EINVAL, and in the flock variant any failure, ends at a return false (the explicit conditions about LOCK_NB with EACCES/EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK only decide whether the unused debug code path is taken; both paths set errno = save_errno and return false). EINTR is not returned as the final error. It opens, closes and allocates nothing.

functions.name: smdb_ndbm_open
functions.prose_contract: smdb_ndbm_open(database, db_name, mode, mode_mask, sff, type, user_info, db_params) opens an ndbm map; the packet name smndbm_open does not exist, the function is at smndbm.c:488-630. It sets *database to NULL and returns SMDBE_UNKNOWN_DB_TYPE if type is NULL; calls smdb_setup_file for the .dir and then the .pag extension (an error is returned); remembers lockcreated if either file does not exist and O_CREAT is in mode; locks the .dir file with smdb_lock_file (error returned). If the files are being created it also locks and closes the .pag file with O_EXCL semantics (on failure it closes the .dir lock descriptor and returns the error) and changes mode to O_TRUNC without O_CREAT/O_EXCL. It allocates the database and dbm wrapper objects (an allocation failure only sets result to SMDBE_MALLOC; it does not return at once). If result is still SMDBE_OK it stores the lock descriptor and calls dbm_open(db_name, mode, DBMMODE): failure gives the errno value or SMDBE_BAD_OPEN. It then fails with SMDBE_GDBM_IS_BAD if the dir and pag descriptors are the same, and runs smdb_filechanged on both files. If everything succeeded it fills in the smdbm_* method table, stores the wrapper in smdb_impl, sets *database and returns SMDBE_OK. Otherwise it closes dbm if opened, unlocks via db->smndbm_lock_fd, frees db and the database object and returns result; this error path dereferences db without a NULL check, so it is a NULL dereference if smdbm_malloc_database failed.

functions.name: rebuildaliases
functions.prose_contract: rebuildaliases(map) rebuilds the alias database for map and returns true only if the rebuild ran. It returns false at once if the map class is not MCF_REBUILDABLE. It adds safe-file flags from the DontBlameSendmail settings and opens the alias file with safefopen for read/write; if that fails and errno is EACCES or EROFS it tries a read-only open (and, in that case, will skip locking); if both opens fail, or the first fails with another errno, it logs (message unless the map is optional) and returns false. Unless locking is skipped it takes an exclusive non-blocking lock on the file; if that fails it prints a message, waits for the other rebuild by locking with LOCK_EX unless OpMode is MD_INITALIAS, closes the file and returns false. It then calls the class map_open with O_RDWR: if it succeeds it logs (when LogLevel > 7), marks the map MF_OPEN|MF_WRITABLE, records map_pid, calls readaliases (which returns nothing, so no result is checked) and sets success to true; if it fails it prints a diagnostic and success stays false. It closes the alias file, and if the map is flagged MF_OPEN it calls map_close and clears MF_OPEN|MF_WRITABLE|MF_CLOSING. It returns success. The early return false paths (not rebuildable, open failure) happen before the file is opened or the map is touched; the lock-failure path closes the file but does not change the map flags. The success can therefore be true even when the file was opened read-only without a lock.

functions.name: load_if_names
functions.prose_contract: Void, takes no arguments; the packet name was a placeholder and the function is load_if_names at conf.c:4832 (slice 4893-5147 is only its middle). It enumerates the machine's network interfaces and adds their IP addresses to class $=w and calls add_hostnames for each usable one. In the IPv6/SIOCGLIFCONF build (4834-5077) it creates a datagram socket (returns silently if that fails), obtains the interface count (SIOCGLIFNUM/SIOCGIFNUM where compiled; if the count is not positive it closes the socket and returns), reads the SIOCGLIFCONF list (failure: close and return), and for each entry it closes and recreates the socket for the address family (returns if that fails), skips entries whose family is not AF_INET or AF_INET6, and, only where SIOCGLIFFLAGS is compiled, skips entries when the flags ioctl fails or IFF_UP is not set. For an IPv6 address it prints a warning and skips the interface if the address is unspecified; for an IPv4 address it warns and skips if it is INADDR_ANY or INADDR_NONE; otherwise the text form "[addr]" is built, and if it is not yet in class w it is added with setclass. Then, only where SIOCGLIFFLAGS is compiled, if DontProbeInterfaces is DPI_SKIPLOOPBACK and IFF_LOOPBACK is set it skips the interface before add_hostnames (the loopback address text has already been added to class w by then); otherwise add_hostnames(sa) is called. At the end it frees the buffer and closes the socket. In the non-IPv6 SIOCGIFCONF build (5078-5300) the structure is the same with SIOCGIFFLAGS/IFF_UP and IFF_LOOPBACK checks; I read that half only by its returns and conditions.

functions.name: hostnamebyanyaddr
functions.prose_contract: hostnamebyanyaddr(sap) returns a printable host name for a socket address, a pointer that the caller must not free as if it were its own allocation (it can point to static storage or, see below, to whatever denlstring returned). The packet name hostnamebyaddr does not exist; the function is at daemon.c:4651-4751. With NAMED_BIND it temporarily shortens the resolver retry count so retry*retrans does not exceed 20 (at least 1) and restores it after the lookup. It calls sm_gethostbyaddr according to sa_family (AF_INET, AF_INET6, AF_ISO where compiled, AF_UNIX gives no host entry, other families use sa_data). If a host entry was found, its name does not start with '[' and it is not a literal IPv6 address (inet_pton) and not a literal IPv4 address (inet_addr), the name is passed through denlstring(name, true, true) and returned; in IPv6 builds, if denlstring returned the same pointer as h_name the name is first copied into a function-static MAXNAME buffer and the host entry is freed, so the returned name is that static buffer or whatever denlstring returned otherwise. In builds without NETINET6 the entry is not freed there and the returned pointer is the denlstring result (possibly pointing into the resolver's own storage). Otherwise it frees the host entry (FREEHOSTENT), returns "localhost" for an AF_UNIX address whose path starts with NUL, and else formats "[address]" with anynet_ntoa into a function-static 203-byte buffer and returns it. I did not read denlstring.

functions.name: starttls
functions.prose_contract: starttls(m, mci, e, implicit, [DANE args]) performs the client side of STARTTLS and returns an exit status; the packet name starttlsclt does not exist, the function is at deliver.c:7481-7742. It returns EX_TEMPFAIL if the client TLS context is NULL and initclttls(true) fails, if TLS_set_engine fails, or if SSL_new fails. It then calls get_tls_se_features: a non-EX_OK result is the return value after the fail label frees the SSL object. Unless implicit it sends STARTTLS and reads the reply: a 4xy reply gives EX_TEMPFAIL, a reply of -1 gives -1, a 5xy reply gives EX_UNAVAILABLE, any other reply that is not 220 gives EX_PROTOCOL (all via the fail label). It stores the TLS info with SSL_set_ex_data (failure is a fail exit) and, with DANE compiled in, may enable DANE and set the SNI host name (failures there are logged or only affect the DANE flags, not the result), sets SNI for STS if configured, sets the read and write descriptors (failure is a fail exit), and runs SSL_connect, retrying through tls_retry while that says to retry; if the connect finally fails it logs and takes the fail exit. After a successful connect it stores the SSL object in mci->mci_ssl, calls tls_get_info (its result is not examined) and sfdctls to switch the streams to TLS; if sfdctls returns 0 it returns EX_OK. At the fail label it frees clt_ssl with SM_SSL_FREE and returns EX_SOFTWARE if the status variable is still EX_OK, else that status; because mci->mci_ssl was assigned before sfdctls, a sfdctls failure leaves mci->mci_ssl pointing at the freed SSL object.

functions.name: sendenvelope
functions.prose_contract: sendenvelope(e, mode) (void) delivers or verifies the recipients of an envelope. It returns without doing anything else except setting EF_CLRQUEUE when e has EF_FATALERRS and OpMode is MD_SMTP or MD_DAEMON. It returns silently, with no other change, if the envelope is not EF_RESPONSE and the return-to-sender timeout for its class is NOW, or a deliver-by return time has already passed. Otherwise it zeroes e_nsent, sets EF_GLOBALERRS, defines the {envid} and {bodytype} macros and, if e is not already split (EF_SPLIT), saves e_sibling, clears it, calls split_by_recipient(e) (if that returns false and EF_FATALERRS is set it sets EF_CLRQUEUE in SMTP and daemon modes and returns, leaving e_sibling as split_by_recipient left it), queues up each new sibling, then closes the transcript, unlocks the queue and drops the data file of each sibling and restores e_sibling to the saved list (this restore is skipped on the early return). It then loops over e->e_sendqueue: in SM_VERIFY mode it only sets e_to and prints a "deliverable" message for addresses for which QS_IS_SENDABLE holds (not for every address); otherwise, for addresses with QS_IS_OK state, it checkpoints the queue every CheckpointInterval sent addresses (queueup, resetting e_nsent) and calls deliver(e, q) (result ignored). If any address was delivered it sets e_dtime to now and increments e_ntries.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: main(argc, argv, envp) is sendmail's entry point (main.c:163-3024, about 2900 lines). Partly read: I read the part shown in the slice and the main control skeleton to the end (queue-run branch, daemon startup, getrequests and the final send loop) by control flow only; the option parsing, configuration reading and initialisation in the first ~2100 lines were not read. From the part read: in the one-shot queue-run case the process labels itself "Queue control", resets SIGCHLD to the default, and while CurChildren > 0 it waits with sm_wait (stopping early if wait fails with ECHILD, ignoring stopped children, otherwise calling proc_list_drop) and then calls finis(true, true, ExitStat), which does not return. If OpMode is MD_DAEMON or QueueIntvl > 0 it forks into the background unless run_in_foreground or the debug flag 99.100 is set (a fork failure is a syserr; the parent of a successful fork calls finis(false, true, EX_OK)), records daemon information, and if QueueIntvl > 0 starts the queue runner (runqueue, or run_work_group for a specific queue group); in non-daemon mode with persistent queue runners it then monitors the runner children itself and finally calls finis(true, true, ExitStat). Otherwise, for MD_SMTP or MD_DAEMON it goes on to serve requests through getrequests (which returns in a child process unless the 93.100 debug flag is set). Later parts include a verify-mode branch, calls to finis(true, true, EX_USAGE) on collection errors, a send loop calling sendall, a final adjustment of ExitStat to EX_USAGE if Errors > 0 and ExitStat is EX_OK, and the final finis(true, true, ExitStat) with a return of ExitStat that is only reached if finis returns. Most paths therefore end in finis rather than returning.

functions.name: milter_data
functions.prose_contract: milter_data(e, state) runs the end-of-message phase of every input milter and returns the reply text (or NULL) while storing the final disposition in *state. It first sets *state to SMFIR_CONTINUE itself, so no caller precondition on *state is needed. For each filter in InputFilters it stops the loop if *state is already something other than continue or accept; resets *state to continue; skips a filter whose connection is closed or not in the open/in-message state (a filter in error state is handled through MILTER_CHECK_ERROR or ends the loop); sets mf_state to SMFS_INMSG; sends headers (unless SMFIP_NOHDRS), the end-of-headers command (unless SMFIP_NOEOH), and the body (unless SMFIP_NOBODY or there is no data file), checking the results after each (MILTER_CHECK_RESULTS, which I did not read); sends the end-of-body command and reads replies until *state leaves continue, a read error occurs, or the EOM timeout expires (then milter_error and the loop ends). Replies handled: replycode, reject, discard and tempfail set *state and mark the filter done; continue and accept set *state to accept (or tempfail if a body replacement failed) and mark it done; progress does nothing; quarantine stores the reply text (an empty string if none) in e->e_quarmsg and the {quarantine} macro; add/insert/change header, change sender, add recipient (with or without parameters) and delete recipient are applied even if the filter did not declare the capability (only logged); replace body is rejected and marked as a failed replacement if the filter lacks the capability, otherwise the data file is reopened on first use and replaced chunk by chunk; any other reply is logged and milter_error is called. After each reply that is not a replycode the response buffer is freed and set to NULL, so the quarantine empty string does not survive as the return value. After the loop, if a replacement failed, *state becomes tempfail when it was continue or accept, and the reopened data file is closed and EF_HAS_DF cleared. Then it resets or rewinds the data file as needed; if that fails it sets ExitStat to EX_IOERR, forces tempfail when the state was continue or accept, and calls syserr. It finishes with MILTER_CHECK_DONE_MSG and returns response, which, from the reply loop, is non-NULL only when the last processed reply was a replycode (response values set by the MILTER_CHECK_RESULTS macros before the loop were not examined).

functions.name: mime7to8
functions.prose_contract: mime7to8(mci, header, e) rewrites a 7-bit encoded text/plain body (base64 or quoted-printable) as 8-bit while writing it to the mailer connection; the function starts at mime.c:1033 (slice cut the head). It looks up the Content-Transfer-Encoding header value and parses it with prescan. If the header is missing or cannot be parsed it calls syserr, sets EF_DONT_MIME, writes the header "Content-Transfer-Encoding: value" only when a value exists (so a missing header produces no CTE line), writes an empty line to end the headers, clears MCIF_INHEADER, copies the whole data file with putxline using PXLF_MAPFROM, and returns true (false if any write fails). Otherwise it copies the encoding name, sets MCIF_INHEADER, writes "Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit" and an "X-MIME-Autoconverted: from <cte> to 8bit by <host> id <id>" header and the blank line, clears MCIF_INHEADER, then decodes the body from e->e_dfp: base64 (read four characters at a time, skipping whitespace, handling '=' padding) or, for any other encoding, quoted-printable (soft line breaks and =XX escapes), writing each decoded line with putxline. It finishes with an extra empty line (the decoded text may lack a final newline) and returns true; a write failure at any putline or putxline goes to the writeerr label and returns false. I read the control flow and returns, not each decoding step.

functions.name: invalidaddr
functions.prose_contract: invalidaddr(addr, delimptr, isrcpt) checks the address string for bad characters and for excessive length and returns true if it is invalid, false otherwise; the function starts at parseaddr.c:277 (slice cut the head). If delimptr is non-NULL it saves *delimptr and, if that is not NUL, writes NUL there so the scan ends at delimptr; the saved character is written back at the end (including after the too-long exit) when delimptr is non-NULL and the saved character was not NUL. It scans addr in place. In builds without USE_EAI, when EightBitAddrOK is false each byte in the 0x80-0x9f range calls setstat(EX_USAGE), sets the result to true and permanently overwrites that byte with BAD_CHAR_REPLACEMENT in the caller's string; this happens before the length test for the same byte. It counts length with XLEN and as soon as the count exceeds MAXNAME - 1 it temporarily NULs the current byte, prints "553 5.1.0 Address ... too long" with usrerr, restores the byte, sets the result to true and jumps to the exit (skipping the 501 message). If the scan finished and the result is true it prints one 501 error naming the address, code 5.1.3 when isrcpt is set and 5.1.7 otherwise. In USE_EAI builds there is no 8-bit replacement in the loop. It returns the result.

functions.name: occ_close
functions.prose_contract: occ_close(e, mci, host, addr) decrements the open-connection count for a connection that was counted. It returns false at once if the global occ is NULL or e is NULL, or if mci is NULL, is in MCIS_CLOSED state, is flagged MCIF_CACHED, or does not have MCIF_OCC_INCR set. Otherwise it clears MCIF_OCC_INCR in mci_flags, takes the current time, runs conn_limits(e, now, addr, SM_CLFL_EXC, occ, -1, -1) between SEM_LOCK and SEM_UNLOCK (the result of conn_limits is ignored; the semaphore macros are compiled in only with _FFR_USE_SEM_LOCKING and SM_CONF_SEM, and I did not read whether they skip locking when no semaphore is available) and returns true. The host argument is not used.

functions.name: split_by_recipient
functions.prose_contract: split_by_recipient(e) splits an envelope into siblings by queue group and by recipient count. It returns true immediately if OpMode == SM_VERIFY (as written in the code), the envelope's queue group is not valid, or EF_SPLIT is already set. Otherwise it calls split_across_queue_groups(e): SM_SPLIT_FAIL returns false. It remembers firstsibling = e->e_sibling, optionally allocates a log buffer for the new envelope ids (only if n > 1 and LogLevel is high), and for each of the n - 1 siblings calls split_within_queue(ee): on SM_SPLIT_FAIL it sets e->e_sibling back to firstsibling, frees the log buffer and returns false (changes made by earlier splits, including split_across_queue_groups and previously split siblings, are not undone); otherwise it sets EF_SPLIT on that sibling and appends its id to the log text. It then logs the split (if enabled), calls split_within_queue(e) for the envelope itself, sets EF_SPLIT on e if that did not fail, and returns whether it did not fail. When it returns false in the last step e_sibling is not restored.

functions.name: dsntoexitstat
functions.prose_contract: dsntoexitstat(dsncode) maps the leading part of an enhanced status code string to an exit status; it reads the string beyond its first character, so it needs a NUL-terminated string. If the first character is '2' it returns EX_OK, if '4' EX_TEMPFAIL, and if it is not '5' EX_CONFIG. For '5' it skips an optional '.', reads the next number code2, skips to the next '.', reads code3, and switches on code2: 0 gives EX_UNAVAILABLE; 1 (address) gives by code3 0 EX_DATAERR, 1 or 6 EX_NOUSER, 2 or 8 EX_NOHOST, 3 or 7 EX_USAGE, 4 EX_UNAVAILABLE, 5 EX_CONFIG; 2 (mailbox) gives 0, 1, 2, 4 EX_UNAVAILABLE and 3 EX_DATAERR; 3 gives EX_OSERR; 4 (network/routing) gives 0 and 2 EX_IOERR, 1, 3, 5 EX_TEMPFAIL, 4 EX_PROTOCOL, 6 EX_CONFIG, 7 EX_UNAVAILABLE; 5 gives EX_PROTOCOL; 6 gives EX_UNAVAILABLE; 7 gives EX_DATAERR. A first character of '5' with any code2 or code3 not listed for it falls to the final return EX_UNAVAILABLE.

functions.name: udbexpand
functions.prose_contract: udbexpand(a, sendq, aliaslevel, e) tries to expand address a through the user database. Partly read: the control flow and returns were read, but the UDB_DBFETCH, UDB_HESIOD and UDB_FORWARD bodies only partly in detail (the DB version ifdefs were skimmed). It returns EX_OK without changes if a is not QS_IS_SENDABLE, if UdbSpec is empty, if the user name starts with a backslash or a colon, or if the key would not fit in the key buffer; it sets e->e_to to the address text when sendable. It returns EX_TEMPFAIL if the one-time _udbx_init(e) returns EX_TEMPFAIL, or a database or Hesiod lookup fails with a temporary error. It then loops over the UdbEnts. For a UDB_DBFETCH entry it looks up the key "user:maildrop"; if found it clears QSELFREF, and if EF_VRFYONLY is set it sets q_state QS_VERIFIED and returns EX_OK, otherwise it expands the stored value with sendtolist, logs, and sets q_state QS_EXPANDED when addresses were produced and the address is not marked as a self reference; it also looks up "user:mailname" to set q_owner and marks the address QDELIVERED|QEXPANDED when it finds one. When the lookup finds nothing (UDB_DBFETCH), it breaks out of that entry at once, before the QSELFREF clear and without changing q_state, and the loop moves to the next entry. The UDB_HESIOD case does the same through Hesiod; UDB_FORWARD handles forward entries and can set QS_VERIFIED (returning EX_OK in verify-only mode) or QS_EXPANDED; UDB_REMOTE does nothing here. After the loop it returns EX_OK, so a no-match, remote or self-reference outcome returns EX_OK without setting QS_VERIFIED or QS_EXPANDED.

functions.name: smtpinit
functions.prose_contract: smtpinit(m, mci, e, onlyhelo) (void) starts an SMTP/LMTP session on an open connection. It sets SmtpNeedIntro, clears e_rcode/e_renhsc/e_text and resets map-changed flags, then switches on mci->mci_state: MAIL, RCPT or DATA first call smtprset and fall through to OPEN; OPEN returns at once if onlyhelo is false (no greeting or HELO is exchanged), and continues if onlyhelo is true; ERROR, QUITING and SSD call smtpquit and fall through; CLOSED calls syserr("451 4.4.0 smtpinit: state CLOSED") and returns without calling smtpquit; OPENING continues. With onlyhelo it jumps straight to the HELO/EHLO step; otherwise it sets MCIS_OPENING and reads the greeting: a read failure (r < 0) goes to tempfail1, a 4xy reply to tempfail2 and any non-2xy reply to unavailable. It then sends LHLO, EHLO or HELO according to the mailer and retry rules, and reads the reply: failure goes to tempfail1, a 5xy reply to unavailable (or retries with HELO when falling back), another non-2xy reply to tempfail2. It checks the host name in the greeting and, if the mailer is not exempt and the name equals MyHostName, reports a 553 config loop error, records EX_CONFIG and calls smtpquit. If configured it sends VERB (failure goes to tempfail1). If the state is not CLOSED it sets MCIS_OPEN and returns. tempfail1 and tempfail2 record EX_TEMPFAIL (4.4.2 and 4.5.0) and call smtpquit unless the state is CLOSED; unavailable records EX_UNAVAILABLE (5.5.0) and calls smtpquit. The function returns nothing; results are recorded in mci status. I did not read the HELO name expansion and the extension parsing between 160-250 in detail.

functions.name: attemptauth
functions.prose_contract: attemptauth(m, mci, e, sai) tries one SASL mechanism and returns an exit status; it is compiled only with SASL. It sets (*sai)[SASL_MECH] to NULL at the start (before a mechanism is chosen), disposes of any existing mci_conn, creates a new client connection with sasl_client_new (failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL), sets security properties with SASL_SEC_NOPLAINTEXT and the external SSF/auth id and the IP properties (each sasl_setprop failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL), and calls sasl_client_start against the server's mechanism list; a result other than SASL_OK or SASL_CONTINUE returns EX_TEMPFAIL (logging when no mechanism qualifies). It stores the chosen mechanism in (*sai)[SASL_MECH], sends "AUTH mech" with or without an initial response (a base64 encoding failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL), and then loops: reply 235 records {auth_type} and returns EX_OK; reply -1 returns EX_IOERR; a 5xy reply returns EX_NOPERM; any other reply that is not 3xy returns EX_TEMPFAIL; for a 3xy reply it calls sasl_client_step: if that fails (not OK or CONTINUE) it sends "*" to abort, reads the reply and returns EX_NOPERM (not EX_TEMPFAIL); if base64 encoding of the step output fails it sends "*" and returns EX_TEMPFAIL; otherwise it sends the encoded response and reads the next reply. The loop has no other exit.

functions.name: smtpauth
functions.prose_contract: smtpauth(m, mci, e) runs SMTP AUTH using attemptauth and returns an exit status; compiled only with SASL. It clears mci->mci_sai, calls getauth: EX_TEMPFAIL is returned at once; if getauth returned EX_OK but gave no SASL_AUTHID it returns EX_OK without authenticating and without setting mci_sasl_auth; if getauth did not return EX_OK it returns EX_UNAVAILABLE when SASLInfo is NULL, otherwise it calls readauth and returns its result if that is not EX_OK. It returns EX_UNAVAILABLE if the password is empty, or if both the authid and the user are empty. It fills the callback contexts, sets a default realm and mechanism list, intersects the mechanism list with the server's capabilities, and calls init_sasl_client (failure returns EX_TEMPFAIL if getauth supplied the data, else EX_UNAVAILABLE). Then it loops calling attemptauth: EX_OK sets mci_sasl_auth to true and ends the loop; EX_TEMPFAIL or EX_NOPERM removes the failed mechanism from mci_saslcap and, if none are left, returns that result when getauth supplied the data or EX_UNAVAILABLE otherwise, else tries the next mechanism; any other result is returned at once (without removing a mechanism). It returns the final result, EX_OK on success.

functions.name: smtpmailfrom
functions.prose_contract: smtpmailfrom(m, mci, e) sends MAIL FROM and returns an exit status; the function starts at usersmtp.c:2055 (slice cut the head). If mci_state is MCIS_CLOSED it sets errno from mci_errno and returns EX_TEMPFAIL without recording a status. It returns EX_DATAERR (after usrerrenh and mci_setstat EX_NOTSTICKY) when the message needs SMTPUTF8 and it is disabled or not offered by the server, or when 8-bit data is present and the server does not support 8BITMIME; it builds the option string (SIZE, BODY, DSN, AUTH and others) and the sender address, sets mci_state to MCIS_MAIL, sends MAIL From:<addr> options, and reads the reply: r < 0 records EX_TEMPFAIL (4.4.2) and returns EX_TEMPFAIL; SMTPCLOSING returns EX_TEMPFAIL; a 4xy reply records EX_NOTSTICKY and returns EX_TEMPFAIL; a 2xy reply returns EX_OK; 501 and 553 record EX_NOTSTICKY and return EX_DATAERR; 552 records EX_NOTSTICKY and returns EX_UNAVAILABLE (and may clear the size option flag); any other 5xy reply records EX_NOTSTICKY and returns EX_UNAVAILABLE; any other reply logs, records EX_PROTOCOL (5.5.1), calls smtpquit and returns EX_PROTOCOL. Partly read: the option-string construction in 2085-2290 was not read line by line.

functions.name: smtprcpt
functions.prose_contract: smtprcpt(to, m, mci, e, ctladdr, xstart) sends RCPT TO for one recipient and returns an exit status; the function starts at usersmtp.c:2384. With PIPELINING it first reads any replies already waiting: while mci_nextaddr is non-NULL and the input is readable it calls smtprcptstat for that address, and on a non-EX_OK result calls markfailure and giveresponse for it, then advances mci_nextaddr (e_to is restored afterward). If mci_state is MCIS_CLOSED it sets errno from mci_errno and returns EX_TEMPFAIL directly, before any smtprcptstat call for this recipient. It builds the NOTIFY/ORCPT option string for DSN-capable servers, sends "RCPT To:<addr>options", sets mci_state to MCIS_RCPT, and, when pipelining is enabled (MCIF_PIPELINED set), returns EX_OK without reading the reply; otherwise it returns smtprcptstat(to, m, mci, e), whose result can be EX_TEMPFAIL (state closed or a 4xy/failed read), EX_OK (2xy), EX_NOUSER, EX_UNAVAILABLE (other 5xy) or EX_PROTOCOL (after recording the protocol error). Partly read: the option building (2441-2500) was read only for the NOTIFY part.

functions.name: smtpdata
functions.prose_contract: smtpdata(m, mci, e, ctladdr, xstart) sends the DATA command and message body and returns an exit status; the function starts at usersmtp.c:2652. If mci_state is MCIS_CLOSED it returns EX_TEMPFAIL (it does not require the connection to be open). With PIPELINING it first drains the pending RCPT replies, calling smtprcptstat for each, markfailure and giveresponse on failures and setting QS_RETRY on EX_TEMPFAIL ones; if the connection closed meanwhile it returns EX_TEMPFAIL. It sends DATA, sets MCIS_DATA and reads the reply: r < 0 or a 4xy reply returns EX_TEMPFAIL (calling smtpquit in the failed-read case); a 5xy reply returns EX_TEMPFAIL if no recipients were accepted (mci_okrcpts <= 0) and mci_retryrcpt is set, else EX_UNAVAILABLE; any other reply that is not 3xy records EX_PROTOCOL and returns EX_TEMPFAIL under the same no-recipients-and-retryrcpt condition, else EX_PROTOCOL. If mci_okrcpts > 0 it writes the message body with a write timeout; a write failure ends at the writeerr label (errno saved, MCIS_ERROR, EX_TEMPFAIL or EX_NOTSTICKY recorded, data file rewound, syserr 451 message, smtpquit, return EX_TEMPFAIL). A reply arriving before the final dot gives EX_PROTOCOL with MCIS_ERROR and smtpquit, and an error on the final flush gives EX_IOERR with MCIS_ERROR and smtpquit. After the final dot it returns EX_OK without a reply when no recipients were sent; otherwise it reads the final reply: failure gives EX_TEMPFAIL, 4xy EX_TEMPFAIL, 2xy EX_OK, a protocol error EX_PROTOCOL, 5xy EX_UNAVAILABLE and anything else EX_PROTOCOL (the final-dot paths do not apply the retryrcpt rule), recording the mci status and the status message. Partly read: the body-writing section 2767-2850 was only skimmed by its returns.

functions.name: xconnect
functions.prose_contract: xconnect(inchannel) handles sendmail's X-CONNECT (and optionally HAProxy PROXY) preamble and returns an int; the function is at util.c:3042-3257 (packet name xconnect_handler does not exist). It consults the x_connect ruleset with rscap on the peer name and address: EX_UNAVAILABLE or any other non-EX_OK status returns 0 (the latter also logged), and a result starting with CANONNET returns 0. With _FFR_HAPROXY a ruleset result "haproxy1" selects PROXY mode. With _FFR_XCNCT > 1 a ruleset result starting "220" makes it print a 220- greeting line and flush OutChannel. It then reads one line from InChannel with the to_nextcommand timeout. In PROXY mode it returns -1 if the line is NULL or does not start with "PROXY ", returns -2 for "UNKNOWN" (logged and ignored), and accepts "TCP4 " or "TCP6 " (otherwise returns -1); in the normal mode it returns -1 unless the line starts with "X-CONNECT ", then skips spaces. It reads an address token of alphanumerics, '.' and ':', and accepts an IPv4 address (inet_addr) or an IPv6 address (inet_pton, if compiled); any other token returns -1, and on success the address is copied into RealHostAddr. In PROXY mode it skips the destination-address token and takes the port from the next token (the source port) into RealHostAddr, frees RealHostName and returns D_XCNCT. Otherwise, if the address token is not followed by a space it returns D_XCNCT; else it reads a host name token (letters, digits, '.', '-'), returns D_XCNCT if it is empty, replaces RealHostName with a copy of the name, and if no space follows returns D_XCNCT; if the rest of the line starts with 'M' it returns D_XCNCT_M, otherwise D_XCNCT.

functions.name: nbns_rq
functions.prose_contract: nbns_rq(rqp) sends a NetBIOS name service request and parses the reply header; the function is at nbns_rq.c:329-381. It sets rqp->nr_if to the global interface list head and calls nbns_rq_opensocket (an error is returned at once); then it loops with retrycount 3: nbns_rq_send (an error is returned at once), nbns_rq_recv; if recv fails with an error other than ETIMEDOUT or no retries remain, then for a broadcast request (NBNS_NMFLAG_BCAST) with a next interface it closes nr_fd, advances to the next interface and restarts from opening a socket, otherwise returns that error (which can be ETIMEDOUT, an errno, or -1 from select inside recv); on an ETIMEDOUT with retries left it decrements the count and sends again, so there are up to four send/receive attempts per interface. After a received reply it returns NBERROR(NBERR_INVALIDRESPONSE) if the reply is shorter than 12 bytes or its transaction id differs from nr_trnid. It then parses the flags into nr_rpnmflags and nr_rprcode (returning NBERROR(nr_rprcode) if the response code is non-zero), skips the question count and reads the answer, authority and additional counts into nr_rpancount, nr_rpnscount and nr_rparcount, and returns 0. The mb_get_* return values are not checked. nr_fd is not closed on the success or error returns (only before moving to the next interface).

functions.name: smb_open_rcfile
functions.prose_contract: smb_open_rcfile() reads the smb configuration files and returns an errno-style int. It takes $HOME, and if set builds "$HOME/.nsmbrc" in a malloc'ed buffer (malloc result unchecked), calls rc_open on it in read mode into the global smb_rc and frees the buffer; its result is only stored in a local variable and is overwritten. It then calls rc_merge(SMB_CFG_FILE, &smb_rc), again without checking the result, and if smb_rc is still NULL it prints "Warning: no cfg file(s) found." with printf and returns ENOENT; otherwise it returns 0. It never returns the rc_open or rc_merge error codes.

functions.name: ScanOneEntry
functions.prose_contract: Static helper of Jim's scan command: ScanOneEntry(interp, str, pos, str_bytelen, fmtObj, idx, valObjPtr) scans one format entry against str. It first sets *valObjPtr to 0. If the entry has a prefix it matches it against str from pos (whitespace in the prefix skips any whitespace in the input): it returns -1 if the input is used up, and 0 if the prefix did not match completely. Unless the type is 'c', '[' or 'n' it skips whitespace; then for 'n' it stores the current position as an integer object; otherwise if the input is exhausted it returns -1; for 'c' it stores the next UTF-8 character code as an integer object and returns the number of bytes consumed since the entry start. For other types it optionally limits the token to the field width (a temporary string object), and converts: d, o, x, u, i parse an integer (base 10, 8, 16, 10 and auto), e, f, g parse a double; on success the value object is stored and the consumed count includes the characters converted, on failure to convert the result is 0 if there is remaining text and -1 if the token is empty. s and [ use JimScanAString with the entry's character-set argument, set *valObjPtr to the string it returns (an empty string object, not NULL, if no characters match) and add its length. A temporary width-limited object is freed before returning. It returns the number of bytes consumed from anchor (including leading whitespace), 0 for a mismatch, or -1 at end of input.

functions.name: Jim_EvalObj
functions.prose_contract: Jim_EvalObj(interp, scriptObjPtr) evaluates a script object and returns a Jim return code. If the object is a list with no string representation it returns JimEvalObjList(interp, scriptObjPtr) at once (not read here). Otherwise it increments the script object's reference count, gets the parsed script with JimGetScript and, if the parse reports a missing closing delimiter (JimParseCheckMissing returns JIM_ERR), sets the error stack, drops the reference and returns JIM_ERR; so an unparseable script returns JIM_ERR. It then sets an empty interpreter result; with JIM_OPTIMIZATION it returns JIM_OK immediately for an empty script (result stays empty) and has a fast path for a three-token "incr var" script on an unshared integer variable, which increments the variable in place, sets it as the result and returns JIM_OK. Otherwise it marks the script in use, pushes an eval frame, clears errorFlag and evaluates each command line: it builds argv from the line's words (string/escape tokens as they are, variables via Jim_GetVariable, expression sugar and nested [commands] evaluated recursively, dict sugar, interpolated words, and {*} expansion of lists), stops the loop as soon as retcode is not JIM_OK or a word could not be produced (then retcode becomes JIM_ERR if it was OK), and for each complete line calls JimInvokeCommand and then JIM_SIGNAL if Jim_CheckSignal reports a signal. The result code of the last command is propagated, so JIM_RETURN, JIM_BREAK, JIM_CONTINUE, JIM_EXIT, JIM_ERR and JIM_SIGNAL are returned as they occur; the loop ends after the first non-OK code. It releases the argument references and any heap-allocated argv per line, sets the error stack when the code is JIM_ERR, pops the eval frame, converts the object back to a script type holding the parsed script, drops its reference and returns the code.

functions.name: JimCallProcedure
functions.prose_contract: JimCallProcedure(interp, cmd, argc, argv) calls a Tcl-style procedure and returns a Jim return code. It returns JIM_ERR (after JimSetProcWrongArgs sets the error message) if the argument count is below the required arity, or above required plus optional arity when the procedure has no args parameter, before any frame exists; returns JIM_OK at once if the body is empty (no frame created, procLevel not changed); returns JIM_ERR with "Too many nested calls. Infinite recursion?" if the current frame level equals maxCallFrameDepth (again before any frame exists). Otherwise it creates a call frame (argv, argc, argument and body objects, static variables), increments interp->procLevel, increments the references of the argument list and body, makes the new frame current, and binds the parameters in order: an args parameter receives the remaining arguments as a list, required and supplied optional parameters are set from argv with JimSetProcArg, and unsupplied optional parameters get their default values with Jim_SetVariable; a failure while binding jumps to the cleanup label with that code. If there is no trace callback or the trace callback (JimTraceCallback "proc") returns JIM_OK it evaluates the body with Jim_EvalObj. At the cleanup label (reached after binding, after a failed trace, and after the body) it runs deferred calls with JimInvokeDefer, restores the parent frame and frees the call frame with JimFreeCallFrame (reuse flag); then, if the code is JIM_RETURN, it decrements interp->returnLevel and, when that reaches 0 or below, replaces the code with interp->returnCode and resets returnCode to JIM_OK and returnLevel to 0. It decrements interp->procLevel and returns the code. So the frame and procLevel are only created and decremented on the paths that get past the arity, empty-body and depth checks, and procLevel is incremented before argument binding.

functions.name: Jim_ForCoreCommand
functions.prose_contract: Implements the Tcl "for start test next body" command. It returns JIM_ERR with a wrong-args message unless argc is exactly 5. It evaluates the start script with Jim_EvalObj and returns that code unchanged if it is not JIM_OK. It evaluates the test expression (Jim_GetBoolFromExpr); with JIM_OPTIMIZATION and when the test is "var < n" or "var <= n" (n an integer literal or a variable) and the next script is "incr var" on the same variable, it runs a specialised loop that increments the integer variable in place; if any of those shape checks fail, or the variable is not an integer, it falls back to the general loop. The general loop runs while the test is true and the code is JIM_OK or JIM_CONTINUE: it evaluates the body, then the next script, then the test again. After each body evaluation JimCheckLoopRetcode is applied: for JIM_BREAK or JIM_CONTINUE it decrements interp->break_level and, if it is still above 0, the loop ends at once and that code (JIM_BREAK or JIM_CONTINUE) is returned unchanged to the caller. Otherwise on exit, if no such propagation happened and the code is JIM_OK, JIM_CONTINUE or JIM_BREAK, it sets an empty result and returns JIM_OK; any other code (for example JIM_ERR, JIM_RETURN, or an error from the start script, next script or test) is returned unchanged. The reference counts it took on the loop and limit variable names are released before return.

functions.name: Jim_LoopCoreCommand
functions.prose_contract: Implements "loop var ?first? limit ?incr? body". It returns JIM_ERR with a wrong-args message if argc is below 4 or above 6. It evaluates the numeric arguments with Jim_GetWideExpr (a failure of the first or second is returned; the increment's result is ignored, so an invalid increment leaves 1), with the 4-argument form using the first number as the limit and 0 as the start. It sets the variable to the start value and loops while (i < limit and incr > 0) or (i > limit and incr < 0) and the code is JIM_OK: it evaluates the body; JimCheckLoopRetcode on the result returns JIM_BREAK or JIM_CONTINUE immediately when break_level stays above 0 after decrementing; for JIM_OK or JIM_CONTINUE it advances i by incr and stores it into the variable (JIM_ERR returned if the variable cannot be set in the in-place path). On exit, a final code of JIM_OK, JIM_CONTINUE or JIM_BREAK becomes an empty result and JIM_OK; any other code (such as JIM_ERR or JIM_RETURN) is returned unchanged.

functions.name: JimForeachMapHelper
functions.prose_contract: Shared helper for foreach (doMap = 0) and lmap (doMap = 1). It returns JIM_ERR with a wrong-args message unless argc >= 4 and argc is even. It initialises a list iterator for each of the varList and list arguments (heap-allocating the iterator array when there are more than two); if any varList is empty it sets the result "foreach varlist is empty" and returns JIM_ERR. For lmap it creates a result list, otherwise it uses the empty object. Each pass first checks whether all value lists are finished and stops if so; it then assigns the next values to the variables of each pair (missing values become the empty string, a failure of Jim_SetVariable ends the function with that code) and evaluates the script. JimCheckLoopRetcode on the result can end the function with that code when break_level stays above 0. JIM_OK appends the script's result to the lmap list; JIM_CONTINUE continues; JIM_BREAK leaves the loop as success; any other code (JIM_ERR, JIM_RETURN and so on) ends the function and is returned as it is. On normal completion or a break it sets the interpreter result to the result list (empty for foreach) and returns JIM_OK; on the error paths the result list is not set as the result. The iterator array is freed when it was allocated.

functions.name: Jim_ForeachCoreCommand
functions.prose_contract: Calls JimForeachMapHelper(interp, argc, argv, 0) and returns its result; it implements foreach and adds nothing of its own. Result codes and the interpreter result are those of the helper: JIM_ERR for wrong arguments or an empty variable list, the loop body's code when that is not OK, continue or break, and JIM_OK with an empty result otherwise.

functions.name: Jim_LmapCoreCommand
functions.prose_contract: Calls JimForeachMapHelper(interp, argc, argv, 1) and returns its result; it implements lmap. On success (end of lists or a break) the helper sets the interpreter result to the list of results of the iterations whose body returned JIM_OK (iterations ended by continue contribute nothing) and returns JIM_OK; JIM_ERR for wrong arguments or an empty variable list; any other non-OK, non-continue, non-break code from the body is returned unchanged.

functions.name: Jim_UplevelCoreCommand
functions.prose_contract: Implements "uplevel ?level? command ?arg ...?". With argc < 2 it returns JIM_ERR with a wrong-args message. Otherwise, if the first argument starts with a digit or '#' it takes the call frame for that level (Jim_GetCallFrameByLevel) and drops the argument, else it uses the default (one level up); a NULL frame returns JIM_ERR. If after dropping the level fewer than two arguments remain, it returns JIM_ERR with the wrong-args message. It makes the target frame current, evaluates the single script (argc == 2) or the concatenation of the remaining arguments with Jim_EvalObj, restores the original frame pointer and returns the evaluation's code unchanged.

functions.name: Jim_DictCoreCommand
functions.prose_contract: Implements the "dict" command; it dispatches on the subcommand in argv[1] (argv[0] is the command name), with the subcommand table and argument-count limits declared with JIM_DEF_SUBCMD (create, get, getdef, getwithdefault, set, unset, exists, keys, size, info, merge, with, append, lappend, incr, remove, values, for, replace, update). A bad subcommand or a wrong argument count returns JIM_ERR through the subcommand parser. Partly read: I read the dispatch skeleton and the return statements, not the individual subcommand implementations. From it: get, getdef/getwithdefault and exists, unset, size and keys/values return JIM_ERR when the underlying dict operation fails and JIM_OK otherwise (keys/values return the result of Jim_DictMatchTypes); merge with argc == 2 (no dictionaries) returns JIM_OK without setting a result (so the interpreter result is whatever it already was); create returns JIM_OK; update with fewer than six arguments or an odd argument count is redirected to the usage handling.

functions.name: JimWaitPid
functions.prose_contract: JimWaitPid(pid, status, nohang) is the Windows (MinGW) variant at jimsh0.c:23735-23748: if pid > 0 it opens a process handle h with OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | SYNCHRONIZE) and, if that succeeds, calls waitpid(h, status, nohang) (a local variable named pid shadows the parameter), then CloseHandle(h) unconditionally; if that waitpid result is greater than 0 it returns h (a handle value that has already been closed by the CloseHandle just before), otherwise it returns JIM_BAD_PHANDLE. It returns JIM_BAD_PHANDLE also when pid <= 0 or OpenProcess fails. *status is only written by waitpid. A separate POSIX definition elsewhere is a macro for waitpid (jimsh0.c:1242).

functions.name: JimCreatePipeline
functions.prose_contract: JimCreatePipeline(interp, argc, argv, pidArrayPtr, inPipePtr, outPipePtr, errFilePtr) (jimsh0.c:5690-6142) starts the processes of an exec pipeline and returns the number of processes, or -1 on error with the interpreter result set. Partly read: I read the redirection setup and the per-process loop by returns, gotos and descriptor handling, not the argument parsing from 5690 to 5780. It parses redirection words (<, <<, <@, >, >>, >@, 2>, 2>@, >&, |&) into input, output and error targets; bad arguments return -1 through badargs. It sets up the input descriptor (a temporary file for here-strings, a file, a channel descriptor, or a pipe when the caller wants one through inPipePtr), the final output descriptor (file, channel, or a pipe through outPipePtr) and the error descriptor (a file, channel, the output descriptor, or a temporary file reported through errFilePtr), each failure going to the error label. For each command stage it creates a pipe when it is not the last stage, starts the process (JimStartWinProcess on MinGW, or vfork/fork, with the child redirecting stdin/stdout/stderr with dup2 and closing the other descriptors), stores the handle in the pid array and closes the parent's copies of the stage's input and output descriptors. A fork or start failure goes to the error label. On success it closes the remaining inputId, lastOutputId and errorId descriptors, restores the environment and returns numPids. The error label closes the caller-visible descriptors (*inPipePtr, *outPipePtr, *errFilePtr), the pipe pair still held in pipeIds, detaches the started pids and frees the pid array, sets numPids to -1 and goes through the common cleanup. It does not close outputId (the current stage's output descriptor) at the error label; in the last stage lastOutputId has been moved into outputId (5979-5980), so a failure to start the last stage leaves that descriptor open.

functions.name: JimParseVar
functions.prose_contract: JimParseVar(pc) parses the text after a '$' for the Jim tokenizer and returns JIM_OK or JIM_ERR. It advances past the '$'. With EXPRSUGAR_BRACKET defined and '[' next it parses a command and sets the token type to JIM_TT_EXPRSUGAR, returning JIM_OK. Otherwise it records tstart and the token type JIM_TT_VAR; for ${name} it scans to the closing '}' (counting newlines), sets tend to the last character before it, and skips the '}' if present. Otherwise it scans a name of alphanumerics, '_', bytes >= 0x80 and '::' runs; if '(' follows it scans to the matching ')' (handling backslashes), sets the token type to JIM_TT_DICTSUGAR, and if no match is found and some ')' was seen it rewinds to just after the last ')'; when EXPRSUGAR_BRACKET is not defined a name starting with '(' becomes JIM_TT_EXPRSUGAR. It sets tend to the last character consumed. Finally, if no characters were consumed (tstart equals the current position) it backs up one character and returns JIM_ERR, otherwise JIM_OK; the braced form ${} consumes the braces, so it returns JIM_OK with an empty name (tend before tstart), not JIM_ERR.

functions.name: idxPopulateStat1
functions.prose_contract: Static function idxPopulateStat1(p, pzErr) in the sqlite3expert code of shell.c (14556-14654); the packet's placeholder name was an unnamed excerpt. Returns an SQLite result code. If p->iSample is 0 it returns SQLITE_OK without doing anything. It finds the largest index (idxLargestIndex): if that fails or nMax <= 0 it returns that code. It then runs "ANALYZE; PRAGMA writable_schema=1" on p->dbm, allocates an IdxRemCtx sized for nMax slots, registers two SQL functions (sqlite_expert_rem on p->db when iSample is 100 or on p->dbv otherwise, and sqlite_expert_sample on p->db), prepares three statements and loops over all indexes of tables: for each (skipping rows with NULL names), when iSample < 100 and the table changed it builds the sample table (a failure ends the loop), then calls idxPopulateOneStat1. After the loop, if rc is OK and iSample < 100 it runs "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp.<unique table>" on p->dbv and stores its result in rc (so a failure of that DROP is returned). It finalizes the three statements (merging their errors into rc), frees the context slots and context, and if rc is OK runs "ANALYZE sqlite_schema" on p->dbm. On the paths that get past the three early returns it removes the two registered functions from p->db and drops the temporary table on p->db at the end, ignoring those results, and returns rc. Any error code from an earlier step is returned instead of continuing, except that the cleanup after the loop runs in every case that got past the allocation.

functions.name: sqlite3_intck_step
functions.prose_contract: sqlite3_intck_step(p) advances an incremental integrity check by one step and returns p->rc. If p->rc is not SQLITE_OK at entry it does nothing and returns that code. Otherwise it frees any previous message and sets zMessage to NULL. If bCorruptSchema is set it sets rc to SQLITE_DONE (without checking any further objects). Else if there is no active check statement it calls intckFindObject: if rc is still OK and there is an object it builds and prepares the check SQL (rc may become an error from preparing) and frees the saved key, and if there is no object left it sets rc to SQLITE_DONE; if intckFindObject returned SQLITE_CORRUPT it converts rc to SQLITE_OK, sets zMessage to "corruption found while reading database schema" and sets bCorruptSchema so that the next step returns SQLITE_DONE. If a check statement exists it steps it: a row is the normal case and changes nothing; otherwise it finalizes the statement, clears it, resets nKeyVal, and if the finalize result is SQLITE_CORRUPT it sets rc back to SQLITE_OK and records "corruption found while scanning database object %s" in zMessage. It returns p->rc, so after this call the result can be SQLITE_OK (more to do or a message to read), SQLITE_DONE (nothing more to check, reached when all objects are finished or the schema was found corrupt) or another error code; corruption is reported through the message with rc OK, and zMessage is freed only at the start of the next step (it stays set after an error return).

functions.name: shell_callback
functions.prose_contract: shell_callback(pArg, nArg, azArg, azCol, aiType) is the sqlite3_exec row callback of the shell and always returns 0 (lines 22887 and 23301); the packet name was outside the slice but the function starts at shell.c:22877. If azArg is NULL it returns 0 at once, writing nothing and leaving p->cnt unchanged (this is the first statement of the function). Otherwise it switches on p->cMode and writes to p->out: MODE_Count and MODE_Off write nothing; MODE_Line prints each column as name = value with a row separator between rows (p->cnt++ > 0); MODE_Explain and MODE_ScanExp print a header on the first row (p->cnt++ == 0) and then the row; MODE_Semi and MODE_Pretty print schema text (pretty-printed with indentation for MODE_Pretty); MODE_List, MODE_Www/MODE_Html, MODE_Tcl, MODE_Csv, MODE_Quote and MODE_Ascii print an optional header on the first row (when p->showHeader, or always for MODE_Www) and then the row in their format, with p->cnt incremented in each; MODE_Insert prints an INSERT statement; MODE_Json prints a JSON object per row; MODE_EQP calls eqp_append with atoi of azArg[0] and azArg[1] and azArg[3]. The azArg == NULL checks inside several cases are therefore never true when execution reaches them, because of the early return. Partly read: I read the structure and the per-mode counter handling, not each mode's formatting code. Modes handled in separate columnar code (column, box, table, markdown) have no case in this switch.

functions.name: do_meta_command
functions.prose_contract: do_meta_command(zLine, p) executes one dot-command and returns an int; the function spans shell.c:28804-32444 and the packet slice (31746-32016) is a fragment of it. Partly read: I read the head, the tail, and the slice's .testcase and .testctrl parts, not the other ~3000 lines of command bodies. At entry, if an expert session is open it finishes it. It tokenizes zLine in place from index 1 into at most 51 arguments (single or double quotes group a token; backslashes are resolved in double-quoted tokens) and terminates the list with NULL; with no tokens it returns 0. It clears the temp file and then runs one if/else chain keyed on the first letters of the command name (names may be abbreviated). Unknown commands print "unknown command or invalid arguments" and set rc to 1. Most command errors set rc = 1 and go to meta_command_exit, which decrements p->outCount (resetting output when it reaches 0), resets p->bSafeMode to p->bSafeModePersist and returns rc; commands that end the process or need an immediate exit use other paths. In the part read: .testcase redirects output to testcase-out.txt; if that file cannot be opened it prints "cannot open 'testcase-out.txt'" and the command still ends with rc 0 (no rc = 1 in that branch); .testctrl parses its option and may set rc = 1 on usage errors (goto meta_command_exit at 31871, 31888, 31979), and for the cases that call sqlite3_test_control it records rc2 and isOk (isOk 1, 2 or 3 selects how the result is printed, with 3 meaning no output, not an error code). The return value is therefore 0 on success, 1 on usage or command errors, and the per-command values I did not read.

functions.name: do_meta_command
functions.prose_contract: Same function as the previous entry (do_meta_command(zLine, p), shell.c:28804-32444); this slice (32017-32274) is a fragment of its .testctrl dispatch and following commands. The function tokenizes the dot-command line in place, returns 0 for an empty line, runs the matching command and exits through meta_command_exit, which decrements outCount (resetting output at 0), restores bSafeMode from bSafeModePersist and returns rc. Unknown commands print an error and give rc 1; usage and execution errors normally set rc = 1; some helper-based commands return the helper's code and some commands exit the process. In the .testctrl part, each handled control calls sqlite3_test_control with the arguments of its case and sets isOk to say how the value is printed (1 for a plain number, 3 for nothing printed, as seen at 32013-32150); an unrecognised or bad usage prints help and sets rc = 1. Partly read: the .import and other command bodies in this fragment were not read, so I do not state what a .import with no columns returns.

functions.name: doAutoDetectRestore
functions.prose_contract: doAutoDetectRestore(p, zSql) implements the shell's state machine that detects a database dump being restored; it returns an SQLite result code (SQLITE_OK unless a statement fails). Nothing happens when p->eRestoreState >= 7. State 0: if safe mode is off and zSql starts with "PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF;" it moves to state 1, otherwise to 7. State 1: if zSql starts with "BEGIN TRANSACTION;" it prepares and steps "SELECT 1 FROM sqlite_schema LIMIT 1" on p->db (rc may be set by the prepare/finalize); the input is treated as a dump only if the database is empty and rc is OK; for a dump it reads the DEFENSIVE and DQS_DDL settings, turns defensive off and DQS_DDL on, and sets eRestoreState to (defensive ? 2 : 0) + (dqs ddl ? 4 : 0), so the value can be 0, 2, 4 or 6; otherwise (not a dump or rc not OK) it sets state 7. Any state from 2 to 6 uses the default branch: once sqlite3_get_autocommit says no transaction is open, it restores defensive mode if bit 2 is set and turns DQS_DDL off if bit 4 is set, and sets state 7; while a transaction is still open it changes nothing. A state value of 0 produced by state 1 (both settings were off) is handled by the state 0 case on the next call, not by the default branch.

functions.name: re_match
functions.prose_contract: re_match(pRe, zIn, nIn) runs the compiled regular expression pRe over the nIn-byte UTF-8 input and returns 1 if some match is accepted, 0 if not, and -1 if allocating the state sets fails (sqlite3_malloc64 returning NULL); the function starts at shell.c:7274. If the regex has a literal prefix (nInit > 0) it skips forward to the first position where that prefix occurs and returns 0 if none exists; the matching then starts at that first occurrence only, so a later occurrence of the prefix is not tried separately by this skip loop (the pattern's own states may still match later). It uses stack space for the state sets when pRe->nState is small, otherwise heap memory freed before returning.
