On TRUE, thread_count is its old value plus one.

functions.name: ccs_cache_collection_handle_message
functions.prose_contract: Dispatches one request message for the CCAPI server's cache collection (ccs_cache_collection.c:1010-1109; the real name is ccs_cache_collection_handle_message). It starts with err = 0 and will_block = 0. It sets err to ccErrBadParam if either pipe is invalid or io_cache_collection, in_request_data, out_will_block or out_reply_data is NULL; if no error so far it creates a reply stream with krb5int_ipc_stream_new. Then, for the message id in_request_name, it calls the matching handler: the old release message does nothing (empty reply), and sync, get_change_time, wait_for_change (which can set will_block), get_default_ccache_name, open_ccache, open_default_ccache, create_ccache, create_default_ccache, create_new_ccache, new_ccache_iterator, lock (which can set will_block) and unlock go to their ccs_cache_collection_* functions with the request data and the reply stream; any other id sets ccErrBadInternalMessage. If err is still 0 it stores will_block in *out_will_block and, when will_block is 0, hands the reply stream to the caller in *out_reply_data (the caller must release it), or, when will_block is non-zero, sets *out_reply_data to NULL. In every case the function releases the reply stream if it still owns it (that is, on all errors and in the will-block case) and returns cci_check_error(err), the error code. On an error return *out_will_block and *out_reply_data are not written.

functions.name: check_once_cc_context_open_default_ccache
functions.prose_contract: Test helper in the CCAPI test suite (test_ccapi_context.c:498-549) that calls cc_context_open_default_ccache once and checks the outcome; the arguments are a context, an optional pointer to a ccache variable, the expected error code and a description. Inside BEGIN_CHECK_ONCE/END_CHECK_ONCE (not read) and only when the cc_context_open_default_ccache API is defined (otherwise it does nothing and returns 0), it calls cc_context_open_default_ccache(context, ccache), or with NULL when ccache is NULL, and checks the returned error against expected_err and the list of five possible codes with check_err. If the call returned 0 it checks that *ccache is not NULL, reads the opened cache's name with cc_ccache_get_name and the default name with cc_context_get_default_ccache_name (the first result is overwritten by the second, so err ends up as the result of cc_context_get_default_ccache_name), records a test failure if both names exist and differ, releases any obtained name strings, and then, if *ccache is non-NULL, releases the ccache and sets *ccache to NULL, whether or not the verification calls failed. The function returns err: the error of the open call when that failed (with *ccache not modified), otherwise the result of cc_context_get_default_ccache_name. Failures of cc_ccache_get_name or name mismatches are recorded as test failures, not returned.

functions.name: k5_kinit
functions.prose_contract: Static function of the MIT kinit client (kinit.c:639-852) that obtains, validates or renews credentials according to opts->action (INIT_PW, INIT_KT, VALIDATE, RENEW) using the context, principal k5->me and output cache k5->out_cc from k5. It returns 1 if it reached the point after the credentials were obtained (and, for VALIDATE and RENEW, stored) and 0 otherwise. It allocates init-cred options (failure goes to cleanup silently), sets lifetime, renew life, forwardable, proxiable, canonicalize, anonymous, address list (from krb5_os_localaddr; failure prints a message and goes to cleanup), armor ccache and PAC options, and resolves the keytab for INIT_KT (a KDB: keytab first sets up the KDB; failures print a message through com_err and go to cleanup), sets any pre-authentication options (failure prints and goes to cleanup), and sets the in-ccache and out-ccache on the options (these two failures go to cleanup without printing anything). It then calls the matching krb5 routine for the action; on failure it prints either "Password incorrect while ..." (for KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_BAD_INTEGRITY, or a preauth failure after a password prompt) or a com_err message and goes to cleanup. For VALIDATE and RENEW it creates a temporary MEMORY cache, initialises it, stores the credentials and moves it into k5->out_cc (each failure prints and goes to cleanup); on success the temporary cache pointer is cleared. It then sets the success flag (notix = 0) and, if k5->switch_to_cache is set, calls krb5_cc_switch; if that fails it prints an error and goes to cleanup, but since the flag is already set the function still returns 1. Cleanup tears down the KDB keytab state (non-Windows), destroys the temporary MEMORY cache if it was not moved, frees the options object, avoids freeing k5->me through the credentials, frees and clears opts->pa_opts, frees the credential contents and closes the keytab; the address list obtained from krb5_os_localaddr is not freed in the code shown.

functions.name: get_best_princ_for_target
functions.prose_contract: ksu helper (heuristic.c:505-740; the real name is get_best_princ_for_target, lower case) that chooses the Kerberos principal ksu should use as the client for switching to target_user. It sets *path_out to 0 and returns 0 immediately if *client is already non-NULL. It reads the default principal of cc_source if that cache is initialised (failure goes to cleanup), and parses target_user and source_user into principals (failures to cleanup). If source_uid is 0 it sets *client to the target principal when target_uid is non-zero, else to the cache's default principal if there is one, else to the target principal, and finishes; if source_uid is non-zero and equals target_uid it sets *client to the default principal if present, else to the target principal, and finishes. Otherwise it calls krb5_seteuid(0) and then krb5_seteuid(target_uid); if either fails it returns errno (the effective uid is then unchanged if the first call failed, or 0 if the second failed; the function never restores it on any path, so on the later paths the effective uid stays target_uid). If neither the .k5login nor the .k5users file can be stat'ed it sets *client to the target principal, sets *path_out to NOT_AUTHORIZED only when cmd is non-NULL, and returns 0. Otherwise it reads the authorized principal list (an error returns that error); an empty list sets *path_out to NOT_AUTHORIZED, leaves *client unchanged and returns 0. It then builds the service principal for hostname and tries three candidate principals in order (the cache's default, the target, the source), looking each up in the list and, when listed, checking for a ticket (find_either_ticket); the first with a ticket is copied into *client and the function finishes. Next it tries each listed principal for an existing ticket and stores the first found in *client. Then it falls back to the first candidate that was merely found in the list and copies it into *client; with PRINC_LOOK_AHEAD compiled in it also tries the closest listed principal to each candidate. If none works it sets *path_out to NOT_AUTHORIZED and returns 0 with *client unchanged. Any intermediate error returns its code, and in all cases the temporary principals are freed; a principal stored in *client is owned by the caller.

functions.name: k5_htonll
functions.prose_contract: Static inline function in k5-platform.h (lines 776-786) that converts a 64-bit host-order value to big-endian (network) order. Its body is chosen at compile time: when K5_BE is defined it returns val unchanged; when K5_LE and SWAP64 are defined it returns SWAP64(val), the byte-swapped value; in any other configuration it returns load_64_be applied to the bytes of its local copy of val, which reads the object's bytes as a big-endian number (equal to val on a big-endian host and byte-reversed on a little-endian host). It has no side effects and takes no locks.

functions.name: k5_ntohll
functions.prose_contract: Static inline function in k5-platform.h (lines 787-791) that converts a 64-bit big-endian (network) order value to host order. It returns k5_htonll(val) (the comment notes the two swaps are identical), so the value is unchanged on a big-endian build (K5_BE) and byte-reversed on a little-endian build with SWAP64, or loaded through load_64_be otherwise. It has no side effects and takes no locks.

functions.name: process_tl_data
functions.prose_contract: Static reader in kadmin's dump.c (lines 565-594) that fills the tagged-data nodes of a principal being loaded from a dump file; fname and lineno are used only in messages, filep is the open stream and tl_data the list of preallocated krb5_tl_data nodes. For each node in list order it reads "type<TAB>length<TAB>" with fscanf; if two values are not read it calls load_err and returns EINVAL; if the type is outside INT16_MIN..INT16_MAX or the length is above UINT16_MAX it calls load_err and returns EINVAL. Otherwise it stores the type and length in the node and calls read_octets_or_minus1 to read the contents into tl_data_contents; if that fails it calls load_err and returns EINVAL. It returns 0 after all nodes were processed (also for an empty list). On a failure the nodes before the failing one are complete, the failing node may already have its type and length set (when the failure is in the contents read) and its contents pointer is whatever read_octets_or_minus1 left, and later nodes are untouched.

functions.name: process_k5beta7_princ
functions.prose_contract: Static loader for one principal record of a kdb5_util "beta 7" dump (dump.c:598-790). It callocs a database entry, returning 1 at once if that fails. It increments *linenop (read_string can add to it), reads five size tokens with fscanf, and returns -1 after cleanup when fscanf returns EOF; any other mismatch or invalid size (name length above UINT_MAX/2, tl_data count above UINT16_MAX, key count above INT16_MAX, extra data size above UINT16_MAX) prints a message through load_err and goes to fail, while memory allocation failures for the name, the tl_data list and the key array go to fail without printing. It reads and parses the principal name (com_err message on parse failure), reads the eight attribute fields into the entry and sets the load mask, reads the tagged data through process_tl_data and, for KRB5_TL_KADM_DATA items, decodes the policy information to set mask bits, reads each key's version, kvno, types, lengths and contents (messages through load_err for unsupported versions, bad kvno or lengths and read errors), reads the extra data, reads the record end, and stores the entry with krb5_db_put_principal (failure: com_err message and fail). On success it prints the principal name when verbose and sets the result 0. Every path after the allocation reaches the cleanup code, which frees the key array copy, the name and the entry with krb5_db_free_principal; the function returns 0 on success, 1 on the failure paths (the fail label sets the result to 1) and -1 at EOF. A read_octets_or_minus1 failure inside, including an allocation failure there, is reported through load_err by this function (it prints "cannot read ..." messages), so not all allocation failures are silent.

functions.name: kdb5_purge_mkeys
functions.prose_contract: The kdb5_util purge_mkeys command (kdb5_mkey.c:1004-1287; the real name is kdb5_purge_mkeys), returning void and reporting failures by incrementing the global exit_status. It first checks that the master key list is initialised (krb5_db_mkey_list_alias non-NULL); otherwise it prints an error, increments exit_status and returns. It parses the options -f (force), -n (dry run, which implies force) and -v (verbose) with getopt; an unknown option calls usage() and returns. It fetches the master key principal entry (failure: message, exit_status++, cleanup). Unless force is set it asks for confirmation and, if fgets returns NULL or the answer is not exactly "yes\n", increments exit_status and returns silently. If the entry has a single key version it returns (with a notice only if verbose, and without incrementing exit_status). Otherwise it allocates an array of the key versions (ENOMEM: message and exit_status++), records each version's kvno and calls krb5_db_iterate with find_mkvnos_in_use to count their use (failure: message, exit_status++). It then prints the versions that are unused (use_count 0); an unused kvno equal to master_kvno gives a KRB5_KDB_STORED_MKEY_NOTCURRENT message and exit_status++ and stops. If all versions are in use it prints "All keys in use, nothing purged." and returns without changing exit_status; in dry-run mode it prints how many would be purged and returns without modifying anything. Otherwise it looks up the active-kvno list and the mkey_aux list (failures: message, exit_status++), allocates a new key_data array for the versions in use (on failure it reports ENOMEM, with master_entry->key_data already set to NULL by the failed malloc assignment and the old array no longer referenced from the entry), moves the in-use keys into it, removes the list entries of the purged versions, frees the old key data and array, and calls krb5_dbe_update_actkvno, krb5_dbe_update_mkey_aux, krb5_timeofday and krb5_dbe_update_mod_princ_data (each failure reports a message, increments exit_status and returns without writing the database), sets the KEY_DATA and TL_DATA mask bits and writes the entry with krb5_db_put_principal (failure: message, exit_status++), printing "N key(s) purged." on success. Cleanup frees the entry, the kvno array and both lists.

functions.name: do_iprop
functions.prose_contract: Incremental propagation loop of kpropd (kpropd.c:634-1003). It takes no arguments and uses the globals kpropd_context, realm, params, db_args, keytab_path, runonce and debug. It gets the primary's kiprop service name, builds and unparses the local kiprop service principal (any failure prints a message and goes to done), then initialises kadm5 with the keytab (label reinit). A kadm5 initialisation failure does not return: KADM5_RPC_ERROR frees any handle, sleeps with an exponential backoff and jumps back to reinit; other failures do the same after a message, except that KADM5_BAD_CLIENT_PARAMS and KADM5_BAD_SERVER_PARAMS call usage() first, which normally exits the process. After a successful initialisation it loops: it reads the local update log header (failure: message, done), calls iprop_get_updates_1; a NULL result destroys the handle and jumps to reinit. By the result code it handles UPDATE_FULL_RESYNC_NEEDED (requesting a full resync with full_resync unless one was requested within iprop_resync_timeout; a failed RPC reinitialises; UPDATE_PERM_DENIED and UPDATE_ERROR go to error and then done), UPDATE_OK (ulog_replay of the updates, only logging a failure), UPDATE_PERM_DENIED and UPDATE_ERROR (go to error), UPDATE_BUSY (backoff counter), UPDATE_NIL and unknown results (reset counters). If runonce is 1 and the result was not UPDATE_FULL_RESYNC_NEEDED it goes to done; otherwise it sleeps for the backoff time or the poll interval and repeats. At done it frees the service strings, principal and default realm, destroys the kadm5 handle, calls krb5_db_fini, ulog_fini and krb5_free_context(kpropd_context) (so the context is unusable afterwards) and returns 0 if runonce equals 1 and 1 otherwise, whether or not an error occurred. With runonce not equal to 1 it therefore returns 1 only after one of the error exits (it does not return on the normal polling path).

functions.name: process_stream_connection_read
functions.prose_contract: Verto read-event callback for a TCP connection of the KDC/kadmind network server (net-server.c:1359-1454). It gets the struct connection from the event's private data. If fewer than 4 bytes of the length prefix have been read it reads the missing prefix bytes; a read error or EOF goes to kill_tcp_connection, which deletes the event (freeing the connection and closing the socket through the event's private data). A short read just advances conn->offset and returns with the event still active. Once 4 bytes are present it takes msglen from them; if msglen is larger than bufsiz - 4 it logs, builds a FIELD_TOOLONG error response (failure: log and kill_tcp_connection), calls prepare_for_dispatch (which allocates a tcp_dispatch_state, detaches the connection and socket from the event, removes and deletes the event; if the allocation fails it frees the response and goes to kill_tcp_connection) and then calls process_stream_response with that response. process_stream_response does not delete the event: it stores the response, and either queues a write event for the connection (then frees the state) or, if the response is missing, there was an error code or the write event could not be made, decrements stream_data_counter, frees the connection, closes the socket and frees the state. If the length prefix is complete and within bounds the function returns and waits for the next event. If the prefix was already complete it reads the rest of the message (msglen - (offset - 4) bytes); read error or EOF kill the connection, a partial read advances the offset and returns with the event active, and a complete message calls prepare_for_dispatch (failure: kill_tcp_connection), sets the request to the buffer after the prefix, calls getsockname for the local address and dispatches the request asynchronously with process_stream_response as callback; if getsockname fails after prepare_for_dispatch has already deleted the event and detached the connection, the code still goes to kill_tcp_connection and calls verto_del(ev) again on that event, and the state and connection are not freed here.

functions.name: shsUpdate
functions.prose_contract: Absorbs count bytes from buffer into the SHA-1 state shsInfo (shs.c:246-333; the slice began mid-function). It first adds count << 3 (the number of bits) to shsInfo->countLo, masks it to 32 bits, increments countHi on carry and adds count >> 29 to countHi, so countLo and countHi hold the total number of bits processed, not bytes. It computes how many bytes were already buffered from the old low count ((countLo >> 3) & 0x3F). If some bytes are buffered it completes the partial 32-bit word and the remaining words of the 16-word block data array from buffer in big-endian order (when buffer has fewer bytes than needed it stores what remains, zero-padding the last word, and sets count to 0), and calls SHSTransform(digest, data) when count was large enough to fill the block. It then processes every remaining full 64-byte (SHS_DATASIZE) chunk of buffer by loading it big-endian into data and calling SHSTransform. Any remaining bytes (fewer than 64) are loaded into the start of data as big-endian words, with the last partial word zero-padded, and stay buffered. buffer is only read; the function returns void. When count is 0 no bytes are read.

functions.name: generic_gss_copy_oid_set
functions.prose_contract: Makes a deep copy of a GSS OID set (oid_ops.c:497-550; the real name is generic_gss_copy_oid_set). If minor_status is non-NULL it sets *minor_status to 0, and this is the only value it stores there (the release on the error path uses a local variable). If new_oidset is non-NULL it sets *new_oidset to GSS_C_NO_OID_SET. It returns GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_READ if oidset is GSS_C_NO_OID_SET and GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_WRITE if new_oidset is NULL, in both cases without allocating anything. Otherwise it callocs a set descriptor, callocs an array of oidset->count element descriptors (a zero count is passed to calloc as is), and for each element mallocs in->length bytes and copies them with memcpy, setting the element length. If any allocation fails it sets the result to GSS_S_FAILURE and releases the partial copy with generic_gss_release_oid_set (*new_oidset then stays GSS_C_NO_OID_SET). On success it stores the copy in *new_oidset and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE; the caller releases it with gss_release_oid_set.

functions.name: kg_accept_krb5
functions.prose_contract: Accepts a Kerberos GSS security context (accept_sec_context.c:667-1246). On entry it initialises the Kerberos context (failure: *minor_status = code, GSS_S_FAILURE), clears *src_name, *mech_type, *delegated_cred_handle and the output token, and uses a default acceptor credential when verifier_cred_handle is GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL. It resolves the credential with kg_cred_resolve, requires its usage to be GSS_C_ACCEPT or GSS_C_BOTH (otherwise GSS_S_NO_CRED), and parses the token header with parse_init_token. A token with a wrong token id gives GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED with minor KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_MSG_TYPE; a malformed header (G_BAD_TOK_HEADER) is not rejected: the whole input is treated as a raw AP-REQ without the GSS framing (no_encap); any other parse error gives GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN. It decodes the AP-REQ (failure: GSS_S_FAILURE), sets up an auth context (replay cache, addresses, permitted enctypes), calls krb5_rd_req_decoded (failure: GSS_S_FAILURE), and then, in the part I did not read line by line (835-1060), checks the authenticator and channel bindings, builds the security context and delegated credential, and decides the flags. With mutual authentication it builds an AP-REP token; for DCE-style contexts it stores the context in *context_handle with established cleared, returns the AP-REP in output_token and returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED; otherwise the context is established, the AP-REP token is built in output_token (empty without mutual authentication) and the function sets the optional outputs (source name copy, mech type, lifetime, flags, delegated credential) and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with *minor_status 0 and *context_handle set to the new context. On the fail path a failure (any result other than COMPLETE, or CONTINUE_NEEDED without the MSG_TYPE code) deletes the partially built context, delegated credential, token and name, stores code in *minor_status, and, when a credential and a decoded request exist and mutual authentication was requested (by the flags or the request) or the result was CONTINUE_NEEDED, it builds a KRB-ERROR token and puts it in output_token, so output_token is not always empty on error. The done label frees the decoded request, unlocks the credential lock, releases a default credential and frees the Kerberos context unless it was handed to the new security context. *context_handle is set only on COMPLETE or the DCE CONTINUE_NEEDED return.

functions.name: kg_cred_resolve
functions.prose_contract: Resolves the name and ccache of a krb5 GSS credential (acquire_cred.c:965-1053). It sets *minor_status = 0 and calls krb5_gss_validate_cred_1 on cred_handle; a non-zero result is returned unchanged (the validate function takes the credential lock on success; its failure behaviour was not read). With the lock held, an accept credential, or any credential that already has a name, is returned as GSS_S_COMPLETE without changing its name or ccache. Otherwise (an initiator credential without a name) it resolves them: if target_name is given it selects a cache for it with krb5_cc_select (KRB5_CC_NOTFOUND is tolerated), sets cred->name from the selected principal and scans the selected ccache; if the name is still unset it opens the default ccache, scans it (KRB5_FCC_NOFILE closes the cache and clears it, other errors fail); if the name is still unset it tries the client keytab (failure becomes KG_EMPTY_CCACHE); if a name now exists but there is no ccache it gets one with get_cache_for_name; then it calls maybe_get_initial_cred and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with the credential lock still held. Any of the failing steps goes to kerr, which unlocks the credential, saves the error info, sets *minor_status to the error code and returns GSS_S_NO_CRED.

functions.name: krb5_gss_init_sec_context_ext
functions.prose_contract: Kerberos mechanism's gss_init_sec_context (init_sec_context.c:871-988, which calls the static helpers kg_new_connection at 461-688 and mutual_auth at 695-868, the two of which make up this slice; the packet name krb5_gss_init_sec_context was an inference). For a new context (*context_handle is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT) it initialises a Kerberos context and syncs the ccache name (failure: GSS_S_FAILURE), otherwise it uses the context saved in the existing GSS context. It clears the output token and *actual_mech_type, maps mech_type (NULL OID, krb5, old krb5, wrong krb5 or iakerb OIDs are accepted, anything else gives GSS_S_BAD_MECH with minor 0 after freeing a context it created). For a first call it uses the default credential if none was passed, resolves it with kg_cred_resolve (errors returned with the context freed) and calls kg_new_connection with the credential lock held. kg_new_connection returns GSS_S_NO_CRED (minor 0) when the credential cannot initiate and GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN (minor 0) when an input token of non-zero length is given on the first call; it allocates a context (ENOMEM gives GSS_S_FAILURE), sets flags from req_flags (GSS_C_DCE_STYLE adds GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG; the delegation policy flag is handled), computes the end time, duplicates the local and target names, gets service credentials with get_credentials, builds the AP-REQ with make_ap_req_v1 (KRB5_FCC_NOFILE, KRB5_CC_NOTFOUND and KG_EMPTY_CCACHE give GSS_S_NO_CRED; KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED gives GSS_S_CREDENTIALS_EXPIRED; other failures GSS_S_FAILURE with *minor_status set to the code), creates the subkeys, and on success stores the context in *context_handle and the AP-REQ in *output_token, sets *ret_flags, *time_rec and *actual_mech_type when requested, and returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED with the context not established when GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG is set (including DCE style) or GSS_S_COMPLETE with it established otherwise; on failure it frees the partial context and leaves *context_handle unchanged. For a later call it runs mutual_auth, which fails with GSS_S_FAILURE (code KG_CONTEXT_ESTABLISHED) if the context is already established or has no mutual flag, GSS_S_BAD_NAME if the target name does not match, and GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN for a missing input token (the last two after deleting the context), returns GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN with minor 0 for a bad token header or a token type other than AP-REP or error without deleting the context, passes on a KRB-ERROR token's code, verifies the AP-REP with krb5_rd_rep (one retry with the user-to-user key), sets the receive sequence and the acceptor subkey when present, builds a DCE-style reply when requested, marks the context established, sets ret_flags, time_rec and actual_mech_type when requested and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. All other failures of mutual_auth delete the context (setting *context_handle to GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT) and return GSS_S_FAILURE with the Kerberos code in *minor_status, including the established/no-mutual-flag failure (the fail label deletes the context although a comment says the arguments are unchanged). The mutex of the credential is released after the first-call helper returns.

functions.name: kg_ctx_internalize
functions.prose_contract: Rebuilds a krb5 GSS security context from its serialised form (ser_sctx.c:484-692; the real name is kg_ctx_internalize). Arguments: the krb5 context, the output pointer argp, and *buffer and *lenremain for the input position and remaining length. It reads a 32-bit tag; if the read fails or the tag is not KG_CONTEXT the result is EINVAL and nothing else happens. Otherwise the result starts as ENOMEM, and it stays ENOMEM both when the remaining length is smaller than the fixed header size (17 int32s, two int64s and the seed) and when allocating the context fails, in which case nothing is allocated and *argp is not set. With enough input it zeroes a new context and unpacks the fixed fields (the results of many int32 and byte unpacks are not checked), then the two sequence numbers (failure frees the context and returns that error), then in order the mechanism OID, the two principals as names, the subkey, enc and seq keys, the sequence state (an EINVAL from these optional parts means the part is absent and is turned into success), the krb5 context, the auth context, proto, cksumtype, the acceptor subkey (EINVAL again tolerated), its checksum type, cred_rcache, and an authdata array (calloc failure gives ENOMEM) and the initiator name's authdata context (a missing initiator name gives EINVAL; an EINVAL from the authdata context is tolerated). It finally reads the trailer tag, which must equal KG_CONTEXT or the result is EINVAL. On success it advances *buffer and *lenremain past the trailer, stores the new context in *argp (the caller owns it) and returns 0. On a failure after the allocation it frees the seq, enc and subkey keys, the names there and here and the context structure, and returns the error with *argp, *buffer and *lenremain unchanged; the acceptor subkey, mech OID, k5 context, auth context and authdata entries are not freed.

functions.name: gss_add_cred_from
functions.prose_contract: GSS mechglue function (g_acquire_cred.c:386-582) that adds a credential for one mechanism to a union credential. It first calls val_add_cred_args; any non-COMPLETE status from it is returned. It selects the mechanism with gssint_select_mech_type (its failure is returned) and looks up the mechanism: GSS_S_BAD_MECH if none, GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE if it has no gss_acquire_cred, and GSS_S_DUPLICATE_ELEMENT if the input credential already has a credential for that mechanism; these returns do not set *minor_status in this function. If there is no input credential it allocates an empty union credential (GSS_S_FAILURE if malloc fails); if there is an input and output_cred_handle is non-NULL it works on a copy made with copy_union_cred (failure returned); with output_cred_handle NULL it modifies the input union credential itself. It converts desired_name to the mechanism's internal name (using the union name's own mech name when it matches, otherwise importing; failure gives GSS_S_BAD_NAME), picks the requested time from cred_usage, gets the public OID of the mechanism, and acquires the mechanism credential with gss_acquire_cred_from when the mechanism has it, or with gss_acquire_cred when cred_store is GSS_C_NO_CRED_STORE, otherwise it fails with GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE; a mechanism error status is mapped with map_error and handled as a failure. It then grows the union credential's mechs_array and cred_array with realloc (GSS_S_FAILURE on failure; the arrays can stay reallocated with the count unchanged), writes *acceptor_time_rec and *initiator_time_rec when requested and the usage covers them, copies the mechanism OID, fills *actual_mechs when requested (an error goes to the failure path), stores the new credential, increments the count and, if output_cred_handle is non-NULL, stores the union credential there. On success it releases a name it imported and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE. The failure path releases the mechanism credential, the imported internal name, and, when output_cred_handle is non-NULL, the working union credential, frees the OID buffer and returns the status; however the malloc failure of the OID buffer (line 536-538) jumps to this path with status still holding the GSS_S_COMPLETE value left by the successful acquire, so that case returns GSS_S_COMPLETE even though nothing was added and the new credential was released.

functions.name: addConfigEntry
functions.prose_contract: Static function in g_initialize.c (lines 1486-1618; the real name is addConfigEntry) that registers one mechanism read from the GSS configuration; the caller is expected to hold the mechanism-list lock. Parameters are the mechanism name oidStr, its dotted OID string oid, the library sharedLib, and the optional kernMod, modOptions and modType. It returns void and silently leaves the list unchanged if oid or oidStr is NULL, if the OID string cannot be converted by generic_gss_str_to_oid, if an entry for that OID already has a loaded mech (searchMechList finds an entry with aMech->mech set; the converted OID is released), or if sharedLib is an empty string (the OID is released); sharedLib itself is dereferenced without a NULL check. The library path is sharedLib if it starts with '/' and otherwise MECH_LIB_PREFIX followed by sharedLib (non-Windows, written with snprintf into a fixed buffer). If an entry for the OID exists but is not loaded it frees and clears its kmodName and optionStr, replaces uLibName with a copy of the path when strdup succeeds, sets kmodName and optionStr to copies of kernMod and modOptions when those are non-NULL (a strdup failure leaves them NULL), releases the converted OID and returns; is_interposer is not changed there. Otherwise it callocs a new entry (on failure the OID is released and nothing changes), stores the converted OID in it, copies the path and the name (if either strdup fails it frees what was allocated, the OID and the entry and returns), copies kernMod and modOptions when non-NULL without checking the strdup results, sets is_interposer when modType is "interposer", appends the entry at the tail of the list and makes it the head if the list was empty.

functions.name: gss_store_cred_into
functions.prose_contract: GSS mechglue function (g_store_cred.c:108-238) that stores the credentials of a union credential with the mechanisms' credential stores, optionally into a given cred_store. It first calls val_store_cred_args and returns any non-COMPLETE status from it (the argument checks live there; they were not read), then sets *cred_usage_stored (when non-NULL) to GSS_C_BOTH and starts with GSS_S_FAILURE. With a desired_mech it selects the mechanism with gssint_select_mech_type (a non-COMPLETE result is returned) and gets its interface, returning GSS_S_BAD_MECH if there is none. If the mechanism has no gss_store_cred_into and cred_store is not GSS_C_NO_CRED_STORE, or has neither gss_store_cred nor gss_store_cred_into, it returns major_status at that point, which holds the value of the successful gssint_select_mech_type call, GSS_S_COMPLETE, so nothing is stored but success is reported. Otherwise it fetches the mechanism's credential (GSS_S_NO_CRED if the union credential has none) and stores it through store_cred_fallback (the mechanism's gss_store_cred_into, or gss_store_cred when cred_store is GSS_C_NO_CRED_STORE, otherwise GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE), mapping the mechanism error with map_error on failure, and returns that status with elements_stored and cred_usage_stored filled in by the mechanism. Without a desired_mech it sets *minor_status to 0 and tries every mechanism element of the union credential, skipping elements that lack a mechanism interface, lack the needed store function or have no credential; for each attempted element a failure is mapped and the loop continues, and a success adds the mechanism's OID to *elements_stored when elements_stored is non-NULL (creating the empty set first; an error from these set operations is returned at once). The final result is the status of the last attempted element (GSS_S_COMPLETE when that one succeeded even if an earlier one failed, GSS_S_FAILURE if none was attempted).

functions.name: mech_init
functions.prose_contract: Static function in negoex_ctx.c (lines 276-348) used by the NegoEx initiator to start the first available mechanism. It first sets output_token to empty. If ctx->negoex_step is 1 and the environment variable NEGOEX_NO_OPTIMISTIC_TOKEN is set (checked with secure_getenv) it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE at once with the empty token and no mechanism started. If the mechanism list is empty it sets *minor to ERR_NEGOEX_NO_AVAILABLE_MECHS and returns GSS_S_FAILURE (this test comes after the environment check). It takes the first mechanism and, if a CHALLENGE exchange message exists whose scheme equals that mechanism's scheme, uses its token as the input token; if that first mechanism is already complete it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with an empty output token. Otherwise it loops over the list: it calls gss_init_sec_context for the first mechanism with the input token, marks it complete when the result is GSS_S_COMPLETE, and if the result is not a GSS error returns get_session_keys(minor, mech) (so the result of that call is what the caller sees). On a GSS error it records the major and minor codes of the first mechanism tried, deletes the failed mechanism with negoex_delete_auth_mech, clears the input token (so the CHALLENGE token is only given to the first mechanism) and tries the next one. When all mechanisms have been deleted the loop ends and it returns the first mechanism's major code with *minor set to its minor code.

functions.name: ulog_replay
functions.prose_contract: Replays the update entries received by an incremental propagation client into the local database and update log (kdb_log.c:400-480; the slice started inside this function). INIT_ULOG(context) sets up the log context first (not read). It opens the database read-write with krb5_db_open and returns that error if it fails; the database stays open afterwards. It then loops i from 0 to the number of updates in incr_ret using a pointer upd that starts at the first entry. For an entry whose kdb_commit is false it executes continue without advancing upd, so the next iteration examines the same entry again; if the first entry is uncommitted the loop therefore skips all later entries too. For a committed entry it deletes the principal (the name copied and parsed; krb5int_delete_principal_no_log; KRB5_KDB_NOENTRY is treated as success) when kdb_deleted is set, otherwise converts the entry with ulog_conv_2dbentry and stores it with krb5int_put_principal_no_log and frees it; any error goes to cleanup. It then takes the exclusive ulog lock; if the log header already has entries (kdb_num != 0) and the update's serial number is not kdb_last_sno + 1 it resets the ulog; it stores the update with store_update, releases the lock, and on error goes to cleanup; otherwise it advances upd. At cleanup, on any error it calls ulog_init_header (which resets the ulog under the lock); whether or not there was an error it frees the whole update array with ulog_free_entries when it is non-NULL, and returns retval, which is 0 when all iterations ended without error.

functions.name: ulog_map
functions.prose_contract: Opens and maps the KDC update log file (kdb_log.c:500-577; the real name is ulog_map and the packet slice held it only partly). It creates a log context with create_log_context; if that returns NULL it returns ENOMEM without cleanup. If stat(logname) fails it opens the file with O_RDWR|O_CREAT and mode 0600 and extends it with extend_file_to to sizeof(kdb_hlog_t) + ulogentries * ULOG_BLOCK; if stat succeeds it opens the existing file O_RDWR. A failed open returns errno (through cleanup). It maps MAXLOGLEN bytes of the file read-write and shared (a failed mmap returns errno), stores the mapping and ulogentries in the log context, and takes the exclusive ulog lock (failure returned). If the header magic is not KDB_ULOG_HDR_MAGIC it returns KRB5_LOG_CORRUPT when the magic is non-zero, or resets the log when it is zero. If the log is non-empty and kdb_num exceeds ulogentries or the first or last serial number fails check_sno it resets the log. If kdb_num differs from ulogentries it extends the file to sizeof(kdb_hlog_t) + ulogentries * ulog->kdb_block (failure returned). At cleanup it releases the lock if it was taken and, when an error occurred, calls ulog_fini; it returns the error code or 0. On success the log context, the mapping and the file descriptor stay in place for later use.

functions.name: kr_remote_equals
functions.prose_contract: Tests whether the remote RADIUS server rr matches the given addrinfo and shared secret (krad remote.c:503-540). It returns FALSE if strcmp(rr->secret, secret) differs, or if ai_addrlen, ai_family, ai_socktype, ai_protocol or ai_flags differ between info and rr->info. It then compares the socket address bytes with memcmp over info->ai_addrlen; if they differ it returns FALSE unless the family is AF_UNIX, in which case it compares the two sun_path strings with strncmp over the size of sun_path and returns FALSE if they differ (this allows for uninitialised bytes after the path in AF_UNIX addresses). Otherwise it returns TRUE. It has no side effects.

functions.name: begin_get_tgt
functions.prose_contract: Static function in get_creds.c (lines 987-1031; the slice cut the head) that starts obtaining the TGT needed for a TGS exchange. It sets ctx->state to STATE_GET_TGT. It treats the service as local when ctx->start_realm equals ctx->server->realm. If it is not local it looks for a cached TGT for the server's realm with get_cached_tgt; an error is returned immediately (ctx->cur_tgt is then unchanged and may still hold an earlier non-local TGT); if one is found it replaces ctx->cur_tgt with it (freeing the old one) and returns end_get_tgt(context, ctx). Otherwise it frees ctx->cur_tgt, sets it to NULL and fetches the cached local TGT with get_cached_local_tgt into ctx->cur_tgt (error returned, with cur_tgt NULL or whatever that callee left). If the service is local it returns end_get_tgt. Otherwise it builds the realm path with init_realm_path (error returned, with ctx->cur_tgt holding the local TGT), frees and clears ctx->realms_seen, and returns get_tgt_request(context, ctx), which generates the first request towards the realm and does not call end_get_tgt here. The return value is 0 or the first error code of those calls (or the result of end_get_tgt or get_tgt_request).

functions.name: process_pa_data
functions.prose_contract: Static function in preauth2.c (lines 648-729) that runs the client preauth modules over the padata received from the KDC. It makes two passes over in_pa_list (the first, real = 0, for informational padata; the second, real = 1, for real mechanisms). For each entry it skips it when it is a real pass and the type is not allowed (pa_type_allowed), when no module handles the type, when the module's real/informational class differs from the pass, and in the real pass when the type has failed before. It then calls clpreauth_process, which may produce an output list mod_pa. If mod_pa is non-NULL it appends it with grow_pa_list to *out_pa_list (updating *out_pa_list_size) and frees the array; if the append fails it frees mod_pa with krb5_free_pa_data and returns the error from grow_pa_list. Note that this append assignment overwrites ret, so the module's own return code is replaced by 0 whenever it produced output padata and the append succeeded, which masks a module error (including KRB5_LIBOS_PWDINTR) in that case. If ret is KRB5_LIBOS_PWDINTR it returns it at once. If ret is 0 in the real pass it sets *out_type to the entry's type and returns 0. A failed real entry saves the error context for the first failure and calls k5_preauth_note_failed (ret is replaced by its result and returned if non-zero). After both passes, if must_preauth is true it returns KRB5_PREAUTH_FAILED (wrapping the saved error message when one was saved). If must_preauth is false it returns the value of ret left by the last module call or note_failed (0 if none ran), which for informational entries is that module's own return code. It clears the saved error info on exit.

functions.name: k5_privsafe_check_seqnum
functions.prose_contract: Checks the received sequence number in_seq of a KRB-PRIV or KRB-SAFE message against the expected number ac->remote_seq_number (privsafe.c:225-304; the packet's name seq_check and the slice, which also contains k5_privsafe_check_addrs, point to this function). The context argument is unused. It returns a krb5_boolean. If KRB5_AUTH_CONN_SANE_SEQ is set it returns whether in_seq equals the expected number, with no flag change. Otherwise, when in_seq is in 0xFF800000..0xFFFFFFFF, it returns true for an exact match if the expected number is also in that range, or if KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ is not set; else it calls chk_heimdal_seqnum(exp_seq, in_seq) (which accepts the three Heimdal wrap-around patterns for an expected value in 0x80..0xFF, 0x8000..0xFFFF or 0x800000..0xFFFFFF) and, if that accepts, sets KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ and returns true; otherwise it returns false. For any other in_seq, an exact match returns true, and also sets KRB5_AUTH_CONN_SANE_SEQ when the expected number is in one of the three ambiguous Heimdal ranges (masks 0xFFFFFF80 = 0x80, 0xFFFF8000 = 0x8000, 0xFF800000 = 0x800000). If the expected number is 0 and KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ is not yet set, an in_seq of 0x100, 0x10000 or 0x1000000 sets KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ and returns true (the assignment to the local exp_seq has no effect on ac->remote_seq_number), and any other in_seq returns false. Everything else returns false.

functions.name: rd_req_decoded_opt
functions.prose_contract: Static worker in rd_req_dec.c (lines 473-787; the real name is rd_req_decoded_opt and the packet slice is its middle) behind krb5_rd_req_decoded, verifying an already decoded AP-REQ req for the accepting principal server with an optional keytab; check_valid_flag selects whether invalid-flag checking and authdata verification are done. Arguments include *auth_context (must be initialised), optional *ap_req_options and **ticket outputs. It first decrypts the ticket's encrypted part: with a key in the auth context (user-to-user) it decrypts with it, frees that key and clears the field (keeping the key contents in a local decrypt_key when check_valid_flag is set); otherwise it uses decrypt_ticket with the keytab and takes the server from the ticket. Failures go to cleanup with their error. It decrypts the authenticator, returns KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_BADMATCH if the authenticator's client differs from the ticket's client, and KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_BADADDR if the auth context has a remote address that is not in the ticket's address list. If there is no replay cache and KRB5_AUTH_CONTEXT_DO_TIME is set it opens the default one (error returned). It then applies the cross-realm policy (under the default build: when the ticket's transit policy was not checked and its transited field is non-empty, krb5_check_transited_list; the other two build variants return KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_ILL_CR_TKT for non-empty transit or a foreign realm) and stores the authenticator in the replay cache with k5_rc_store when a cache exists (error returned). It then checks the ticket times (krb5int_validate_times) and the clock skew of the authenticator time; with check_valid_flag it also returns KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_INVALID for an invalid ticket, initialises the authdata context and verifies the authdata. It decodes the RFC 4537 etype list from the authenticator, builds the desired etype list (adding the authenticator subkey's and the ticket session key's enctype; ENOMEM on allocation failure), obtains the permitted enctypes unless KRB5_AUTH_CONTEXT_PERMIT_ALL is set, and negotiates the enctype into negotiated_etype (failure returned). It sets remote_seq_number from the authenticator, creates recv_subkey and send_subkey from the authenticator subkey when present (freeing the recv key if the send key creation fails, else setting both to NULL), creates the session key reference in (*auth_context)->key, and XORs local_seq_number with remote_seq_number when mutual authentication was not requested and the remote number is non-zero. If ticket is non-NULL it copies the ticket (error returned). If ap_req_options is non-NULL it sets it to req->ap_options & AP_OPTS_WIRE_MASK, ORed with AP_OPTS_ETYPE_NEGOTIATION when an RFC 4537 list was present and AP_OPTS_USE_SUBKEY when the negotiated enctype differs from the key's enctype. It returns 0 on success. Cleanup frees desired_etypes, a permitted list obtained locally, and the local decrypt_key contents when check_valid_flag is set; on a failure the auth context may keep fields set before the failing step (keys already created are not released).

functions.name: k5_internalize_auth_context
functions.prose_contract: Rebuilds a krb5 auth context from its serialised form (ser_actx.c:250-397; the real name is k5_internalize_auth_context). Arguments: the output pointer argp and *buffer and *lenremain as input position and remaining length. It reads a 32-bit tag; if the read fails or the tag is not KV5M_AUTH_CONTEXT the result is EINVAL and nothing is allocated. Otherwise the result starts as ENOMEM; it stays ENOMEM if fewer than 5 int32s remain or the calloc of the context fails (argp is then not set). With enough input it unpacks the flags, the remote and local sequence numbers and the two checksum types (the results of these unpacks are not checked), then the cstate length and bytes (alloc_data and unpack errors propagate), then a tag-driven sequence of optional parts, each present only when its tag matches: remote address, remote port, local address, local port, key, send subkey, and, if the next tag is TOKEN_RSKBLOCK, the receive subkey (otherwise the tag bytes it consumed are put back by moving the position back four bytes). It then reads the authenticator (an EINVAL from k5_internalize_authenticator is turned into success, i.e. an absent authenticator) and the trailing tag, which must be KV5M_AUTH_CONTEXT or the result is EINVAL. On success it advances *buffer and *lenremain past the trailer, sets the magic and stores the new context in *argp (the caller owns and frees it with krb5_auth_con_free); on any failure after allocation it frees the partly built context with krb5_auth_con_free and returns the error with *argp, *buffer and *lenremain unchanged.

functions.name: start_connection
functions.prose_contract: Static helper in sendto_kdc.c (lines 885-990) that opens a non-blocking socket to the server in state->addr and registers it in selstate. It creates the socket (type from the transport); if socket() fails it returns -1 without touching state (no descriptor exists). It sets close-on-exec and non-blocking mode, and for TCP a zero linger. It calls connect: if that fails with an error other than EINPROGRESS or EWOULDBLOCK it closes the socket, sets state->state to FAILED (state->fd is not updated) and returns -2; EINPROGRESS or EWOULDBLOCK stores the socket in state->fd with state CONNECTING, and an immediate success stores it with state WRITING. If a callback_info is given it calls its callback with state->fd; on failure it closes the socket, sets state->fd to INVALID_SOCKET and state to FAILED and returns -3, otherwise the callback's buffer replaces the message. It then calls set_transport_message; on failure it closes state->fd, sets it to INVALID_SOCKET, state to FAILED and returns -4. For UDP it sends the initial datagram; a failed or short send closes the socket, sets fd INVALID_SOCKET and state FAILED and returns -5, and a successful send sets state READING. It then adds the descriptor to selstate with cm_add_fd; if that fails it closes the socket, sets fd INVALID_SOCKET and state FAILED and returns -1. Finally it registers the descriptor for writing when the state is CONNECTING or WRITING and for reading otherwise, and returns 0.

functions.name: authunix_refresh
functions.prose_contract: Refresh callback of the AUTH_UNIX client handle (auth_unix.c:245-284) for a rejected credential. If auth->ah_cred.oa_base already equals au->au_origcred.oa_base (the original credential is in use) it returns FALSE immediately without changing anything. Otherwise it increments au->au_shfaults (there is no limit check on it), decodes the original credential bytes with xdr_authunix_parms into a local struct, and if that fails goes to done. On success it sets aup_time to the current time, rewinds the XDR stream to the start, re-encodes the parameters in place over the original credential buffer, and if that fails goes to done; on success it sets auth->ah_cred to au->au_origcred and calls marshal_new_auth to rebuild the marshalled form. At done it frees the decoded parameters with an XDR_FREE pass, destroys the stream and returns the last xdr status: TRUE after a complete refresh, FALSE if either xdr_authunix_parms call failed (in the second-call failure case the original credential buffer may already have been partly overwritten, and ah_cred is left unchanged).

functions.name: clntraw_call
functions.prose_contract: RPC call routine of the "raw" in-process client (clnt_raw.c:133-222) that sends a call through the in-memory buffer to a server running in the same process. It reads the module-global clntraw_private into clp and computes &clp->xdr_stream before testing clp (a pointer computation, not a read); if clp is NULL it returns RPC_FAILED. At call_again it sets the XDR stream to encode and position 0, increments the message xid, and writes the pre-built call header bytes, the procedure number, the auth marshalled credentials (AUTH_MARSHALL) and the arguments (xargs); if any step fails it returns RPC_CANTENCODEARGS. It then runs the server side with svc_getreq(1), sets the stream to decode at position 0, and decodes the reply message with xdr_replymsg into msg with the result pointers; if that fails it frees what was decoded (an XDR_FREE pass) and returns RPC_CANTDECODERES. Otherwise it translates the reply with gssrpc__seterr_reply and takes the status from it. If the status is RPC_SUCCESS it validates the reply verifier with AUTH_VALIDATE (a failure makes the status RPC_AUTHERROR); for any other status it calls AUTH_REFRESH and, if that returns true, jumps back to call_again (retrying with a new xid). For a status still RPC_SUCCESS the validation is run a second time (lines 211-214) and the reply verifier is freed with xdr_opaque_auth. It returns the resulting status, which can be RPC_SUCCESS, a server-reported error status from the reply, or RPC_AUTHERROR.

functions.name: clnt_broadcast
functions.prose_contract: Broadcasts a portmapper CALLIT request for (prog, vers, proc) and passes each reply to a callback (pmap_rmt.c:228-416; the slice cut the head). It creates a default AUTH_UNIX handle, creates a UDP socket (failure: perror and RPC_CANTSEND) and enables SO_BROADCAST (failure: RPC_CANTSEND), collects the broadcast network addresses with getbroadcastnets, builds a call message with an xid derived from the pid and time and encodes the call header and the remote-call arguments into outbuf (failure: RPC_CANTENCODEARGS). It then makes rounds with select timeouts of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. In each round it sends the packet to every broadcast address with sendto (a send that does not return exactly the packet length gives RPC_CANTSEND); if eachresult is NULL it then returns RPC_SUCCESS right after the first round's sends. Otherwise it waits with select: a timeout sets the status to RPC_TIMEDOUT and starts the next round; EINTR retries the select; another select error gives RPC_CANTRECV. When the socket is readable it calls recvfrom (EINTR retried; another error gives RPC_CANTRECV); a datagram shorter than 4 bytes is ignored and the wait continues; for a longer one it decodes the reply and, if the xid matches, the reply is MSG_ACCEPTED and the accept status is SUCCESS, it sets the port in the reply address and calls eachresult(resultsp, &raddr), taking its non-zero return as done. For every datagram of at least 4 bytes it then frees the decoded reply with an XDR_FREE pass and invokes xresults with the XDR_FREE stream on resultsp. If done is set it returns RPC_SUCCESS; otherwise it waits for more replies in the same round. When all six rounds time out the loop ends and the last status, RPC_TIMEDOUT, is returned. On every return after the call handle was created, done_broad closes the socket (including after a failed socket() call) and destroys the AUTH handle with AUTH_DESTROY, which is not guarded against a NULL handle returned by authunix_create_default.

functions.name: svc_do_xprt
functions.prose_contract: Static function in svc.c (lines 447-536) that serves the requests ready on one transport. It allocates three buffers (raw credential and raw verifier of MAX_AUTH_BYTES each and a cooked credential area of RQCRED_SIZE); if any allocation fails it returns at once, leaking the ones that succeeded and leaving the transport untouched. It then loops: it calls SVC_RECV(xprt, &msg) and, if that fails, goes to call_done without dispatching; otherwise it fills a struct svc_req from the message and calls gssrpc__authenticate. If authentication fails it sends svcerr_auth with the reason and goes to call_done; if it succeeds but sets no_dispatch it goes to call_done without replying here. Otherwise it searches the registered callouts for the program and version: an exact match calls its dispatch function and goes to call_done; if the program exists with other versions it sends svcerr_progvers with the lowest and highest registered versions, and if the program is unknown it sends svcerr_noprog. At call_done it reads SVC_STAT(xprt): if the transport has died (XPRT_DIED) it calls SVC_DESTROY(xprt) and leaves the loop; otherwise, if xprt->xp_auth is non-NULL and its ops are not the GSS ops, it sets xp_auth to NULL. The loop repeats while the status is XPRT_MOREREQS. After the loop (not on the early allocation-failure return) it frees the three buffers.

functions.name: gssrpc__svcauth_gss
functions.prose_contract: Server-side RPCSEC_GSS authentication for one received call (svc_auth_gss.c:387-555), returning an auth_stat and possibly setting *no_dispatch. It first resets the transport verifier xp_verf to the null auth. If the transport has no auth or svc_auth_none it callocs an auth and a data structure and installs them in xp_auth (an allocation failure returns AUTH_FAILED, and a failure of the second calloc leaks the first block); otherwise it uses the existing data. An empty credential gives AUTH_BADCRED; the credential is decoded into the svc_req's cooked credential area (a decode failure gives AUTH_BADCRED). The remaining checks free the decoded credential on exit. A wrong gc_v version or an invalid gc_svc service gives AUTH_BADCRED. For an established context: a sequence number above MAXSEQ gives RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM; the replay window is updated (a newer number shifts the window), and a number outside the window or already seen sets *no_dispatch to 1 and gives RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM; otherwise the sequence is recorded; the client name and context are copied into the request. Then by gc_proc: for RPCSEC_GSS_INIT and RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT a call procedure other than NULLPROC, a failed credential acquire or a failed verifier generation gives AUTH_FAILED, a failed context accept gives AUTH_REJECTEDCRED; otherwise it sets *no_dispatch, sends the init reply (a failed send gives AUTH_FAILED), releases the buffers, and marks the context established when the major status is GSS_S_COMPLETE. For RPCSEC_GSS_DATA it validates the request MIC (failure gives RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM) and builds the next verifier (failure AUTH_FAILED). For RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY it requires NULLPROC (else AUTH_FAILED), validates the MIC (RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM on failure), builds the verifier (AUTH_FAILED), sets *no_dispatch, sends an empty reply (its result is not checked), destroys the auth handle and sets xp_auth to &svc_auth_none. Any other procedure gives AUTH_REJECTEDCRED. The successful cases return AUTH_OK.

functions.name: gssrpc__svcauth_gssapi
functions.prose_contract: Server-side AUTH_GSSAPI (the older GSS RPC flavor) authentication of one call (svc_auth_gssapi.c:156-660; the real name is gssrpc__svcauth_gssapi). It cleans up expired client records, sets xp_auth to &svc_auth_none and decodes the credential from the message. An empty credential gives AUTH_BADCRED, an undecodable one AUTH_BADCRED (after freeing it), and a version other than 2 gives AUTH_BADCRED. For an AUTH_GSSAPI_INIT call with auth_msg set it requires an empty client handle (else AUTH_FAILED) and creates a client record (AUTH_FAILED on failure); otherwise it requires a non-empty handle (AUTH_FAILED) and looks the client up (AUTH_BADCRED if unknown). It then sets xp_auth to the client's svcauth. If the context is not yet established it returns AUTH_REJECTEDCRED when auth_msg is false, AUTH_FAILED unless the procedure is AUTH_GSSAPI_INIT or AUTH_GSSAPI_CONTINUE_INIT, and AUTH_BADCRED when the init arguments cannot be decoded; an unsupported init version gives AUTH_BADCRED (versions 1 and 2 are accepted with a warning, 3 and 4 are used as is) and, for version 3 and later, a missing local address gives AUTH_FAILED; these two failure returns do not free the decoded init arguments (only the credential is freed at the error label). It then runs gss_accept_sec_context, trying the client's server credentials or each configured credential in turn, and frees the init arguments. If the accept fails (major status neither COMPLETE nor CONTINUE_NEEDED) it calls badauth, releases the output token, sends the init reply, sets *no_dispatch to TRUE and returns AUTH_OK (the error label then returns ret, which is AUTH_OK). Otherwise it stores the output token, on completion seals the initial sequence number (failure: release the token, AUTH_FAILED), sends the reply, sets *no_dispatch, and marks the client established when the status is GSS_S_COMPLETE. For an established context it unseals the verifier sequence number (failure: AUTH_BADVERF), requires it to equal the stored number plus one (else AUTH_REJECTEDVERF, calling log_badverf), releases the previous verifier and seals the response sequence number (failure: AUTH_FAILED); for an auth_msg call it then handles AUTH_GSSAPI_MSG (decode arguments, BADCRED on failure, process the token, AUTH_FAILED unless the status is GSS_S_COMPLETE, reply and set *no_dispatch) and AUTH_GSSAPI_DESTROY (reply and set *no_dispatch, then clean up the client), and any other procedure gives AUTH_FAILED. Success returns AUTH_OK; the credential is freed on the exit paths.

functions.name: krb5_decode_princ_entry
functions.prose_contract: Decodes a stored V1 principal record content into a new krb5_db_entry (kdb_xdr.c:225-442; the real name is krb5_decode_princ_entry). It sets *entry_ptr to NULL, allocates the entry (the allocation error is returned) and walks the content bytes while tracking sizeleft. A record shorter than KRB5_KDB_V1_BASE_LENGTH gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD. It reads the length, attributes, lifetimes, expiration times, last success and failure times, failure count and the tl_data and key_data counts; a negative n_tl_data or n_key_data gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD. If the stored length exceeds the base length it copies the extra bytes as e_data (length len - base length) with k5memdup, without checking them against sizeleft (an allocation failure returns that error). It then requires at least 2 bytes for the name length and a NUL-terminated name of that length with no embedded NUL inside the declared size (else KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD) and parses it with krb5_parse_name (its error is returned). It reads each tl_data node (4 bytes header; a short header or a length beyond sizeleft gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD, a failed malloc gives ENOMEM, contents copied with k5memdup) and allocates the key_data array (ENOMEM) and reads each key: a short 4-byte header gives KRB5_KDB_TRUNCATED_RECORD, a key_data_ver outside 0..KRB5_KDB_V1_KEY_DATA_ARRAY gives KRB5_KDB_BAD_VERSION, and for each of the ver parts it reads type and length (truncation checks against sizeleft) and copies non-empty contents with k5memdup. On success it stores the entry in *entry_ptr and returns 0; on any error it frees the partly built entry with krb5_db_free_principal, leaves *entry_ptr NULL and returns the error code.

functions.name: kdb5_ldap_create_policy
functions.prose_contract: Implements the kdb5_ldap_util create_policy command (kdb5_ldap_policy.c:92-310, void return); argv[1..] hold the options and the policy DN. A usage error occurs when argc is outside 2..16, when -maxtktlife or -maxrenewlife has no following value, when a ticket-flag option name is matched but its first character is neither '+' nor '-', when the DN is given twice (any argument that is not a known option is taken as the policy DN) and when no DN was given. A usage error sets print_usage (and suppresses the generic message) and leads to cleanup, where db_usage(CREATE_POLICY) is called, with retval 0 so exit_status is not incremented. It callocs the policy parameters (ENOMEM: goes to cleanup with the generic message "while creating policy object" and exit_status++). It parses -maxtktlife and -maxrenewlife with get_date (an unparsable value sets EINVAL, prints "while providing time specification" and increments exit_status), computes the lifetime as the date minus now, and sets or clears the ticket-flag bits for the +/- options (allow_postdated, allow_forwardable, allow_renewable, allow_proxiable, allow_dup_skey, requires_preauth, requires_hwauth, allow_svr, allow_tgs_req, allow_tix, needchange, password_changing_service), recording the fields in the mask. For the DN it duplicates the argument (strdup failure: ENOMEM message "while creating policy object", exit_status++). It then calls init_ldap_realm (failure: message "while reading realm information", exit_status++) and krb5_ldap_create_policy (failure: its error is printed once with "while creating policy object" and exit_status++). cleanup frees the parameters with krb5_ldap_free_policy, prints usage if requested, and increments exit_status whenever retval is non-zero. On success it returns with exit_status unchanged.

functions.name: kdb5_ldap_modify_policy
functions.prose_contract: Implements the kdb5_ldap_util modify_policy command (kdb5_ldap_policy.c:420-669, void return; the real name is kdb5_ldap_modify_policy). If argc is outside 3..16 it goes to the usage path. Pass 1 scans all arguments only to find the policy DN: -maxtktlife and -maxrenewlife skip their following argument, the known ticket-flag option names (matched on argv[i] + 1) are ignored, and any other argument is the DN; a second DN gives a usage error, a strdup failure gives ENOMEM with the message "while modifying policy object" and exit_status++, and no DN gives a usage error. It then calls init_ldap_realm (failure goes to cleanup, which prints "while modifying policy object" and increments exit_status) and reads the existing policy with krb5_ldap_read_policy (failure: message "while reading information of policy '<DN>'", exit_status++). Pass 2 re-scans the arguments, skipping the DN: -maxtktlife and -maxrenewlife without a following value are usage errors, an unparsable date prints "while providing time specification" with exit_status++, otherwise the new lifetime is the date minus now; each ticket-flag option sets or clears the matching bit in the policy flags, with a first character other than '+' or '-' being a usage error; the changed fields are recorded in out_mask. It then calls krb5_ldap_modify_policy with out_mask (failure: cleanup prints "while modifying policy object" and increments exit_status). The usage path prints the modify_policy usage via db_usage without incrementing exit_status. cleanup always frees the policy parameters and the duplicated DN. On success it modifies on the server only the attributes recorded in out_mask and leaves exit_status unchanged.

functions.name: kdb5_ldap_create
functions.prose_contract: Implements the kdb5_ldap_util create command (kdb5_ldap_realm.c:357-664, void return; the real name is kdb5_ldap_create). It callocs realm parameters (ENOMEM goes to cleanup) and parses the options: -subtrees, -containerref, -sscope, -s (stash), and ticket-policy options through get_ticket_policy, recording the chosen fields in mask; a missing option value or an unknown argument is a usage error. Unless a master password was already set it reads it with krb5_read_password (failure: message path). It then takes the LDAP context from the DAL handle (a NULL context goes to cleanup), reads the Kerberos container DN with krb5_ldap_read_krbcontainer_dn (or takes it from a given location), creates the container (krb5_ldap_create_krbcontainer) and the realm object (krb5_ldap_create_realm); after the realm object exists it sets realm_obj_created. It re-reads the realm parameters (a failure prints "while reading information of realm" and sets no_msg), replaces realm_name with a strdup of global_params.realm (ENOMEM on failure), builds the master key principal with krb5_db_setup_mkey_name, derives the master key from the password (salt with krb5_principal2salt, then krb5_c_string_to_key; each failure prints a message and sets no_msg), temporarily clears the realm's containerref and calls create_special_princs (restoring containerref afterwards; a failure prints "while adding entries to the database"), and then sets create_complete. If -s was given or KADM5_CONFIG_STASH_FILE is in the global mask it stores the master key with krb5_db_store_master_key using the user-specified kvno or 1; on failure it prints "while storing key" and a warning, but retval keeps the failing code. At cleanup it deletes the realm object with krb5_ldap_delete_realm when realm_obj_created is set and create_complete is not, frees the realm parameters, zeroes pw_str, prints usage if requested, and when retval is non-zero prints "while creating realm '<name>'" unless no_msg is set and increments exit_status. Afterwards it frees the master key contents and the master principal. Therefore a failed stash, which happens after create_complete, does not delete the realm but still prints the generic message and increments exit_status.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of kdb5_ldap_util (kdb5_ldap_util.c:235-608) returning the global exit_status. It sets progname, initialises the Kerberos context (failure: message, exit_status++, cleanup) and allocates the sub-command argument array (ENOMEM: message, exit_status++). It parses the global options: -P (master password), -r (realm, also set as default realm), -k (enctype; an invalid one gives EINVAL, exit_status++ and cleanup), -kv (key version; the IGNORE_VNO value gives EINVAL and exit_status++), -M, -sf, -m, -D (bind DN), -w (password, strdup'ed), -H (server), --help (sets a flag), the first recognised sub-command name, and collects all other arguments as sub-command arguments; a second sub-command name, no sub-command, or --help frees the argument array and calls usage() and goes to cleanup without incrementing exit_status, so these paths can return 0. For sub-commands other than list and stashsrvpw it requires a default realm (failure: message and exit_status++). It reads the LDAP configuration section name from the profile, retrieves the config parameters (failure: message, exit_status++), initialises the LDAP library, allocates the LDAP context and fills in the bind password (prompting with krb5_read_password when only -D was given; a failed or empty read is reported with ENOMEM), the server list entry and the bind DN (each allocation failure: message, exit_status++). If the configured enctype is not valid it only prints a com_err message and continues. It then sets up the DAL library handle, installs the LDAP context in it, reads the server parameters (failure: message, exit_status++), opens the database when the sub-command needs it (failure: message, exit_status++), and runs the sub-command function with its arguments; the sub-command itself reports its failures by incrementing exit_status. Cleanup zeroes and frees the password, frees an unused LDAP context, frees the config params (unless static), finishes and frees util_context, frees the argument array, prompt and section name, and returns exit_status. usage_print is never set to a non-zero value in this function.

functions.name: populate_krb5_db_entry
functions.prose_contract: Fills a krb5_db_entry from an LDAP entry (ldap_misc.c:1410-1702; the real name is populate_krb5_db_entry, called with context, ldap_context, ld, the LDAP message ent, the principal princ and the output entry; no arguments are handed over to it). It copies princ into entry->princ, and when the LDAP entry has krbprincipalname values it unparses princ, counts the values if one matches, reads the entry DN (failure: LDAP error mapped and returned), records a standalone-object type tl_data if the objectclass list contains krbprincipal, and stores the principal count and DN in a local tl_data list. It then reads, each with its attribute-presence bit recorded in a local mask, krbLastSuccessfulAuth, krbLastFailedAuth, krbLoginFailedCount, krbmaxticketlife, krbmaxrenewableage, krbticketflags, krbprincipalexpiration and krbpasswordexpiration into the entry; the krbticketpolicyreference and krbpwdpolicyreference names (converted from DNs, failures returned); the password history (krb5_decode_histkey) and the kadm5 policy data (krb5_update_tl_kadm_data); the secret keys (krb5_decode_krbsecretkey, and the master key version with krb5_dbe_update_mkvno when non-zero); the last password change and last admin unlock times; the constrained-delegation values as KRB5_TL_CONSTRAINED_DELEGATION_ACL tl_data appended to entry->tl_data; the link references and krbExtraData items as tl_data; and the authentication indicators with get_ldap_auth_ind. It stores the mask as a KDB_TL_MASK tl_data and updates the entry's tl_data. A nsAccountLock attribute equal to "TRUE" (case-insensitive) sets KRB5_KDB_DISALLOW_ALL_TIX in entry->attributes. It then reads the ticket policy with krb5_read_tkt_policy and finally sets entry->len to KRB5_KDB_V1_BASE_LENGTH. Any failing step goes to cleanup with its error code (ENOMEM or the callee's code), leaving the entry partly filled in. Cleanup frees the DN, the LDAP value lists, the temporary tl_data contents, the policy names and strings, the unparsed name and the temporary policy record, and returns the code, 0 on success. The password history pointer ber_key_data is freed at line 1559 without being cleared, so a failure of krb5_update_tl_kadm_data before ber_key_data is assigned again would free it again at cleanup.

functions.name: verify_securid_data_2
functions.prose_contract: KDC-side verification of a SecurID SAM-2 preauth response (securid2.c:274-666; only built with ARL_SECURID_PREAUTH). It sets *sc2_out to NULL, unparses the client name (failure: message and immediate return of that error), and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED for an empty response ciphertext. It finds and decrypts the client key, decrypts the response (k5alloc, krb5_c_decrypt, decode failures returned) and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED for a nonce mismatch, an empty SAD or a SAD longer than the passcode buffer; it copies the SAD to passcode and the user name without the realm into securid_user (ENOMEM on strdup failure). If the response carries a track id it decrypts it (errors returned), requires the track data to be at least the structure size (KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED), returns KRB5KDC_ERR_DISCARD when its host id differs from gethostid(), and switches on its state: SECURID_STATE_INITIAL jumps to the initial check; NEW_PIN_AGAIN compares the repeated PIN with the stored one (mismatch: KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED), calls SD_Pin and SD_Close and on ACM_NEW_PIN_ACCEPTED sets TKT_FLG_HW_AUTH and TKT_FLG_PRE_AUTH in enc_tkt_reply and returns 0, else KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED; NEW_PIN builds a "new PIN again" challenge (random nonce failure, track-data encryption failure and sam_make_challenge failure are returned), stores it in *sc2_out and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED; NEXT_CODE calls SD_Next and SD_Close and sets the two flags and returns 0 on ACM_OK, else KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED. A track state not listed here leaves the earlier result, 0, and returns it without setting the flags. Without track data it initialises the SecurID handle (SD_Init failure, then SD_Lock failure: KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED), calls SD_Check: ACM_OK closes the handle, sets the two flags and returns 0; ACM_ACCESS_DENIED closes the handle and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED; ACM_NEW_PIN_REQUIRED or ACM_NEXT_CODE_REQUIRED builds a challenge (the handle is kept in the encrypted track data and not closed; a random nonce or track-encryption failure is returned), and a failure of sam_make_challenge there is only logged: the code then still stores sc2p in *sc2_out and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED; any other SD_Check result returns KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED. On every path after the name was unparsed, cleanup frees the client key contents, the scratch buffer, the decoded response, the user strings, the track data and any unused challenge.

functions.name: getopt_long
functions.prose_contract: Fallback getopt_long for systems without one (getopt_long.c:157-231), built on getopt_internal (72-130) which keeps a static scan pointer and the globals optind, optopt, optarg and opterr. getopt_internal returns -1 when there are no more options, when the word does not start with '-', when the word is a lone "-" (a '-' option letter not listed in the option string), BADCH ('?') for an unknown or ':' option letter (advancing optind when the word is finished, with a diagnostic when opterr is set and the option string does not start with ':'), BADARG (':') (with the diagnostic only when the option string does not start with ':', in the else-branch of its test) for a short option missing its argument, the option letter otherwise (setting optarg to NULL, to the attached text, or to the next word and advancing optind), and -2 for a word beginning with "--" (leaving optind unchanged). For any other value getopt_long returns it unchanged. For -2 it takes the text after "--" from nargv[optind] and increments optind; an empty text (a bare "--") returns -1. It splits off a '=' value if present and searches long_options for the first entry whose name starts with the given text (the user text is a prefix of the option name; strncmp over the user text's length), preferring an entry whose name has exactly that length, with no check for ambiguity. If nothing matches it prints an "illegal option" diagnostic (when opterr is set and *options is not ':') and returns BADCH. For a match with required_argument or optional_argument it sets optarg to the text after '=' if there was one, else to nargv[optind] and increments optind (this reads nargv[optind] even when optind is at nargc, which relies on the vector being NULL-terminated; an optional argument therefore consumes the next word even if it looks like an option); for no_argument entries optarg is left as it was. A required_argument whose optarg is NULL prints the "requires an argument" diagnostic (opterr set and *options not ':') and returns BADARG; *index is not stored on the BADCH and BADARG returns. Otherwise if the entry has a flag pointer it stores the entry's val through it and returns 0, else it returns val, and stores the match index through *index when index is non-NULL.

functions.name: mkstemp
functions.prose_contract: Fallback mkstemp (mkstemp.c:67-73) that calls _gettemp(path, &fd) and returns fd when _gettemp returns non-zero and -1 otherwise. path is modified in place by _gettemp. On success fd is a descriptor opened O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_RDWR with mode 0600 on the generated name, which the caller must close. A template without trailing 'X' characters is not rewritten and is opened as given. On failure no descriptor is returned and path may have been changed (trailing X characters replaced, or truncated at the last '/' when the directory check failed).

functions.name: _gettemp
functions.prose_contract: Static helper of the fallback mkstemp (mkstemp.c:75-138). It takes the pid, scans to the end of path and then backwards over trailing 'X' characters, replacing each with a decimal digit of the pid (least significant digit last X first). A path made only of X characters makes this backward scan run before the start of the string, which is undefined behaviour; a path without trailing X is left unmodified by this step.
