It then always returns digest_dynamic2(obj, dyn_rpath, dyn_soname, dyn_runpath): that returns false if obj->z_origin is set and obj_resolve_origin(obj) fails; otherwise it sets obj->runpath (or, if there is no runpath, obj->rpath) from the string table with $ORIGIN substitution, adds the soname as a name of obj with object_add_name when there is one, and returns true. The wrapper therefore returns true or false, and obj is modified by the two callees.

functions.name: _rtld
functions.prose_contract: Dynamic linker main routine (the real name is _rtld): it is called from the entry stub with the initial stack pointer sp and returns the program's entry point, storing rtld's exit procedure in *exit_proc and the main object in *objp. It parses argc, argv, the environment and the auxiliary vector from sp, initialises rtld itself (init_rtld from AT_BASE, which must be present), sets up error reporting, the environment-variable table and (for HardenedBSD) the PaX flags. If AT_EXECFD is given the main program is loaded from that descriptor; otherwise, when AT_PHDR is rtld's own program header it is direct-exec mode: a tainted process is refused (error then rtld_die), the arguments are parsed (a missing binary, a failing fstat or a missing execute permission give an error and rtld_die), and the argv, envp and auxv are moved down over the interpreter arguments and main_argc reduced; in the other case the already-mapped main program is described by digest_phdr (rtld_die if that fails). It then loads or digests the main object (rtld_die on failure), sets its path, processes its dynamic section (rtld_die if digest_dynamic fails), links main and rtld objects into the lists, loads preload objects and the needed objects (rtld_die on failure) and builds the main initial object list. A failure of rtld_verify_versions calls rtld_die only when LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS is not set; with tracing it continues. With LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS it prints the loaded objects and calls exit(0); the LD_DUMP_REL_PRE and LD_DUMP_REL_POST options dump relocations and exit(0). Otherwise it allocates TLS offsets, relocates the main object and does copy relocations (rtld_die on failure), runs ifunc setup, allocates the initial TLS, sets the program variables, builds the init list, notifies the debugger, in direct-exec mode sets the process osrel with sysctl (result ignored), takes the bind lock for writing, runs ifunc initialisation and the init functions, loads filtees where requested, enforces RELRO (rtld_die on failure), releases the lock, and returns obj_main->entry with *exit_proc and *objp set. Most error paths do not return: they call rtld_die() or exit().

functions.name: tftp_send
functions.prose_contract: Sends the open file to the TFTP peer over the socket peer in segsize-byte DATA blocks with a sliding window of up to windowsize blocks, numbering them from *block, and returns 0 on success or -1 on failure; ts->amount is cleared at the start and ts->blocks, ts->amount, ts->retries, ts->rollovers and ts->tstop are updated as it goes. For each block it records the file offset and block number in the window table, reads segsize bytes (a negative read_file result logs, sends a TFTP ERROR packet with errno + 100 and returns -1), and sends the DATA packet with send_data, retrying a failed send up to maxtimeouts times and returning -1 after logging when the retries are used up. When the window is full or the block just read is shorter than segsize it waits for an answer with receive_packet: a timeout gives -1 after maxtimeouts consecutive timeouts, otherwise it counts a retry, seeks the file back to the start of the window and resends from there (a failing seek sends an ERROR packet and returns -1); any other receive error returns -1 (logged only when DEBUG_SIMPLE is set). An ACK whose block number is not in the window triggers synchnet, a seek back to the start of the window and a resend (seek failure returns -1); an ACK inside the window counts the acknowledged blocks into ts->blocks and ts->amount and resets the timeout count, and if it acknowledges only part of the window the file is repositioned to the first unacknowledged block and sending resumes from there. A received packet that is not an ACK is not examined further and does not stop the loop. After each block *block is incremented before its acknowledgement is known (so *block ends one past the last block sent); on wrap-around it is set to 0, or to the client's rollover option value, and ts->rollovers is incremented; ts->tstop is updated. The loop ends when the block just sent was shorter than segsize and its window has been fully acknowledged, and the function returns 0.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of adjkerntz, which keeps the kernel's timezone offset and the RTC settings consistent with the local time zone; it takes -i (initial call), -a (adjustment call) and -s (sleep mode), exactly one of -i and -a, otherwise it calls usage() (not read here). It returns 0 at once if the clock file _PATH_CLOCK does not exist. With -i it implies sleep mode; it blocks SIGTERM, ignores SIGHUP and, for -i, calls daemon(), logging and returning 1 if that fails. It then re-tests whether _PATH_CLOCK exists to set wall_clock, and for -i without sleep mode it turns the call into an -a call and returns 0 when the clock is not a wall clock. It reads machdep.adjkerntz (return 1 on failure) and calls gettimeofday(&tv, &tz) (return 1 on failure), computes the local offset with mktime; a mktime failure (nonexistent local time) returns 1 when not in sleep mode and otherwise logs, sleeps REPORT_PERIOD seconds and restarts. It computes the difference between the new offset and the timezone in the kernel; when non-zero it recomputes for the corrected time (possibly repeating once when the DST flag differs; a second mktime failure is handled like the first), and may mark the time to be set. If the timezone info is non-zero it is scheduled to be cleared. It reads machdep.disable_rtc_set and sets it to 1 when it was 0 (a failing sysctl returns 1), calls settimeofday for the new time and zone when needed (re-reading the time with gettimeofday, whose result is not checked, and adding the difference; a settimeofday failure returns 1), sets machdep.adjkerntz when it differs (return 1 on failure), sets machdep.wall_cmos_clock (return 1 on failure), restores machdep.disable_rtc_set when it changed it (return 1 on failure), and then, for -i with a wall clock, leaves sleep mode, waits in sigsuspend for a signal and restarts, otherwise returns 0.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of bsdlabel: it prints a deprecation warning, parses the options (-A all fields, -B and -b xxboot (install boot code), -f (the operand is a file), -m arch (only i386 or amd64 are accepted, otherwise errx(1, "Unsupported architecture")), -n (no write), -R restore, -e edit, -r accepted and ignored, -w write) and sets the operation; a second operation option or an unknown option calls usage(). It then requires at least one operand (usage otherwise) and requires that a -m option was given (errx(1) otherwise). With -f the target is argv[0] as a file; otherwise it resolves the device path with g_device_path (warning and return 1 if NULL), opens it read-only (warning and return 1 on failure), gets the provider name with g_providername (warning, close and return 1 if NULL) and closes the descriptor. With no operation option the operation is WRITEBOOT if -B was given and READ otherwise. READ requires one operand (usage otherwise), reads the label, displays it and sets error to the result of checklabel. EDIT requires one operand, reads the label, fixes it and sets error from edit(). RESTORE requires two operands (usage otherwise), opens the file argv[1] (err with status 4 if that fails), reads the current label, parses the file with getasciilabel (exit(1) if it fails) and sets error from writelabel(). WRITE takes one or two operands (a name argv[1] or "auto"; usage otherwise), reads the label, builds it with makelabel, fixes it and, if checklabel returns 0, sets error from writelabel(). WRITEBOOT reads the label, fixes it, runs makelabel with argv[1] when there are two operands, and, if checklabel returns 0, sets error from writelabel(). It ends with exit(error); it does not return normally.

functions.name: scsiattrib
functions.prose_contract: Implements the camcontrol attrib command: it parses the sub-options from argv with getopt using combinedopt, issues a SCSI READ ATTRIBUTE to device and prints the result, returning 0 on success and 1 on any error (error and warning messages go to stderr). It allocates a CCB (cam_getccb) and a data buffer of 65534 bytes with malloc (return 1 after a warning if either fails). The options are -a attribute number, -c cached, -e element address, -F output format (numeric, or a comma-separated list of names), -p partition, -r read service action (looked up by name), -s starting attribute, -T element type, -V logical volume and -w; an invalid number or name, or an ambiguous name, gives a warning and return 1, and -w only prints "writing attributes is not implemented yet" and returns 1. If neither or both of read and write are selected it prints "Must specify either -r or -w" and returns 1 (so a case with write only does not reach the read step). With -r it builds the READ ATTRIBUTE command with the requested service action, partition, element, starting attribute and output flags, sends it with cam_send_ccb (return 1 on failure) and returns 1 if the CCB status is not CAM_REQ_CMP (printing the CAM error first when verbosemode is non-zero). It then decodes the reply by service action: for attribute values, a reply shorter than the header prints "No attributes returned." (return 0), otherwise each attribute is formatted into an sbuf with scsi_attrib_sbuf (an error returns 1), filtered to attr_num when -a was given, and printed; for the attribute lists it prints the list of attribute IDs with descriptions, or a "No ..." message if the reply is short; for the logical volume or partition list it prints the first number and the count, or a "No ... list returned" message. It then frees the CCB and the buffer and returns error.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of camcontrol: it parses the subcommand and generic options, opens the device when the command needs one, runs the command handler and exits with its status; it does not return. With fewer than 2 arguments it calls usage(0) and exit(1). The subcommand argv[1] is looked up with getoption; an ambiguous or unknown name prints a warning, calls usage(0) and exits with 1. The generic option letters C, E, n, Q, t, u, v (plus the subcommand's own letters) are combined; for commands other than rescan, reset, devtree, usage and debug a device is opened: argv[2], when it does not start with '-', is either a numeric bus:target[:lun] (parse_btl; fewer than two fields is an errx(1)) or a device name (cam_get_device; errx(1) with the CAM error on failure). The generic options are then read: -C a retry count (errx(1) if negative), -E error recovery, -n device name, -Q a task attribute number or name (errx(1) if invalid or ambiguous), -t a timeout in seconds (errx(1) if negative; stored in milliseconds), -u unit, -v verbose. For commands that open a device, errx(1) is called if no valid device identifier was given or the device cannot be opened (cam_open_btl or cam_open_spec_device with O_RDWR). It then switches on the command and calls the handler with the parsed values, storing its return in error (modepage's return value is not stored); CAM_CMD_USAGE calls usage(1), which only prints and returns, leaving error at 0; an unrecognised command calls usage(0) and sets error to 1. It finally closes the device if one was opened and calls exit(error).

functions.name: scanlun_or_reset_dev
functions.prose_contract: Re-scans (scan non-zero) or resets (scan zero) the single device at bus:target:lun and returns 0 on success or 1 on failure. It returns 1 after a warning if bus, target or lun is the corresponding wildcard value (CAM_BUS_WILDCARD, CAM_TARGET_WILDCARD, CAM_LUN_WILDCARD). It builds a CCB with function code XPT_SCAN_LUN or XPT_RESET_DEV, the path, a 5000 ms timeout and priority 5. For a scan it opens XPT_DEVICE read-write (return 1 with warnings on failure) and sends the CCB with the CAMIOCOMMAND ioctl (return 1 and close on failure); for a reset it opens the device with cam_open_btl (return 1 with the CAM error text if that returns NULL) and sends the CCB with cam_send_ccb (return 1 and close the device on failure). It then closes the descriptor or device. If the CCB status masked with CAM_STATUS_MASK is CAM_REQ_CMP, or, for a reset only, CAM_BDR_SENT, it prints "Re-scan" or "Reset" of bus:target:lun "was successful" to stdout and returns 0; any other status prints the status code to stdout and returns 1.

functions.name: get_device_type
functions.prose_contract: Classifies the device dev into *devtype and returns 0 on success or the non-zero result of get_cgd (1) on failure. It first calls get_cgd, which allocates a CCB, sends XPT_GDEV_TYPE and copies the result; a failure to allocate the CCB or to send it prints a warning and returns 1, and a CCB status other than CAM_REQ_CMP returns 1 and prints the CAM error only when the global CAM_ARG_VERBOSE flag is set; in every failure case *devtype is left unchanged. On success it sets *devtype by protocol: CC_DT_ATA for PROTO_ATA, PROTO_ATAPI and PROTO_SATAPM, CC_DT_NVME for PROTO_NVME, CC_DT_MMCSD for PROTO_MMCSD and CC_DT_UNKNOWN for other protocols not listed, each returning 0. For PROTO_SCSI with retry_count == -1 it uses only cached identify data: CC_DT_SATL if the first byte of the serial, revision or model string is non-zero, otherwise CC_DT_SCSI; with any other retry_count it calls dev_has_vpd_page for the ATA Information VPD page and sets CC_DT_SATL if that returns 1 and CC_DT_SCSI otherwise (including when it returns -1 for an error), then returns 0.

functions.name: mmcsdcmd
functions.prose_contract: Implements the camcontrol mmcsdcmd command for MMC/SD devices: it parses options (bus width 4 or 1, -S speed high/std, -I info, -F frequency, -c opcode, -a argument, -f flags, -l data length, -W write, -b data byte), then either changes transport settings, prints controller information, or sends one MMC command. It returns 1 without doing anything else if the CCB cannot be allocated (cam_getccb). A negative opcode, argument, flags value or a data length that is not positive prints a warning, sets error to 1, frees the CCB and returns 1. If the flags are not given they are chosen from the opcode (and for some opcodes the argument is rewritten). A bus width, frequency or speed option sends an XPT_SET_TRAN_SETTINGS CCB, prints "Parameters set OK" or "Speed set OK" when the send and CCB status succeed (otherwise a warning), frees the CCB and returns the cam_send_ccb result (negative on send failure, non-negative otherwise, even if the CCB status was not CAM_REQ_CMP). The info option sends XPT_GET_TRAN_SETTINGS: on send or status failure it warns and returns the send result without freeing the CCB; on success it prints the host controller capabilities and current settings and returns 0, also without freeing the CCB. Otherwise it prints the command, allocates and zeroes a data buffer when a data length was given (the malloc result is not checked), fills the MMC I/O CCB with the retry count and a timeout (5000 when none given), sends it, prints a warning (and the CAM error text when verbose) if the send or the status failed (the return value is not changed by this), and when the status is CAM_REQ_CMP prints the command response and a command-specific decoding or hexdump of the data. It frees the CCB and the data buffer and returns error, which is 0 for this path even when the send failed.

functions.name: smpreportgeneral
functions.prose_contract: Implements the camcontrol smprg command: sends an SMP REPORT GENERAL request to the expander on device and prints the decoded response; it returns 0 or 1. It returns 1 after a diagnostic if the CCB cannot be allocated (cam_getccb). It parses the options (a long-response flag among them), allocates the request and response structures with malloc (a failure prints a diagnostic and sets error to 1, then cleans up), builds the SMP request with smp_report_general using retry_count and timeout (with the long-response bit when requested), and sends the CCB; if cam_send_ccb fails or the CCB status is not CAM_REQ_CMP it prints a diagnostic (and the CAM error details when verbose is set), sets error to 1 and cleans up. If the response has SMP_RG_LONG_RESPONSE set and long response was not requested, it clears the CCB, sets long_response to 1 and sends the request again (once, since long_response is then 1). On a good response it creates an sbuf with sbuf_new_auto and formats the response with smp_report_general_sbuf; if sbuf_new_auto or sbuf_finish fails it prints a diagnostic and goes to the cleanup with error still 0; the printed output is the sbuf contents. At the cleanup it frees the CCB, request, response and sbuf (each if non-NULL) and returns error.

functions.name: smpphycontrol
functions.prose_contract: Implements the camcontrol smpphycontrol command: sends an SMP PHY CONTROL request for one expander phy and returns 0 or 1 (a non-negative cam_send_ccb result on success). It returns 1 after a diagnostic if the CCB cannot be allocated. Options: -a, -A, -s and -S select slumber/partial enable or disable (any argument other than "enable" or "disable" gives return 1), -d the attached device name, -l long response, -m and -M the minimum and maximum link rate (0 or above 0xf gives return 1), -o the phy operation (a second -o gives return 1; a number of 0 or above 0xff gives return 1; a name is looked up with getoption, and an ambiguous or unknown name prints a warning, calls usage(0), which prints and returns, and then returns 1), -p the phy number (converted with atoi), -T the partial pathway timeout (above 15 gives return 1). It returns 1 if no phy was given, which includes -p -1 since -1 is the unset marker, and if -d and the setdevname operation are not used together. It allocates the request and response buffers (return 1 on failure), builds the SMP PHY CONTROL request with smp_phy_control and sends it; if cam_send_ccb fails or the CCB status is not CAM_REQ_CMP it prints a diagnostic (and CAM error details when verbose) and returns 1. In all cases it frees the CCB, request and response and returns retval (the cam_send_ccb return value on the success path, normally 0).

functions.name: send_discover
functions.prose_contract: Timeout handler that sends a DHCPDISCOVER on the interface ipp (a struct interface_info) and schedules itself again; it returns nothing. It computes interval = cur_time - client->first_sending; if that is larger than config->timeout it calls state_panic(ip) and returns without sending or scheduling anything. Otherwise, when no lease has been offered yet and a media list is configured, it advances client->medium to the next medium (increase = 0 in that case), wrapping to the head of the media list with increase = 1 when it runs off the end (the "No valid media types" error call is guarded by a variable fail that is initialised to 0 and never changed, so it cannot run), logs the medium, runs the MEDIUM script with script_init and script_go; if script_go returns non-zero it jumps back to the label at 1355 and tries the next medium (a loop that ends when script_go returns 0). It then sets client->interval: with increase set, to config->initial_interval if it is 0, otherwise it adds a random amount below twice itself, and if the result exceeds config->backoff_cutoff it is replaced by backoff_cutoff / 2 plus a random value modulo backoff_cutoff (so it can still exceed backoff_cutoff); without increase it is only set to the initial interval when it is 0. If cur_time plus the interval would pass first_sending plus config->timeout, the interval is cut to end one second past that time. It stores the elapsed seconds (capped at 65535) in the packet's secs field, logs the send, transmits the stored discover packet to the broadcast address with send_packet_unpriv, and schedules send_discover again with add_timeout at cur_time plus the interval.

functions.name: send_request
functions.prose_contract: Timeout handler that sends a DHCPREQUEST for the active lease on the interface ipp and schedules itself again; it returns nothing. It computes interval = cur_time - client->first_sending. If the state is S_REBOOTING or S_REQUESTING and interval is greater than config->reboot_timeout, or if the state is S_REBOOTING, no medium is set, the active lease has a medium and the MEDIUM script fails (script_go non-zero), it sets the state to S_INIT, cancels the pending send_request timeout, calls state_init(ip) and returns without sending anything. When the MEDIUM script succeeds it records the lease's medium. If the state is not S_REQUESTING and cur_time is past the active lease's expiry, it runs the EXPIRE script (with the old and alias parameters) and the PREINIT script, sets the state to S_INIT, calls state_init(ip) and returns without sending a packet or scheduling a timeout. Otherwise it sets client->interval (the initial interval if it was 0, else adds a random amount below twice itself) and, if it exceeds backoff_cutoff, replaces it with backoff_cutoff / 2 plus a random value modulo the interval; when the state is not S_REQUESTING it limits the interval so the next send is at most one second past the lease expiry (this clamp is not applied in S_REQUESTING). It chooses the destination: broadcast in S_REQUESTING or S_REBOOTING or after the rebind time, otherwise the server address; the source is the active lease address except in S_REQUESTING and S_REBOOTING (then 0.0.0.0). The seconds field is the saved client->secs in S_REQUESTING and the elapsed interval (capped at 65535) otherwise. It logs, sends the stored request packet with send_packet_unpriv and schedules send_request again at cur_time plus the interval.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of dumpon: it configures (or removes) the kernel dump device or a netdump target and does not return. Options: -C cipher, -c client address, -g gateway, -i insert index, -k public key file, -l list, -r remove, -s server, -v verbose, -Z zstd, -z gzip; an unknown option calls usage(). It exits with EX_USAGE (errx) for an unrecognised cipher, for -C when built without crypto, for -i outside 0 to KDA_APPEND-2, for -z together with -Z, for -i together with -r, and, with crypto, for -C given without a public key file; a failed OpenSSL initialisation (when -k is given) exits with EX_UNAVAILABLE, as does -k when built without crypto. With -l it calls listdumpdev() and exits EX_OK. Without -l it requires exactly one operand (usage() otherwise). If both server and client are given the device is the netdump device and the operand is the interface name; if neither is given the operand is the dump device ("off" means remove with /dev/null, and for /dev/null any netdump configuration is first removed through an ioctl, exiting with 1 on failure); any other combination calls usage(). It opens the device with opendumpdev, checks its size unless netdump, compression or removal is in use, and fills the kernel-dump request (remove or insert index, compression zstd, gzip or none). For netdump it resolves the server with getaddrinfo (exit EX_OSERR or EX_NOHOST on failure), copies the interface name and parses the server, client and gateway addresses (the gateway is looked up or defaults to the server), exiting with EX_USAGE for an invalid interface name or address. With a public key it generates the encryption key with genkey. It issues DIOCSKERNELDUMP, retries without compression when it fails with EINVAL and -z or -Z was given (with a warning if the retry succeeds), checks the link status after a netdump success, wipes and frees the key material, and on a final failure exits with EX_OSERR (with a specific message for ENODEV on netdump). On success it lists the dump devices when -v was given and exits with EX_OK.

functions.name: write_s0
functions.prose_contract: Writes the in-memory MBR (mboot.bootinst with its partition table) to the disk and returns 0 or -1. If the global iotest is set it only prints the table with print_s0 and returns 0 without writing. Otherwise it encodes the NDOSPART partition entries from mboot.parts into mboot.bootinst at DOSPARTOFF, stores the DOS magic (DOSMAGIC, little-endian) at DOSMAGICOFFSET, and calls write_disk for each of mboot.bootinst_size / secsize sectors. It returns -1 after a warning if write_disk returns -1, but write_disk (fdisk.c:794-812) returns only 0 on success and EINVAL on a failed or short pwrite (after printing a warning), never -1, so in practice a failed write is not detected here: the loop continues and the function returns 0 at the end.

functions.name: checkfstab
functions.prose_contract: Checks the filesystems listed in /etc/fstab by pass number: docheck decides whether an entry is checked and checkit checks one filesystem; flags is a mix of CHECK_PREEN, CHECK_DEBUG, CHECK_VERBOSE and DO_BACKGRD. It returns 8 if the checklist cannot be opened (setfsent fails). For each pass (starting at 1 and following the next higher fs_passno) it scans the fstab entries of that pass that docheck accepts. When CHECK_PREEN is clear, or the pass is 1, or DO_BACKGRD is set, each entry is checked synchronously with checkit and a non-zero result is returned immediately; an entry without a device name returns 8 in preen mode and is skipped otherwise. In preen mode in later passes an entry without a device name prints "BAD DISK NAME" and ORs 8 into the status, and other entries are queued per disk (with the failok option). After such a pass it starts the per-disk checks with startdisk (returning its non-zero error code immediately) and waits for the children: for each child that exited normally the exit status is used, except that it is 0 for entries with failok (with a message), and a child killed by a signal counts as 8; a failed entry is kept in the bad list and its status is ORed into the sum, a good one is freed, and the next partition of that disk is started (startdisk error returned immediately). After all passes: if CHECK_PREEN is clear it returns 0; if the accumulated status is non-zero it prints the list of failed filesystems (when there is one) and returns the status; otherwise it calls endfsent and returns 0.

functions.name: allocdir
functions.prose_contract: Allocates a new directory inode for fsck_ffs, creates its first block with "." and ".." entries, links it under parent, and returns the new inode number or 0 on failure. The arguments are the parent inode number, the requested inode number (0 for any, as accepted by allocino) and the permission bits mode, which are combined with IFDIR. It returns 0 if allocino returns 0. Otherwise it fills the shared directory template with ino as "." and parent as "..", reads the inode's first block with getdirblk; if that buffer has errors (b_errs non-zero) it calls freeino(ino) and irelse and returns 0. It copies the template into the block, fills the rest of the fragment with empty directory chunks, marks the buffer dirty, sets the inode's link count to 2 and marks the inode dirty. For the root inode (UFS_ROOTINO) it caches the inode info with parent as parent and dotdot, marks it new, sets its type to DT_DIR and its link count, releases the inode and returns ino without checking the parent. For any other inode it first checks INO_IS_DVALID(parent); if the parent is not a valid directory it calls freeino(ino), releases the inode and returns 0. Otherwise it caches the inode info, records the parent, depth (parent's depth plus one, stored in the inode) when the parent's info is found (an unknown parent calls pfatal("allocdir: UNKNOWN PARENT DIR") and continues), sets the type DT_DIR, copies the parent's state, and when that state is DSTATE sets the new inode's link count and increments the parent's link count in the tables. It then increments the parent inode's on-disk link count (for "..") and returns ino. The directory block buffer obtained from getdirblk is not released inside this function.

functions.name: checkfilesys
functions.prose_contract: Checks one filesystem (filesys, a device or mount point) with fsck_ffs and returns a status or exits. It initialises the fsck state, resolves the device (the mount source or blockcheck), opens it and reads the superblock (a failure sets sbreadfailed). In background-check mode (bkgrdcheck) it exits 3 if the superblock cannot be read, 4 if the filesystem is flagged as needing fsck or the journal check passes, 5 if soft updates are not in use, 6 if the kernel lacks the adjrefcnt sysctl, 7 if the filesystem is clean, and otherwise 0. With ckclean and skipclean it again exits 3 on a superblock read failure, may open the device for writing, and for a gjournal filesystem exits 0 if it is clean or runs gjournal_check and exits 0 or 4. With bkgrdflag it calls setup_bkgrdchk: -1 goes to the clean report (prints the free counts and returns 0), 0 exits with EEXIT, 1 sets preen and continues. It then calls setup(filesys): 0 prints "CAN'T CHECK FILE SYSTEM" (in preen mode) and returns EEXIT, -1 prints the clean report and returns 0. For a journaled (SUJ) filesystem it may run suj_check and exit 0 or 4. It may offer to add check-hash protection when not preening and not -y, then runs pass1, pass1b when there are duplicates, pass2, pass3, pass4 and pass5 (pass5 is skipped, with a message, when a cylinder group header is corrupt), prints the statistics, cleans up and calls ckfini(resolved). It then returns ERESTART if a rerun is needed, a restart is wanted and fewer than 10 restarts happened and (preen or the user answers yes); otherwise, if chkdoreload reports a reload it returns 0 when the filesystem was not modified and else syncs and returns 4; the last result is ERERUN if rerun is set and 0 otherwise.

functions.name: pass2
functions.prose_contract: Phase 2 of fsck_ffs (check directory connectivity); it takes no arguments, returns nothing, and relies on pass 1 having filled the inoinfo table and the sorted array inpsort of directories. It first examines the root inode state: unallocated (USTATE) asks to ALLOCATE and calls allocdir; a cleared one asks to REALLOCATE (freedirino then allocdir) or CONTINUE; a non-directory root asks to REALLOCATE or FIX (changing the mode to a directory); a directory state is left; any other state calls errx(EEXIT). If the user declines to allocate or continue it calls ckfini(0) and exit(EEXIT); a failed allocdir calls errx(EEXIT, "CANNOT ALLOCATE ROOT INODE"). It then marks the root DFOUND and the whiteout inode FSTATE (type DT_WHT), sorts inpsort by block with blksort, and for each directory with non-zero size reports progress on signals, fixes a size below MINDIRSIZE (after reply("FIX") for the on-disk size) or not a multiple of DIRBLKSIZ (adjusting it in preen mode or after reply("ADJUST")), builds a temporary directory dinode from the recorded blocks and runs ckinode with pass2check on it. In a second loop, for each directory with a non-zero parent and size: a directory whose parent is DFOUND and which is still unfound becomes DFOUND; when i_dotdot equals i_parent or is (ino_t)-1 nothing more is done; when i_dotdot is 0 it creates the missing ".." entry automatically with makeentry and decrements the parent's link count (no user prompt); otherwise it reports the bad ".." entry and, in snapshot mode, fixes it with the vfs.ffs.setcwd and setdotdot sysctls (on a failure it only prints and skips), or in normal mode fixes it after preen or reply("FIX") with link count adjustments and changeino (a declined fix leaves the entry unchanged). Finally it calls propagate(). The function does not return a status.

functions.name: pass2check
functions.prose_contract: Callback run by ckinode for each directory entry of a directory being checked in pass 2; it returns KEEPON, ORed with ALTERED when it changed the entry buffer, and never returns any other value (a bad inode state calls errx(EEXIT)). idesc->id_dirp is the current entry, id_number the directory inode and id_entryno the position. For entry 0 it checks that the entry is "." with the directory's own inode number and type DT_DIR, fixing them when reply("FIX") agrees, and otherwise offers to add or replace it with "." (either replacing the whole entry or splitting off space), which can be declined, leaving "." missing. For entries 0 and 1 it checks the ".." entry in the same way: an out-of-range inode number is replaced by the recorded parent (or the root) after reply("FIX"), the type is corrected, i_dotdot is set from the entry; a missing ".." is added or replaced after reply, and if the user declines i_dotdot is set to (ino_t)-1; link counts are adjusted when a new entry splits an existing one (the link count of an existing entry's inode is decremented without a range check at lines 360 and 437). A free entry (inode 0) returns KEEPON. Later entries named "." or ".." (entry number 2 or higher) are cleared after reply("FIX"). For other entries it clears them if the inode number is out of range or the user answers REMOVE for an unallocated or cleared inode, fixes whiteout/type mismatches, propagates the DFOUND state from the directory to subdirectories, sets i_parent of a directory's first-found parent (calling fix_extraneous for a directory named a second time, which can ask to remove the entry), corrects the entry type and decrements the inode's link count. If the entry is to be removed it sets d_ino to 0 and returns ret | KEEPON | ALTERED; otherwise ret | KEEPON.

functions.name: fix_extraneous
functions.prose_contract: Called from pass2check when a directory inp already has a recorded parent and another directory entry (idesc, in directory idesc->id_number) also names it. It returns 1 to tell the caller to clear the new entry, or 0. If inp->i_dotdot is 0 it first looks up ".." in the directory named by the new entry with ckinode/findino and records it in i_dotdot when found. In cases 1 to 4 (i_dotdot is 0, or the new entry is in the recorded parent, or i_dotdot differs from the entry's directory, or i_dotdot equals the recorded parent) it prints the extraneous-link message and: in a snapshot (cursnapshot non-zero) removes the new name with the vfs.ffs.setcwd and vfs.ffs.unlink sysctls (reporting a failure) and returns 0 in all sub-cases; otherwise returns 1 in preen mode, and the answer of reply("REMOVE") otherwise. In case 5 (the new entry's directory is the one ".." points to), it prints the message and: in a snapshot removes the old name with the sysctls (a failing sysctl returns 0 without changing anything) and sets inp->i_parent to the new directory without touching the link count, returning 0; otherwise, if not preening and the user declines it returns 0, else it deletes the old entry from the old parent with ckinode and deleteentry, sets i_parent to idesc->id_number, increments the link count of inp's inode in inoinfo and returns 0.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of ggatel (GEOM Gate local provider tool); it does not return. The action comes from argv[1] (create, rescue, destroy or list, case-insensitive); a missing or unknown action calls usage(). Options are parsed with getopt "fo:s:t:u:v": -f (force) only for destroy, -o ro, wo, rw or direct only for create and rescue (any other value is errx(EXIT_FAILURE)), -s sectorsize and -t timeout only for create, -u unit for all, -v verbose except for destroy; an option not allowed for the action calls usage(). The -s, -t and -u values are converted with strtoul/strtol and rejected only when the result is 0 and errno is non-zero, so a non-numeric argument that converts to 0 with errno 0 is accepted as 0. After the options it requires, per action: create needs exactly one operand (the path), loads the module, opens the control device and calls g_gatel_create(); rescue needs one operand and a unit (otherwise "Required unit number." and usage()), opens the device and calls g_gatel_rescue(); destroy needs a unit (same message), sets verbose and calls g_gate_destroy(unit, force) after opening the device; list calls g_gate_list(unit, verbose). Any other state calls usage(). Afterwards it closes the control device with g_gate_close_device() and exits with EXIT_SUCCESS (g_gatel_create and rescue may not return, not read).

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of growfs, which enlarges a UFS filesystem; it returns 0 at the end or exits through err/errx. Options: -N (dry run), -s size (parsed with strtoumax base 0 and scaled: a bare number by DEV_BSIZE, b/B by 1, k/K, m/M, g/G and t/T by powers of 1024; any other suffix is errx(2)), -v (ignored) and -y; an unknown option calls usage(), as does an operand count other than one. It resolves the device with getmntpoint/getdev (errx(2) if it cannot be found), opens it read-only (err(3)), reads the media size (err(3) on failure, errx(2) if below 1) and the superblock with sbget (errx(2) for an unrecognised superblock, errc(3) for a read error), and exits 2 if the filesystem is flagged unclean or needing fsck. The target size is the media size when -s is absent, otherwise the -s value (errx(2) if larger than the media), rounded down to the fragment size. If it is not larger than the current size it exits with errx(0) for equal and errx(2) for smaller. It computes the new superblock size; if the old size is not below the new one it calls errx(3, "we are not growing"). Unless -y it errors out (errx(2)) if active snapshots exist, and unless -y or -N it prints the warning and asks for confirmation (any reply other than "yes" exits 0). Unless -N it suspends a mounted read-write filesystem through the ufssuspend device (err(3) on failure) or opens the device for writing (err(3)); it reads and rewrites the last fragment as a write test, recomputes the cylinder group count (dropping a last group too small to use and exiting errx(3) with "not enough new space" if there is no growth), calls growfs(), closes the descriptors, resumes the filesystem with UFSRESUME and closes the output (err(3) on failure), and for a read-only mount calls chkdoreload and exits 9 if it fails. It then returns 0.

functions.name: ctrl_thread
functions.prose_contract: Thread function of the HAST worker that serves the control connection res->hr_ctrl; arg is the struct hast_resource. It loops forever and returns only by pthread_exit. Each iteration receives a header nvlist with hast_proto_recv_hdr; if that fails it calls pthread_exit(NULL) immediately when sigexit_received is set, and otherwise logs an error, sends SIGTERM to its own process and calls pthread_exit(NULL). It reads the "cmd" field; a message without cmd (value 0) logs an error, frees the message and continues without sending a reply. For the status command it builds a reply with "complete" or "degraded" depending on whether both remote connections exist, the extent size, keepdirty and dirty counts (non-zero only for the primary role) and the statistics counters, calls the resource's output_status_aux, and sets "error" to 0; for the reload command (which asserts the primary role) it calls primary_config_reload and sets "error" to 0; any other command sets "error" to EINVAL. It frees the incoming message; if building the reply failed (nv_error) it logs an error, frees the reply and continues without replying; otherwise it sends the reply with hast_proto_send (a send failure is only logged) and frees it.

functions.name: compression_recv
functions.prose_contract: Decompresses a received HAST data buffer according to the "compression" field of the nvlist nv; the parameters are the resource (unused), the nvlist, the buffer pointer *datap, its size *sizep and the flag *freedatap saying whether *datap is heap-owned. If nv has no "compression" string it returns 0 without changing anything. If the algorithm is "hole" it calls hast_hole_decompress, if "lzf" hast_lzf_decompress, each with the current buffer and a local copy of the size; any other name logs "Unknown compression algorithm" and returns -1 without changing anything. If the decompressor returns NULL it returns -1 leaving *datap, *sizep and *freedatap unchanged. Otherwise it frees the old buffer only when *freedatap was true, sets *freedatap to true, stores the new buffer in *datap, the decompressed size in *sizep and returns 0.

functions.name: main_loop
functions.prose_contract: Main event loop of the hastd parent process; it takes no arguments and does not return. Each iteration calls check_signals(), builds a read set containing the control connection descriptor, every non-NULL listen connection, every resource's event connection and, for resources in the primary role, their hr_conn (asserting the descriptors are valid and fit FD_SETSIZE), and calls select with a REPORT_INTERVAL timeout. After select it calls hook_check() and updates lastcheck when REPORT_INTERVAL seconds have passed since the last check. If select returned 0 or failed with EINTR it starts the next iteration; for any other select error it removes the pid file and calls pjdlog_exit(EX_OSERR). Otherwise it calls check_signals() again, then handles the ready descriptors: control_handle(cfg) for the control connection, listen_accept for each ready listen connection, and for each resource with an event connection: if the event descriptor is ready, event_recv is called and, when it returns 0, the loop goes to the next resource (so the resource's hr_conn is not examined in this iteration), otherwise the event connection and the resource's hr_conn are closed and set to NULL; if the event descriptor is not ready and the role is primary, connection_migrate(res) is called when hr_conn is ready.

functions.name: listen_accept
functions.prose_contract: Accepts one incoming connection on listen entry lst and handles the HAST handshake; it returns nothing. It accepts the connection with proto_accept (on failure it returns), gets the local and remote addresses, sets the protocol timeout, and finds a resource whose configured remote address matches the connecting address (closing the connection if there is none). It receives the handshake header (close on failure) and reads the "resource" name (missing: close), "version" (0 is treated as 1) and the optional "token" (a token of the wrong size closes the connection). It then looks up the resource by name; each of the following failures builds an error message nvlist and goes to fail, which sends it back and closes the connection: unknown resource ("Resource not configured."), address no longer matching ("No access to the resource."), a role other than secondary (with a "wait" flag if the local role is primary), and a token that does not match the stored token. Without a token (the first connection): an existing worker process is signalled with SIGINT, waited for and cleaned up (failures logged), or an existing half-open incoming connection is closed and dropped; the version is capped at HAST_PROTO_VERSION and stored in res->hr_version, a fresh random token is generated into res->hr_token, a reply with the version and token is built and sent (a build or send failure goes to fail), and the connection is stored in res->hr_remotein. With a token (the second connection) the connection is stored in res->hr_remoteout and hastd_secondary(res, nvin) is called (which takes the handshake further). On success it frees the nvlists and clears the log prefix without closing the connection (it now belongs to the resource); on fail or close it frees the nvlists, closes the connection and clears the prefix.

functions.name: remote_recv_thread
functions.prose_contract: Thread of the HAST primary that receives replies from the secondary for component 1 (ncomp = 1); arg is the hast_resource; it loops forever and returns NULL only syntactically. Each iteration waits on hio_recv_list_cond until the receive list is non-empty. If the remote component is not connected (ISCONNECTED false) it removes the first request, sets hio_errors[1] to ENOTCONN and moves it to the done path (goto done_queue). Otherwise it receives the reply header; on failure it logs, closes the remote connection with remote_close and goes to the next iteration. A reply without "seq", or one whose seq matches no request on the receive list (the matching request is removed from the list), frees the nvlist and continues. A reply with a non-zero "error" sets that error in hio_errors[1], logs a warning and goes to the done path. For a BIO_READ it takes the remote lock, goes to the done path without setting hio_errors[1] if the connection is gone, and receives the data with hast_proto_recv_data; a receive failure stores errno in hio_errors[1], closes the connection and goes to the done path (not continue). Other commands carry no data; an unknown command aborts. On success hio_errors[1] is set to 0. For a memsync write the first (memsync) acknowledgment releases hio_writecount, calls write_complete when it reaches zero and hio_errors[0] is 0, marks the request as memsync-acknowledged and, if there was no error, puts the request back at the tail of the receive list and continues to wait for the final reply. Finally it releases hio_countdown; if other references remain it continues, otherwise a sync request (ISSYNCREQ) is completed with SYNCREQDONE under sync_lock and signals sync_cond, and any other request is moved to the done queue.

functions.name: yygetc
functions.prose_contract: Returns the next character for the ipf configuration lexer, from the lookahead buffer yytext or from the current source, using the globals yypos, yylast, yylineNum, pos, string_start/string_end/string_val and yyin; docont non-zero enables backslash-newline continuation. If yypos < yylast it returns yytext[yypos], increments yypos, increments yylineNum if the character is '\n', and leaves yylast unchanged. Otherwise, if yypos == YYBUFSIZ it returns TOOLONG without changing anything. Otherwise it takes the character from string_val[pos - string_start] when pos lies in [string_start, string_end] (incrementing yypos once at that point) or else reads it with fgetc(yyin); for the stream case with docont set, a backslash makes it read the next character and, if that is a newline, count the line and read one more. It increments yylineNum if the character is '\n', stores it at yytext[yypos] and increments yypos again (so in the string_val branch yypos ends two above its old value and the character is stored one slot past the old yypos), sets yylast to yypos, NUL-terminates yytext at yypos and returns the character.

functions.name: bpf_validate
functions.prose_contract: Checks that the BPF program f of len instructions is well formed and returns 1 if it is and 0 otherwise. It returns 1 immediately for len == 0 (without reading f), and 0 for len < 1 after that or len > BPF_MAXINSNS. For each instruction it switches on the class: for load classes the mode must be one of the accepted immediate, absolute, indirect, MSH and length modes, with the scratch-memory mode requiring k < BPF_MEMWORDS and any other mode returning 0; for store classes k must be < BPF_MEMWORDS; for ALU instructions the operation must be a known one, and a division or modulus by the constant 0 returns 0; for jumps the operation must be a known one: an unconditional jump needs from + k not to overflow and to stay below len (from = i + 1), conditional jumps need from + jt and from + jf below len; return, misc classes are accepted; any unknown class returns 0. After the loop it returns 1 only if the class of the last instruction f[len - 1] is BPF_RET. It does not modify f.

functions.name: emitGroup
functions.prose_contract: Part of the ipf rule compiler: it emits C source text for one rule or for the closing of a rule group to the output file; the parameters are the rule number num (negative values mean end-of-group markers, -2 emitting the rule-pointer arrays), the direction dir (0 in, 1 out, -1 none), v (an array of FRC_MAX mc_t records), the rule fr, the group name and the in/out rule counts. It keeps static state: fp (set from cfile when unset; it returns immediately if both are NULL), the saved group name egroup, openfunc, the saved comparison array n, the nesting depth sin and the per-direction header flags. When the group differs from the saved one it prints closing braces for the open nesting levels (sin - 1 down to 1), and if a function is open (openfunc == 1) it prints "return (fr);" and the closing brace, clears openfunc and frees n; it then resets sin and the header flags and saves the new group name. When the group is the same, a function is open and num < 0, it frees n, prints the closing braces and, if still open, the return and brace and clears openfunc. dir == -1 returns here. It finds the matching group in the groups list for the direction; for num == -2 with dir 0 or 1 and header[0] unset and non-zero counts it prints the ipf_rules_in_ or ipf_rules_out_ pointer array (the out case also sets fp to NULL); any num below 0 then returns. For a rule it prints the function header for the group and direction the first time (openfunc = 1, with src/dst variables when needed), marks which of the FRC_MAX comparisons apply from the rule, sorts them, computes the indentation shared with the previous rule's comparisons (closing braces for the levels that end), prints the nested if-tests for the comparisons, prints either a return of the rule (for quick rules) or an assignment to fr, copies the comparison array into n (allocating it if needed) and stores the new depth in sin.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of ipfstat, which displays IPFilter statistics, rules, states or authentication information; it returns 0 after the display, or exits earlier. It first scans the options once (without error reporting) only for -M (memory file) and -N (kernel image), which set live_kernel to 0. For a live kernel it opens the state, auth, NAT and filter devices (perror and exit(-1) if one fails); when -M or -N was given it drops setuid/setgid privileges; for a live kernel it checks the device revision, otherwise it opens the kernel image with openkmem (exit(-1) on failure); it then drops privileges again. It parses the options a second time: -4/-6 (when built with IPv6), -a, -A, -C, -d, -D, -f, -g, -h, -i, -I, -l, -m (an invalid ipf expression exits 1), -n, -o, -O, -P (an unknown protocol exits -2), -R, -s, -S, -t (exits -2 if STATETOP is not built in), -T (a refresh time below 1 exits -2) and -v; an unknown option calls usage(). With IPv6 support, -4 or -6 without -i, -o or -t exits -2, and without either both families are selected. It then reads the statistics with ipfstate_live (zeroing the structures first) or ipfstate_dead. It selects the display by an if/else chain: states (-s) shows the IP states and nothing else; a list option calls showlist and, when both -i and -o are set, clears the output flag and calls showlist a second time; otherwise the frag states (-f), the state-top display (-t, when built in), authentication statistics (-A), groups (-g), or by default the general statistics. It returns 0.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of ipmon, which logs IPFilter events; it returns 0 after the log reading ends, or exits. It initialises the configuration (initconfig) and parses the options (-a all logs, -b, -B binary log file, -C config file, -D daemon, -f/-I filter log, -F flush logs, -L syslog facility (an unknown name exits 1), -n resolve names, -N NAT log, -o/-O log selection, -p, -P pid file, -s syslog, -S state log, -t, -v, -x, -X); an unknown option, -h or -? calls usage(argv[0]). With -s it opens syslog with the program name and facility, initialises the tables, loads the configuration file if one was given (a load_config failure unloads it and exits 1), and defaults the first log source to the IPFilter log (the test of the three source types at lines 1652-1654 repeats logsrc[0] and so does not look at the other two). It calls openlogs, which can exit 1 when a log device cannot be opened or examined. Without -s it opens the output file argv[optind] for append (or uses stdout), exiting 1 if the open fails, and sets it unbuffered; with -s the log pointer is NULL. If -D was given and the output is not stdout, or syslog is used, it calls daemon(0, !syslog) on BSD (the result is not checked) or forks (exit 1 if fork fails, the parent exits 0) elsewhere, closes descriptors 0 and 1 and writes the pid file. It installs handlehup for SIGHUP, calls read_loginfo(&config) until it returns 0, unloads the configuration and returns 0.

functions.name: text_open
functions.prose_contract: Opens the text packet-input source fname for the ipf test reader, using the module's static tfd (descriptor) and tfp (FILE pointer); it returns tfd. If tfp is non-NULL and tfd is not -1 it rewinds tfp and returns tfd without opening anything. Otherwise, for the name "-" it sets tfd to 0 and tfp to stdin; for any other name it opens fname read-only into tfd and, if that succeeded, sets tfp to fdopen(tfd, "r") (which may be NULL if fdopen fails, while tfd keeps the opened descriptor). If the open fails tfd is -1 and tfp is left as it was (it may still hold an earlier stream). It returns tfd (the descriptor, or -1).

functions.name: parseline
functions.prose_contract: Parses one line of the ipf text packet input into the IP packet buffer ip (large enough for ip_t plus the larger of a TCP header and an ICMP header), setting *out to 1 for an "out" line and 0 for an "in" line and, when the line has "on interface", *ifn to a strdup'd interface name; it returns 0 on success and 1 on a parse failure. It first frees *ifn if it is non-NULL (without clearing the pointer, so on a successful line without "on" *ifn is left dangling), zeroes ip and the local TCP, ICMP and option buffers, sets the IP version, header length and TTL 63, and splits the line into up to 19 whitespace-separated tokens. It returns 1 for an empty line, for a first token that does not start with 'i' or 'o' (printing a diagnostic), and (when built with IPv6) hands "in6" and "out6" lines to parseipv6. Each of the following missing tokens returns 1 without a message: the interface name after "on", the protocol, the source and destination addresses. It reads the protocol (tcp, udp or icmp, a numeric protocol, or IP), and for tcp and udp requires a comma-separated port in both the source and destination fields (a missing one prints a diagnostic and returns 1). The addresses go through tx_hostnum. For TCP it reads optional flag letters, seq= and ack=; for ICMP an optional type and code; "opt" adds IP options through buildopts. It copies the TCP, UDP or ICMP header after the IP header, stores the total length in network byte order and returns 0.

functions.name: fill_ip
functions.prose_contract: Parses the address specification av of an ipfw rule into the ipfw_insn_ip instruction cmd; cblen is the space available in the instruction buffer counted in 32-bit words (it is passed to CHECK_LENGTH, which is not read), tstate is the table state, and the function returns nothing, reporting errors by errx. It first clears the length part of cmd->o.len. The word "any" (or an abbreviation) returns leaving the length 0; "me" sets a one-instruction length and returns; a string starting "table(" is handled by fill_table with O_IP_DST_LOOKUP. Otherwise it loops over the comma-separated entries: for each it checks the remaining space, finds a separator among "/:,{", resolves the host part with lookup_host (errx(EX_NOHOST) if unknown), and builds the mask: ":" followed by a dotted netmask (invalid gives EX_DATAERR), "/" followed by a width (0 gives a zero mask, above 32 gives EX_DATAERR), "{" (a set; mask /24 assumed) or none or "," (a /32 mask); the address is ANDed with the mask. For a "{" set it requires that it is the only entry (otherwise EX_DATAERR "address set cannot be in a list"), a mask width from 24 to 31, builds a bitmap of the listed last-octet values and ranges with checks that each lies in the range and that ranges are well formed (an unclosed set, an incomplete range, an out-of-range value, an inverted range or a double '-' is EX_DATAERR), sets opcode O_IP_DST_SET with the map length and returns. An entry with a zero mask (0.0.0.0/0, meaning any) is skipped when more entries follow and, when it is the only entry, returns with a length of 0, except that "not any" gives errx(EX_DATAERR). A single plain host with mask /32 and no other entry sets the length to one ipfw_insn_u32 and returns. Other entries add two words each; at the end a total that exceeds F_LEN_MASK gives EX_DATAERR and the length is stored as the word count plus 1.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of ipfw and dnctl. In Windows/TCC builds it first calls WSAStartup and returns 1 with a message if that fails. It sets g_co.prog to the dnctl or ipfw command line depending on whether the basename of av[0] is "dnctl". If there is more than one argument and the last argument starts with '/', it treats it as a file to preprocess: it calls ipfw_readfile(ac, av) when access(R_OK) succeeds and otherwise calls err(EX_USAGE, "pathname: ...") which does not return. Otherwise it calls ipfw_main(ac, av), and if that returns non-zero it calls errx(EX_USAGE, ...) with a usage message, which does not return. In the remaining cases it returns EX_OK.

functions.name: setup_redir_port
functions.prose_contract: Parses a libalias "redirect_port" argument list into the buffer buf (a nat44_cfg_redir followed by one nat44_cfg_spool per comma-separated local target) and returns the number of bytes used; *ac and *av are the remaining argument count and vector and are advanced past the consumed tokens. It stores the protocol from the first token with StrToProto. The second token is the local target: if it contains a comma it is a load-sharing (LSNAT) list, which sets laddr to INADDR_NONE, lport to ~0, one local port and remembers the list; otherwise for SCTP it must not contain ':' (errx(EX_DATAERR) if it does) and is read as an address, and for other protocols it is read with StrToAddrAndPortRange (errx on an invalid range) giving the local port and the number of local ports. The third token is the public port range, with an optional address (errx on an invalid range); for SCTP the number of local ports and lport are taken from it. An optional following token beginning with a digit is the remote address, with optional port range (invalid range gives errx), otherwise the remote address is any and the remote port range is 0 with a count of 1. It requires the local and public port counts to match and the remote port to be 0 or of equal count (errx(EX_DATAERR) otherwise). For an LSNAT list it then parses each comma-separated target into a spool entry appended to the buffer: for SCTP the target must not contain ':' and its port is the public port; for other protocols it is parsed with StrToAddrAndPortRange and must name a single port, which becomes the spool port; each entry increments spool_cnt. It returns the space used.

functions.name: nat64clat_foreach
functions.prose_contract: Fetches the list of nat64clat instances from the kernel and calls the callback f(cfg, name, set) once for each entry; it returns 0 on success or an errno value. It allocates a zeroed buffer of an initial size (a list header and 16 entries) with calloc and returns ENOMEM if that fails. It then calls do_get3(IP_FW_NAT64CLAT_LIST, ...): on failure it takes the size the kernel reported back in the header, frees the buffer and, if errno is ENOMEM, repeats the whole request with the new size (the calloc of the retry can again return ENOMEM); for any other errno it returns that errno. On success, if sort is non-zero it sorts the entries with qsort and nat64name_cmp, calls f for each of the olh->count entries (stepping by objsize, ignoring the result of f), frees the buffer and returns 0.

functions.name: firmware
functions.prose_contract: Implements "nvmecontrol firmware" (the name of the function is firmware, not firmware_main): it downloads and/or activates an NVMe firmware image; it returns void if arg_parse fails and otherwise ends with exit(0) or an error exit. It returns at once if arg_parse(argc, argv, f) is non-zero. It then validates the options: slot 0, or a slot above 7 (other than the NONE marker), prints a message and calls arg_help; no replace image and no activate request calls arg_help; activation without an image and without a slot calls arg_help (arg_help is not read, so it is not stated whether it returns). It opens the controller (re-opening the controller device when the given device is a namespace), reads the identify data (errx(EX_IOERR) on failure) and exits through errx(EX_UNAVAILABLE) if the controller does not support firmware commands, if an image is to be written to slot 1 and slot 1 is read-only, if the slot is greater than the number of slots the controller supports, or if activation of an existing image is requested for a slot without valid firmware. It reads the image file if one was given, prints a warning and asks "Are you sure ..." until the answer starts with "yes" (continue) or "no" (exit(EX_DATAERR)). It then downloads the image (update_firmware) when given, chooses the activate action (replace and activate, replace only, or activate an existing slot), calls activate_firmware, prints whether a reboot is required or the controller reset needed when activation was requested, closes the device and exits with status 0.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of pfctl; it parses the command line, opens the pf device and performs the requested operations in a fixed order, finishing with exit(exit_val). With fewer than two arguments it calls usage(). It reads the options (-a anchor, -d, -D macro, -e, -q, -F what, -i interface, -k and -K (at most two each, otherwise usage()), -m, -M, -n, -N, -r, -f rules file, -g, -A, -R, -o optimizer, -O, -p, -P, -s what, -S, -t table, -T command, -v, -x debug, -z, -h); a repeated -F, -o, -s, -T or -x selector calls usage(), as does an unknown option or -h. It then calls errx(1) for -N together with -r; usage() when -t and -T are not used together or when operands remain where none are allowed; defaults the load flags; and, for an anchor given with -a, calls errx(1) for an empty name, a name beginning with '_' in write mode (other than for tables), or a name too long (usage() for some read-only combinations). Unless -n (no action) is set it opens the pf device and calls err(1) if that fails; with -n an open that succeeds is closed and a failed open is ignored. It opens the netlink handle (err(1, "Failed to open netlink") if that fails), allocates a path buffer (errx(1) if calloc fails), and runs, in order: disable (-d), the show options (-s), counter clearing, the clear options (-F), state and source-node killing (-k, -K), table commands (-t with -T), optimizer options (-o), loading fingerprints and rules (-f), enable (-e) and the debug level (-x); each failing step sets exit_val to 1 and the later steps still run. It ends with exit(exit_val); it does not return.

functions.name: print_ioctl
functions.prose_contract: Formats the OS fingerprint fp (a struct pf_osfp_ioctl) as text in a static 1024-byte buffer and returns a pointer to that buffer (so the result is overwritten by the next call and the function is not reentrant). The colon-separated fields are: the window size, written as "*" when PF_OSFP_WSIZE_DC is set, "S" for PF_OSFP_WSIZE_MSS, "T" for PF_OSFP_WSIZE_MTU, otherwise the number fp_wsize with a "%" prefix when PF_OSFP_WSIZE_MOD is set; the TTL; the DF flag as 1 or 0; the packet size ("*" or the number, "%"-prefixed when the modulus flag is set); the TCP options from the highest-numbered stored option down, comma-separated, as N (NOP), S (SACK), T (timestamp, followed by 0 when PF_OSFP_TS0), M (MSS, followed by "*" or the possibly "%"-prefixed number) and W (window scale, followed by "*" or the possibly "%"-prefixed number), or "." when there are none (option codes other than these produce nothing); the class, version and subtype names; and a trailing "TcpOpts <count> 0x<hex>" debug field. All appends use strlcat, so output longer than the buffer is truncated.

functions.name: ping
functions.prose_contract: Main routine of ping (the function called from main is named ping(argc, argv), at ping.c:197-1004); it does not return, ending with exit(nreceived ? 0 : 2). The part read here (the end of the function) starts after the options, sockets and destination have been set up: it enlarges the receive buffer, limits the capability rights of the receive socket (CAP_RECV, CAP_EVENT) and the send socket (CAP_SEND), calling err(1, ...) if caph_rights_limit fails, prints the "PING ..." banner, installs the handler onsignal for SIGINT and SIGINFO (and SIGALRM when a timeout is set; err(EX_OSERR) if sigaction fails), sets up the msghdr for receiving, and sends the first request or the preload requests (limited to npackets) with pinger(). It then loops until SIGINT is seen: on SIGINFO it prints a summary to stderr; it waits in pselect up to the interval remaining; when the socket is readable it receives with recvmsg (errors are warned about and ignored), takes the kernel timestamp or the current time, calls pr_pack and leaves the loop when the once option or npackets has been satisfied; when the wait times out (or in flood mode) it advances a sweep if one is configured (stopping when the next size would exceed the maximum), sends another request with pinger() while fewer than npackets have been sent, and otherwise leaves the loop on the second pass after setting a final wait (twice the maximum round trip, or the wait time if nothing was received); it records the largest number of missed replies. After the loop it prints the summary and calls exit(nreceived ? 0 : 2). Many earlier exits for invalid options and socket setup errors (errx with EX_USAGE, EX_NOHOST, EX_OSERR and others) occur in the part of the function that was not read in detail.

functions.name: ping6
functions.prose_contract: Main routine of ping6 (the function called from main is named ping6(argc, argv), at ping6.c:269-1273); the part read here is the end of the function, after the options, sockets and destination have been set up. It adjusts the socket buffers (err(1, ...) if the setsockopt calls for SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF, IPV6_RECVPKTINFO and IPV6_RECVHOPLIMIT fail), limits the capability rights of the two sockets by clearing CAP_SETSOCKOPT (err(1) if caph_rights_limit fails), prints the banner, and sends the first request or the preload requests (limited to npackets) with pinger(). It installs onsignal for SIGINT and SIGINFO (and SIGALRM when a timeout is set), calling err(EX_OSERR) if sigaction fails. In the loop, until SIGINT is seen, it prints a summary to stderr on SIGINFO, waits with pselect for the remaining interval and, when the socket is readable, receives with recvmsg (an error other than EINTR gives a warning and a one-second sleep; a zero-length result checks the path MTU notification and continues; otherwise it calls pr_pack); it leaves the loop when the once option or npackets is satisfied. When the wait times out (or in flood mode) it sends the next request with pinger() while fewer than npackets have been sent, otherwise it leaves the loop on the second pass after setting a final wait, and records the largest number of missed replies. After the loop it ignores SIGINT and SIGALRM, prints the summary, frees the receive packet buffer if set, and exits with 0 if any reply was received, 2 if more requests were sent than failed to send, and EX_OSERR otherwise.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of reboot, halt and nextboot (selected by getprogname()): "halt" in the name sets halting, "nextboot" selects nextboot mode and its option set, anything else is reboot. It parses the options (-a, -c, -D, -d, -e, -f, -k, -l, -n, -N, -o, -p, -q, -r); an unknown option or any remaining operand calls usage(). It exits with errx(1) when the no-shutdown file exists (unless -f or nextboot), for conflicting option combinations (-D with anything else, -d with halt, -N with -n, -c with -p, -r with other options or with -k). With -D it removes the nextboot file (a missing file is fine, an unlink failure only warns) and exits 0. Unless nextboot mode, a non-root caller gets err(1) with EPERM. With -q it calls reboot(howto) directly and calls err(1) if that returns. A -k kernel name is checked (unless -f) to be an existing regular file, then added to the next-boot environment; a non-empty environment is written to the nextboot file with write_nextboot; in nextboot mode it then exits 0. Otherwise it logs the shutdown (unless -l), records a SHUTDOWN_TIME utmpx entry, syncs unless -n or -N, and ignores SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGQUIT, SIGTERM, SIGTSTP and SIGPIPE. With -r it sends SIGEMT to init (err(1) if that fails) and returns 0, the only return of the function. Otherwise it sends SIGTSTP to init (err(1) on failure), SIGTERM to all processes (err(1) on failure other than ESRCH), waits for paging to settle, repeatedly sends SIGKILL (a failure other than ESRCH goes to the restart path, a missing process ends the loop, and after 5 rounds it warns and stops), and calls reboot(howto). The restart path calls errx(1) after trying to send SIGHUP to init; the message mentions "(can't restart init)" only if that kill fails.

functions.name: main
functions.prose_contract: Entry point of recoverdisk, which copies a possibly failing disk to a file or reads it, keeping a worklist of areas still to be read. It makes stdout and stderr unbuffered and parses the options -b big read size, -i interval, -l log file (opened for append, err(1) on failure), -p error pause, -m medium read size, -r read worklist file, -s small read size, -t total size, -u unreadable pattern, -v verbose, -w write worklist file; an unknown option calls usage(), as does a number of operands other than one or two. It opens the first operand read-only (err(1) on failure), determines the total size and the read sizes, allocates the work buffer (asserted), and when a second operand is given opens it for writing with O_CREAT and truncates it to the total size (err(1) on failure), otherwise write_fd is -1. If an unreadable pattern is given it prepares a pattern buffer. It loads the worklist from -r (the done size is the total minus the remaining work) or starts with one lump covering the whole device. If -w was given it installs sighandler for SIGINT. It then loops while aborting is not set: it sleeps for the interval, calls attempt_one_lump, ends when that returns 0 (no more work), counts successful reads and saves the worklist every snapshot period (60 seconds), reports progress, and on a failed read (negative result) adjusts the read sizes and stops with aborting set when errno is EINVAL or ENXIO; otherwise it reports and continues. The loop also ends when SIGINT sets aborting through sighandler (when -w was given). After the loop it saves the worklist, frees the buffers, reports and returns 0 (the return value is marked XXX in the source), so a read error does not change the exit status.

functions.name: setdirmodes
functions.prose_contract: Applies the owner, mode, extended attributes, times and flags recorded in the mode file to the directories restored by restore; flags may contain FORCE. The mode file name modefile is rebuilt from TMPDIR (or _PATH_TMP) and dumpdate when the command is 'r' or 'R'. If modefile starts with '#' it calls panic("modefile not defined") (which terminates the program; the lines after it are unreachable). If fopen fails it prints a diagnostic and returns. It then reads struct modeinfo records until end of file or a read error (a warning and a break); for a record with an extended attribute block it reads it into a malloc'd buffer (if malloc fails the block is skipped with fseek). For each record it looks up the entry by inode number. For the 'i' and 'x' commands: an unknown inode is skipped; an entry that already existed (EXISTED) is skipped, after clearing its NEW flag, unless FORCE is set; and for the root inode it asks reply("set owner/mode for '.'") and skips the entry if the answer is FAIL. For other commands an unknown inode calls panic (terminating). Unless Nflag is set it then chowns (a non-root caller uses its own uid with the recorded gid), chmods, sets extended attributes when present and the buffer was obtained, sets the times with utimensat and the flags with chflags, ignoring their errors. It clears the entry's NEW flag in every non-skipped case, including when Nflag is set. At the end it frees the buffer and closes the file.

functions.name: findinode
functions.prose_contract: Reads tape headers from the dump until a header that describes a file, and fills in the global curfile from it; header is the current header and dumpdate the dump date being restored. It first resets curfile to the name "<name unknown>", action UNKNOWN, mode 0 and ino 0. Then it loops, switching on the header type: for TS_ADDR it skips the data blocks the header lists (reading them with readtape) and reads headers with gethead until one succeeds with the right dump date (counting skipped blocks, with Dflag byte-slide bookkeeping), and the loop repeats; for TS_INODE it copies the mode, owner, flags, rdev, times, size and the inode number from the header into curfile and ends the loop; for TS_END, if tapesread & (tapesread + 1) is non-zero it calls getvol(0) and continues, which re-tests the loop condition and, because the type is not TS_ADDR, ends the loop with curfile.ino still 0, otherwise it sets curfile.ino to maxino and ends; TS_CLRI and TS_BITS set the name to "<file removal list>" or "<file dump list>" (ino stays 0); for TS_TAPE and unknown types it either prints a message (with Dflag) and skips headers with gethead until a good one, or calls panic (terminating) without Dflag. The loop repeats only while the header type is TS_ADDR (while (htype == TS_ADDR)); afterwards, if any blocks were skipped it prints a "resync restore, skipped N bytes/blocks" message and resets the skip count.

functions.name: input
functions.prose_contract: Handles one received RIP packet in routed: input(from, sifp, aifp, rip, cc) returns nothing; the part read here is the RIP_RESPONSE case, ending in the loop that processes the route entries (n points at the first entry and lim at the end). The whole response is discarded with a rate-limited message (and the function returns) when the source port is not the RIP port, when rip_sock is closed, when the sender is one of this host's own addresses on a non-remote interface, when no receiving interface can be found (aifp NULL), when the interface has RIP input off, when the response is empty (n >= lim), when the interface rejects that RIP version (IS_NO_RIPV1_IN or IS_NO_RIPV2_IN), when the interface is marked broken, when it is IS_DISTRUST and the sender is not in the trusted-gateway list, or when authentication is configured, the packet is not RIPv1 and ck_passwd fails. Otherwise it loops over the entries: authentication entries are skipped; an entry of an unsupported address family is skipped with a message; an invalid destination (check_dst) or a metric of 0 or above HOPCNT_INFINITY discards the rest of the packet (return); a next hop is honoured only for RIPv2 on the interface's network, else cleared; the mask is derived (RIPv1 or a zero mask uses the classful mask, a mask inconsistent with the destination skips the entry); the metric is increased by the interface metric and the inbound adjustment, capped at HOPCNT_INFINITY; entries from a trusted gateway outside its allowed nets, and default routes whose metric reaches the interface's default threshold, are skipped; for RIPv1 hosts it may expand a classful route into several subnet routes (not more than 510) and then calls input_route for each destination of the expansion with the new route record (gate, router, metric, tag, time, interface). The function returns void after the loop. The code before line 511 (other commands, the request case) was not read ("partly read").

functions.name: set_rdisc_mg
functions.prose_contract: Joins or leaves the ICMP router discovery multicast groups on the interface ifp (assert ifp != NULL); on non-zero joins as appropriate and on zero leaves; it returns nothing and logs socket errors with LOGERR. If rdisc_sock is not open: it returns if on is zero or the interface has IS_NO_RDISC set, and otherwise opens the socket. If the interface lacks IFF_MULTICAST it clears IS_ALL_HOSTS and IS_ALL_ROUTERS in ifp->int_state and returns. For the all-hosts group: if this host is a supplier, the interface has IS_NO_ADV_IN, or on is zero, it leaves the group when IS_ALL_HOSTS is set (a failing MCAST_LEAVE_GROUP is only logged) and clears IS_ALL_HOSTS in every case, even if the leave failed; otherwise, if IS_ALL_HOSTS is not set, it joins the group and sets IS_ALL_HOSTS only when the join succeeded. For the all-routers group: if this host is not a supplier, the interface has IS_NO_ADV_OUT, or on is zero, it leaves the group when IS_ALL_ROUTERS is set and clears the bit (even if the leave failed); otherwise, if the bit is not set, it joins and sets IS_ALL_ROUTERS on success only.

functions.name: rdisc_age
functions.prose_contract: Ages the table of discovered routers drs[] and re-selects the preferred one; bad_gate is 0 or the address of a gateway that has stopped working; it returns nothing. If this host is a supplier it calls rdisc_sort() when a discovered route is currently in use (cur_drp non-NULL; rdisc_sort may itself remove expired entries), then rdisc_adv() to send advertisements, and returns without any aging or bad-gateway handling. Otherwise, if bad_gate is non-zero, it finds the entry for that gateway and, if its timestamp is later than the value that would make it expire one supply interval from now, moves its timestamp back to that value (so it expires sooner). It then calls rdisc_sol() to send solicitations and rdisc_sort() to age and select, and when the RIP socket is closed and bad_gate is 0 it calls age(0).

functions.name: DoFile
functions.prose_contract: Processes one dump device for savecore: it examines the kernel dump header at the end of the device and, depending on the options, checks for a dump, saves it (possibly compressed, uncompressed or decrypted) into savedir and records it with info and symlinks, and clears the dump header unless keep is set; it returns nothing. It returns early (after a message) when a live core is requested, when the XML output stream cannot be created, when the work buffer cannot be allocated, or when the device cannot be opened. It reads the device size and the last header (a short sector, a failed allocation or seek or read goes to the cleanup that closes the descriptor), and decides from the header magic whether it is a text or regular kernel dump, a cleared header or garbage, checking the version and the header parity; a bad version, parity or non-matching first and last headers makes it stop (go to cleanup) unless force is set, and a cleared or unknown magic stops it unless forced. With -c (clear) it goes to the header-clearing step; with the check option (checkfor) it exits with EXIT_SUCCESS when a valid dump is present.
